E|Idioms & Phrases.why: Idioms & Phrases give about 1.6 questions per shift across 2021-2025 (2.05 in 2021) and about 1.4 in 2025, so expect one or two in a 2026 shift, plus idioms hidden in Sentence Improvement and Cloze items. The bare 'meaning of the given idiom' format dominates and was used for all but one 2025 item. In 2025 about half were literary, such as Hobson's choice and the sword of Damocles.

lines: An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning cannot be worked out from the words themselves, so 'kick the bucket' means to die and has nothing to do with buckets.
Idioms are frozen: you may not swap a single word, so it is 'break a leg' and never 'break an arm', and 'an ace up his sleeve' and never 'up his sheath'.
Since 2025 almost every item has been the bare stem 'Choose the correct meaning of idiom', with long, abstract options.
Every set of options hides one literal picture, one opposite-tone meaning and one half-right near-miss, and you should kill them in that order.
The right meaning explains every word of the idiom, so 'hoist with one's OWN petard' must mention one's own scheme.
Greek myth gives the weak spot of Achilles' heel, the endless weaving of Penelope's web and the troubles let loose from Pandora's box.
The sword of Damocles hung by a single hair, so it stands for a constant threat, while Hobson's choice means taking the horse nearest the door or none at all.
Anger has a whole family, from fly off the handle and hit the roof to see red and in high dudgeon.
Effort has its own family: move heaven and earth, leave no stone unturned, strain every nerve and fight tooth and nail.
Peace is an olive branch or a buried hatchet, while bad blood, daggers drawn and loggerheads all mean bitter hostility.
Trouble comes in hot water, in a soup and in a tight corner, and when the danger passes you are out of the woods.
Deceit draws the longbow and throws dust in your eyes, while honesty calls a spade a spade and stays above board.
Eat humble pie and eat crow mean swallowing your pride, while a feather in your cap and winning your laurels mean honour.
Carrying coals to Newcastle, flogging a dead horse and chasing a wild goose are all ways of wasting effort.
Proverbs count as idioms, and the answer is always the lesson, never the picture.
Learn idioms in themed families with one story or sentence each, because families survive in memory far longer than alphabetical lists.

expand: L: kill the Literal picture first
O: kill the Opposite-tone option next
N: of the Near-misses left, keep the one that explains every word

So Hobson's choice means no real choice at all

chapters.h: What idioms are and how SSC asks them
chapters.intro: An idiom is a fixed group of words with a meaning that the individual words do not reveal. SSC mixes idioms with phrasal verbs, proverbs and pair phrases, and treats them all the same way. Because the words are frozen, both the meaning and the exact wording can be tested, and most idioms also carry a clear tone of praise, blame, warning or luck that helps you eliminate options.

rows: A fixed group of words with a figurative meaning
A verb plus a particle with a special meaning
put off = postpone; give in = surrender; look down upon = despise
A complete saying that gives advice
A rolling stone gathers no moss.
Two words joined by 'and' in a fixed order
ins and outs, by leaps and bounds, bag and baggage, in weal and woe, hand and glove, tooth and nail
blocks.title: Four kinds of fixed expression

rows: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom, with no sentence.
The idiom is underlined in a sentence that gives context.
I only see him once in a blue moon = not very often
Choose the idiom that fits the blank.
fair-weather friend, beside the mark, on the fence, pat myself on the back
Replace plain words with an idiom.
a grave error = Himalayan blunder; for a very long time = donkey's years
Choose the sentence that uses the idiom correctly.
Ranita was not selected as she got cold feet.
Inside Sentence Improvement, one wrong word must be fixed.
make it a day = call it a day; speaks his eye = speaks his mind
blocks.title: The six formats

blocks.body: An idiom is frozen, so 'break a leg' cannot become 'break an arm' and 'blow one's own trumpet' cannot become 'blow one's own saxophone'. SSC tests this rule directly in Sentence Improvement.
blocks.title: Never swap a word

chapters.h: Idioms from Greek myth and ancient history
chapters.intro: Many of the hardest idioms come from ancient stories, and each one is easy once you know the story. The story is the meaning: Achilles was invulnerable except at his heel, so an Achilles' heel is a single weak point. Learn the stories below and a whole class of 2024-2025 questions becomes free marks.

rows: The hero could be wounded only at the heel by which his mother held him.
Greek soldiers hid inside a wooden horse that Troy took in as a gift.
Pandora opened a forbidden jar and released all the evils of the world.
King Midas turned everything he touched into gold.
the ability to make money from anything
Penelope wove a shroud by day and unpicked it by night to delay her suitors.
a task that is never finished
A golden apple marked 'for the fairest' set goddesses quarrelling and led to the Trojan War.
The Trojan princess was cursed so that her true prophecies were never believed.
one whose true warnings are ignored
Alexander the Great cut through a knot that no one could untie.
a very complex problem; cutting it means solving it boldly
The halcyon, a legendary kingfisher, was said to calm the seas while nesting.
a happy, peaceful time in the past
blocks.title: Myth to meaning

blocks.q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom "To square the circle."
steps: The idiom comes from an ancient Greek geometry puzzle: draw a square with exactly the same area as a given circle using only ruler and compass.
This was later proved impossible (π cannot be constructed that way).
So 'to square the circle' means to try to do something that cannot be done.
Answer: To attempt something impossible.
blocks.trick: Easy, quick and perfect drawing are traps built on the literal words; the idiom is about impossibility.

blocks.body: Dionysius, ruler of Syracuse, let the flatterer Damocles sit on his throne for a day, but hung a sword over his head by a single horsehair. Damocles quickly understood that power comes with constant danger, and that is what the sword of Damocles still means.
blocks.title: The sword of Damocles

blocks.body: King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat the Romans but lost so many soldiers that he said another such victory would ruin him. A Pyrrhic victory is a win gained at too great a cost.
blocks.title: A Pyrrhic victory

blocks.q:
Choose the idiom from the given alternatives that best matches the following definition:
"An arbitrary and ruthless standard to which exact conformity is forced, often by using violent, unnatural, or distorting methods to alter the original data or situation."
steps: The definition describes a rigid standard that things are forced to fit by stretching or cutting them.
In Greek myth, Procrustes made every guest fit his bed by stretching the short ones and cutting the tall ones, so 'a Procrustean bed' is exactly this forced conformity.
A Sisyphean task is endless, futile labour; a Gordian knot is a very complex problem; the Sword of Damocles is a constant threat hanging over someone.
Answer: A Procrustean bed
blocks.trick: Forced to fit = Procrustes' bed; the other three myths are about effort, complexity and danger.

chapters.h: Idioms from history, the Bible and literature
chapters.intro: A second group of classic idioms comes from real events, the Bible and famous books. Each is tied to a person or a place, and the place usually tells you the meaning if you know one fact about it. Newcastle was a great coal-mining town, so carrying coal there is pointless.

rows: A Cambridge stable owner let customers take the horse nearest the door or none.
Julius Caesar crossed this river with his army in 49 BC, starting a civil war.
Napoleon suffered his final defeat at Waterloo in 1815.
Emperor Nero is said to have played music while Rome burned.
waste time on trivial things during a crisis
Newcastle in England was a major coal-producing town.
supply something where it is already plentiful
In Hamlet, a bomb-maker is blown up by his own small bomb, the petard.
Saul was converted suddenly on the road to Damascus in the Bible.
a sudden, complete change of view
The apostle Thomas would not believe until he saw proof.
In a parable, a Samaritan stopped to help a wounded stranger.
one who helps a stranger in need
Hatters were popularly linked with madness, and Lewis Carroll's Mad Hatter fixed the image.
blocks.title: Place, person and meaning

items.b: meet someone more powerful than expected

blocks.body: Hobson's choice is not a choice between two evils; that is 'between the devil and the deep sea'. Hobson offers one option or nothing.
blocks.title: Hobson is not a dilemma

blocks.q:
Choose the alternative which gives the correct meaning of the given idiom or phrase.
Read somebody the Riot Act
o: To explain a rule in great detail
To participate in a public protest
To read aloud from a law textbook
steps: The Riot Act was a British law (1714): an official read it aloud to a crowd, ordering them to break up or face punishment.
So 'reading someone the Riot Act' means giving them a stern warning and a severe telling-off.
Eliminate the literal options: reading from a law book and explaining a rule are word pictures, not the meaning; joining a protest reverses the idea.
Answer: To reprimand someone very severely
blocks.trick: Literal 'read a law' options are always the trap; the idiom is about scolding.

chapters.intro: Animal idioms are the largest single family, and each animal tends to carry the same character in every idiom. The cat stands for secrets and risk, the wolf for hunger and hidden danger, the dog for spite and ruin, and the horse for racing, hard work and plain common sense. Group the idioms by animal and they become easy to recall.

rows: a person used as a tool by another
Let the cat out of the bag
take on a dangerous task for others
Rain cats and dogs; a cat and dog life
rain heavily; a life of constant quarrels
waste effort on a hopeless cause
Put the cart before the horse
do things in the wrong order
one who stops others using what he cannot use
do not stir up an old trouble
an enemy pretending to be a friend
Keep the wolf from the door
Bull in a china shop; take the bull by the horns
a clumsy person; face a problem directly
blocks.title: Animal by animal

items.b: a small flaw that spoils something

items.a: Kill two birds with one stone
items.b: achieve two aims with one action

blocks.q:
Select the correct meaning of the given idiom/phrase.
"To beard the lion in his den" means:
o: To confront a powerful adversary boldly on their own territory
To make a futile attempt at subduing a ferocious opponent
To seek refuge from a superior enemy
To incite unnecessary conflict with an authority
blocks.a: To confront a powerful adversary boldly on their own territory
steps: Picture the idiom literally: to 'beard' someone is to grab his beard, that is, to face and defy him to his face.
Doing this to a lion inside its own den means challenging the strongest opponent where he is strongest.
So the idiom praises boldness; it is close to 'take the bull by the horns'.
Eliminate: it is not about failure (futile attempt), running away (seek refuge) or picking a needless fight (incite conflict).
Answer: To confront a powerful adversary boldly on their own territory.
blocks.trick: Ask what quality the picture shows: walking into a lion's den shows courage, so pick the only option about bold confrontation.

blocks.body: In the old fable, a monkey wanted chestnuts roasting in a fire, so it used the cat's paw to pull them out. The cat got burnt and the monkey got the chestnuts, which is why a cat's paw is a person used as a tool by someone else.
blocks.title: Why a cat's paw is a tool

chapters.intro: Idioms built on the body are easy to picture, and the picture usually points straight at the meaning. Cold feet are what you feel just before you back out, and a silver spoon in a baby's mouth means family wealth. Sort them by body part and the list shrinks to a few memorable images.

rows: Hit the nail on the head
Keep a level head; head over heels
See eye to eye; feast one's eyes on; all eyes
agree fully; look at with delight; watching eagerly
Turn a deaf ear; play it by ear
Pay through the nose; follow one's nose
pay too much; go straight ahead
Born with a silver spoon in one's mouth; down in the mouth
Gift of the gab; bite one's tongue
a talent for fluent speaking; stop oneself speaking
Heart in the right place; change of heart; take heart; learn by heart
good-natured; change of opinion; be encouraged; memorise
Get cold feet; put one's foot down; stand on one's own feet
lose nerve; refuse firmly; be independent
Break a leg; pull someone's leg
good luck before a performance; tease
Back against the wall; by the skin of one's teeth; tooth and nail
trapped with no escape; only just; with full force
blocks.title: Head to toe

blocks.body: 'Break a leg' is a wish for good luck before a performance, not a wish for injury. SSC has offered 'break an arm' as a wrong option in Sentence Improvement.
blocks.title: Luck, not injury

chapters.intro: Colours carry fixed moods in English idioms: red for danger, anger and debt, green for inexperience and envy, blue for sadness and rarity, and white for harmlessness or surrender. Numbers are fewer but appear often, especially cloud nine, sixes and sevens and the eleventh hour. Learn the colour code first and the individual idioms follow.

rows: Caught red-handed; see red; in the red
caught in the act; become very angry; in debt
Green with envy; the green-eyed monster
Once in a blue moon; out of the blue; feel blue
a harmless lie; a costly useless possession
Show the white feather; show the white flag
blocks.title: The colour code

blocks.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the following idiom:
Hit the purple patch
o: To experience a period of great success or achievement
To face an unexpected period of failure
To become extremely angry over a minor issue
To withdraw from a difficult situation
blocks.a: To experience a period of great success or achievement
steps: Picture the idiom: a 'purple patch' is a stretch of time that stands out as rich and splendid (purple was the colour of royalty).
In sport and work it means a run of excellent form or good luck.
To 'hit' it is to enter such a phase.
Failure, anger and withdrawal are all negative meanings, so they do not fit.
Answer: To experience a period of great success or achievement.

items.a: Forty winks or a cat nap

blocks.body: Green horn means inexperienced, not uneducated. In CGL 2021 'The new electrician is a green horn' meant he was new to the job.

chapters.intro: Kitchen idioms are homely and vivid, which makes them easy to remember once you link each to a feeling. Humble pie tastes of humiliation, sour grapes taste of jealousy, and a piece of cake tastes of ease. A few old-fashioned ones, like 'keep a good table', surprised candidates in 2025, so learn those carefully.

rows: admit a mistake and accept humiliation
Take with a grain of salt
In a soup; in hot water
pretending not to want what one cannot have
a big fuss over a small matter
blocks.title: From the kitchen

items.a: Too many cooks spoil the broth
items.b: too many people spoil a task
have more important things to do

blocks.body: In CGL 2025 'eat humble pie' was offered with the option 'celebrate one's success'. Humble pie is always about accepting defeat or insult, never about triumph.

chapters.intro: This family covers the whole life of a task: trying hard, succeeding, failing and starting again. Several idioms in it are exact synonyms, so SSC can substitute one for another. Keep the groups below separate in your mind and you will never confuse bite the bullet with bite the dust.

items.title: Trying hard
points: leave no stone unturned
move heaven and earth
strain every nerve
go out of one's way
pull out all the stops
burn the midnight oil (work late at night)
around the clock (day and night)
pull one's socks up (work harder)

items.title: Succeeding
points: a feather in one's cap (an achievement to be proud of)
win one's laurels (gain fame)
come off with flying colours (succeed brilliantly)
bring the house down (win loud applause)

items.title: Failing
points: bite the dust (fail or die)
go down the tubes (fail completely)
go pear-shaped (go wrong)
hit a brick wall (be unable to progress)
miss the boat (miss a good opportunity)
a damp squib (a disappointing failure)
draw a blank (get no result)

blocks.q:
Fill in the blanks with the correct expression:
Far from the applause she expected, her speech ______.
steps: 'Far from the applause she expected' tells us the speech failed to have its intended effect.
'Fall flat' means to fail completely to impress or amuse.
'Fall out' means to quarrel, 'fall off' means to decline, and 'fall foul of' means to come into conflict and needs an object.
Only 'fell flat' fits the meaning and the sentence.
Answer: fell flat.

items.b: gain an advantage by acting first

items.a: Throw one's hat into the ring
Take a leap in the dark
items.b: take a risk with unknown results

blocks.body: 'The doctors tried very hard to save his mother' was rewritten in CGL 2024 as 'The doctors moved heaven and earth'. Any of the trying-hard idioms can be tested this way.

chapters.intro: Idioms about truth and talk split cleanly into two camps: those who speak straight and those who twist the truth. A third small group is about reading meaning correctly. When you meet one of these, first decide which camp it belongs to, because the options usually include one from the opposite camp.

items.title: Honest and plain
points: call a spade a spade (speak plainly)
straight shooter (an honest, direct person)
above board (honest and open)
fair and square (honestly)
make a clean breast of (confess fully)
speak one's mind (say frankly what one thinks)

items.title: Deceitful or exaggerating
points: beat about the bush (avoid the main point) {PYQ 2026}
cock and bull story (an absurd story)
draw the longbow (exaggerate)
tall tales (exaggerated stories)
throw dust in one's eyes (deceive)
pull the wool over someone's eyes (deceive)

items.b: deal with a dangerous or wicked person

blocks.body: Medieval archers loved to boast about impossible shots with their longbows. That is why 'to draw the longbow', asked in CGL 2025, means to exaggerate or tell tall stories.

blocks.q:
Select the correct meaning of the given idiom/phrase.
"To beat around the bush" means:
o: To search carefully for something hidden
To avoid getting to the point of a topic
blocks.a: To avoid getting to the point of a topic
steps: 'Beat around the bush' (also 'beat about the bush') is an idiom about speech, not about real bushes.
It describes someone who talks around a subject instead of saying the main thing directly.
Check the options: searching, physical attack and boasting have nothing to do with indirect talk.
Answer: To avoid getting to the point of a topic.

chapters.intro: This family moves through a quarrel from start to finish: losing one's temper, living in hostility, and finally making peace. The anger idioms are near-synonyms and can replace one another, while the peace idioms all describe a gesture. Remember the story arc and you can place any of these idioms in the right stage.

steps: Anger flares: fly off the handle, hit the roof, lose one's temper, fly into a passion, see red, foam at the mouth, or sit in high dudgeon (deeply offended).
Hostility settles in: bad blood, no love lost between, at loggerheads, at daggers drawn, or at cross purposes (misunderstanding each other's aims).
Things get worse: add fuel to the fire, stir up a hornet's nest, rub someone the wrong way, or get on one's nerves.
Peace returns: break the ice, pour oil on troubled waters, hold out an olive branch, and finally bury the hatchet.
blocks.title: The life of a quarrel

items.a: Throw or pour cold water on

blocks.body: Break the ice is used at a first meeting to ease tension, while bury the hatchet ends an old quarrel. Both are peaceful, but they belong to different moments.

chapters.intro: English has many ways of saying 'in trouble', and SSC treats them as interchangeable. A second group describes risky behaviour, and a third describes facing or surviving difficulty. Keep the three groups apart: being in trouble, walking into trouble, and coming out of it.

items.title: Already in trouble
points: in hot water, in a soup, in a tight corner, in a fix, up the creek
get into a scrape (get into an awkward situation)
back against the wall (no escape)
at one's wits' end (completely puzzled about what to do)

items.title: Taking a risk
points: play with fire
tread or skate on thin ice
between the devil and the deep sea (two equally bad choices)
hanging by a thread (in great danger of failing)

items.title: Facing or escaping it
points: bite the bullet (face something unpleasant bravely) {PYQ 2026}
face the music (accept the consequences)
weather the storm (survive a hard period) {PYQ 2026}
out of the woods (out of danger)

blocks.title: In it, near it, out of it

blocks.q:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Bite the bullet
o: Decide to do something that is difficult
blocks.a: Decide to do something that is difficult
steps: 'Bite the bullet' means to face something painful or unpleasant bravely and get on with it.
It comes from soldiers biting a bullet to bear the pain of surgery without anaesthetic.
So it means deciding to do something difficult that cannot be avoided; harming someone, ruining oneself and peace talks are unrelated.
Answer: Decide to do something that is difficult

blocks.q:
Select the correct meaning of the idiom used in the given sentence.
Despite the challenges, Priya managed to keep her head above water.
o: To remain calm in a stressful situation
To barely manage to survive or cope
blocks.a: To barely manage to survive or cope
steps: Picture someone in deep water who only just keeps his head above the surface: he is not drowning, but only just.
So the idiom means to barely manage to survive or cope, often with money trouble or pressure of work.
In the sentence, 'despite the challenges' supports this: Priya just about coped.
Staying calm, not asking for help and keeping quiet are not what the picture shows.
Answer: To barely manage to survive or cope.
blocks.trick: It is close to 'weather the storm', but stresses only just surviving.

items.b: a small visible part of a large problem
in a weak or depressed state

blocks.body: Hold water means to be valid, but in hot water means to be in trouble. The shared word 'water' is a favourite distractor.

blocks.q:
Select the correct meaning of the idiom used in the given sentence.
Knowing the surgery would be painful, he finally decided to bite the bullet and get it done.
o: To endure a painful or difficult situation with courage
To complain endlessly about a problem
blocks.a: To endure a painful or difficult situation with courage
steps: 'Bite the bullet' means to face something painful or unpleasant bravely.
In the sentence he knows the surgery will hurt, yet decides to go ahead with it.
That is courage in a difficult situation, not cowardice, complaining or delay.
Answer: To endure a painful or difficult situation with courage.

blocks.q:
Fill in the blanks with the correct expression:
When the company started losing money, they decided to ______ and lay off twenty employees.
steps: Translate the blank: losing money, the company had to do something painful but necessary (lay off twenty employees).
'Bite the bullet' means to face an unpleasant situation bravely and do what must be done.
'Cut corners' means to do a job cheaply or carelessly; 'call it a day' means to stop working; 'pull the plug' means to end a project, which does not lead into 'and lay off'.
Only 'bite the bullet' fits the sense of a hard but unavoidable decision.
Answer: bite the bullet.

chapters.intro: These idioms answer the questions when, how often and how. They are short, common and often appear in sentence-context items, where the rest of the sentence confirms the meaning. The frequency idioms are especially important, because SSC tests the exact degree, such as 'occasionally' against 'never'.

rows: Off and on; now and then; by fits and starts
In full swing; on the wane
at the peak of activity; declining
Through thick and thin; in weal and woe
in good times and bad; in prosperity and adversity
blocks.title: When, how often, how fast

blocks.body: 'Off and on' means periodically, not constantly or regularly (CGL 2024). 'Once in a blue moon' means not very often, so monthly and weekly are both too frequent.

blocks.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the following idiom:
Once in a blue moon
o: To be extremely sad or depressed
An event that happens every night
steps: 'Once in a blue moon' answers the question 'how often?'.
A blue moon is an extra full moon that comes only rarely, so the idiom means very rarely.
'Extremely sad' confuses it with 'feel blue'; 'every night' is the opposite; 'achieve the impossible' is unrelated.
Answer: Something that happens very rarely.

chapters.intro: Many idioms are labels for a kind of person, and they usually appear in fill-in-the-blank items after 'a' or 'an'. Each label describes one striking trait. Picture a real person you know for each label and the meaning will stay with you.

items.b: a friend only in good times
a weak person with no substance
one who criticises without practical experience
one who always does the same things
a child very like a parent
a husband dominated by his wife
one who can do many things

blocks.body: In a fill-in item such as 'she turned out to be a/an ___', the blank needs a noun phrase. In CGL 2024 the clue that Sadhna deserted the speaker once trouble came pointed to a fair-weather friend.

chapters.intro: A proverb is a whole sentence of advice, and SSC asks for its meaning exactly as it asks for an idiom's. The wrong options usually describe the picture, such as stones and moss, while the right option states the lesson. Always translate the proverb into a rule for living before you read the options.

rows: A rolling stone gathers no moss.
One who keeps moving gains nothing lasting.
Knowing someone too well lessens respect.
Out of sight, out of mind.
What is not seen is soon forgotten.
Something that seems bad but turns out good.
When life gives you lemons, make lemonade.
Make the best of a bad situation.
If you are not alert, you miss chances.
Money does not grow on trees.
A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
A sure thing is better than a possible bigger one.
And it is done, simple as that.
blocks.title: Picture to lesson

blocks.body: For 'Money does not grow on trees', an option like 'money grows on shrubs' describes the image and is always wrong. The answer is the lesson: money is limited and must be earned.

chapters.h: How to crack an unfamiliar idiom
chapters.intro: Since 2025 about half the idioms have been rare or literary, so you will sometimes meet one you have never seen. You can still reach the answer by reasoning from the image, the tone and every word of the idiom. This routine turns guessing into elimination.

steps: Picture the literal image and ask what quality it suggests: Newcastle was a coal town, so carrying coals there means supplying what is already abundant.
Eliminate the literal option first, such as a buried hatchet, a kicked bucket or someone playing a fiddle, because SSC always includes one.
Match the tone: humiliation idioms such as eat humble pie never mean celebration, and fame idioms such as laurels never mean loss.
Use every word: 'hoist with one's OWN petard' needs 'own scheme', and 'fair-WEATHER friend' needs 'only in good times'.
In sentence items, put each remaining option into the sentence and keep the one that is both logical and grammatical.
blocks.title: Five steps

blocks.body: Old British idioms can mislead. 'Cry stinking fish' does not mean to complain; it means to run down your own goods, like a fishmonger shouting that his own fish stinks. 'Keep a good table' does not mean to keep discipline; it means to serve good meals.
blocks.title: Read old idioms literally, then think of the seller or the host

blocks.q: What does the idiom "the best of both worlds" typically mean?
o: Having advantages of two different things
Being stuck in between two choices
blocks.a: Having advantages of two different things
steps: Picture it: two worlds, and you get the best part of each.
So the idiom means enjoying the advantages of two different things at the same time, without having to give one up.
Eliminate: 'worst situation' is the opposite tone, 'stuck between two choices' is a dilemma, and 'choosing the better option' means picking one, not having both.
Answer: Having advantages of two different things
blocks.trick: 'Both' is the key word: the answer must keep two things, not choose one.

blocks.q: Choose the correct meaning of the idiom "Open the floodgates."
o: To release something that was previously under control
blocks.a: To release something that was previously under control
steps: Read the idiom literally: floodgates hold back water; opening them lets it pour out all at once.
Turn the picture into an idea: something held back is suddenly released in large amounts.
Check options: closing opportunities, stopping people and controlling emotions are all about holding back, the opposite.
Answer: To release something that was previously under control.
blocks.trick: Opening = releasing; reject every option about stopping or controlling.

chapters.intro: The weight of this topic has held steady at one or two items per shift, but its difficulty rose sharply in 2025. Common idioms from 2021-2024 gave way to literary and rare ones with long, abstract options. The good news is that older SSC favourites keep coming back, so a well-learnt list pays off repeatedly.

items.what: CGL favourites included face the music, apple of discord, play second fiddle, not fit to hold a candle to, Achilles' heel, a man of straw, apple-pie order, donkey's years, keep the wolf from the door, chapter and verse, dog in the manger, beside the mark and in black and white.
Idioms peaked at about 2.05 questions per shift, in all six formats.
About 1.6 per shift, mostly common idioms such as kick the bucket, once in a blue moon, spill the beans, bury the hatchet and fair-weather friend, with frequent sentence and fill-in items.
About 1.4 per shift, and 36 of 37 items used the bare stem 'Choose the correct meaning of idiom', with about half being literary or rare.

items.title: The literal option
points: describes the picture: fiddling, burying a hatchet, a spoon in the mouth

items.title: The opposite-tone option
points: reverses the mood: 'celebrate one's success' for eat humble pie

items.title: The near-miss
points: is half right: 'a difficult task' for Penelope's web, which is really an endless task

blocks.body: Idioms also appear inside Sentence Improvement, where plain words are replaced by an idiom, and occasionally inside the Cloze Test, so this list pays off in three question types.

chapters.intro: Idioms gave 15 stand-alone questions across the eight Tier 2 Paper I English sections on the site (2, 3, 6 and 7 March 2023, 26 October 2023, 18 and 20 January 2025, and 19 January 2026), 2 in every paper except 2 March 2023 (1), plus one idiom replacement inside sentence improvement ('at a stone's throw'). The idioms are well known (a pinch of salt, water under the bridge, Achilles' heel, cold feet), but Tier 2 asks them in more ways than Tier 1: the meaning of an idiom in a sentence, the meaning of an idiom alone, the idiom that fills a blank, the idiom that completes a dialogue, and the sentence that shows an idiom's meaning.

rows: Meaning of a highlighted idiom in a sentence
The employee took the manager's remark with a pinch of salt.

Despite their differences, the two politicians decided to bury the hatchet.

blocks.body: The dialogue format tests the exact form of the idiom. The options were 'cold foot', 'cold feet', 'cold hand' and 'hot feet', and 'my cup of coffee', 'not my cup of coffee', 'not my cup of tea' and 'not my cup, not my tea'. An idiom never changes its words or number: it is always 'cold feet' and always 'not my cup of tea'.

blocks.title: Tier 2 idioms with their meanings
items: By the skin of one's teeth: barely, just managing to escape.
Running around in circles: very active but achieving little.
A Catch-22 situation: a problem whose only solution is blocked by the problem itself.
Achilles' heel: a weak or vulnerable point. A chip off the old block: like one's parent in behaviour.
With a pinch of salt: with doubt about its truth. Water under the bridge: past events that no longer matter.
Bite the bullet: face something painful with courage. Bury the hatchet: end a quarrel.
Pull out all the stops: do everything possible to succeed. Sitting on the fence: not taking a side.
Get cold feet: become nervous before an event. Not my cup of tea: not what I like.
A stitch in time saves nine: timely action prevents more work later.
Strain at a gnat and swallow a camel: fuss over small things while ignoring big ones.

formulas.f: Rule 1: an idiom's words are fixed; no word may be swapped
formulas.note: 'Break a leg', not 'break an arm'; 'an ace up his sleeve', not 'up his sheath' (CGL 2023).

formulas.f: Rule 2: the literal option is almost always wrong
formulas.note: 'Cake walk' = something easy, not 'something tasty' (CGL 2021).

formulas.f: Rule 3: match the tone (positive / negative / neutral)
formulas.note: 'Eat humble pie' = accept defeat or insult gracefully, never 'celebrate one's success' (CGL 2025).

formulas.f: Rule 4: the answer must explain every word of the idiom
formulas.note: 'Fair-weather friend' = friend only in good times, hence 'a selfish friend' (CGL 2022).

formulas.f: Rule 5: in a sentence, the context sets the meaning
formulas.note: 'I only see him once in a blue moon' = not very often (CGL 2024).

formulas.f: Rule 6: for fill-in items, the idiom must fit both meaning and grammar
formulas.note: 'She turned out to be a/an ___' needs a noun phrase: fair-weather friend (CGL 2024).

formulas.f: Rule 7: proverbs are tested as idioms; give the lesson, not the picture
formulas.note: 'A rolling stone gathers no moss' = one who keeps moving gains nothing lasting (CGL 2022).

formulas.f: Rule 8: phrasal verbs change meaning with the particle
formulas.note: Put off means postpone, put up with means tolerate, put on means wear or pretend, put out means extinguish, and put down means suppress.

formulas.f: Effort cluster: leave no stone unturned = move heaven and earth = strain every nerve = pull out all the stops
formulas.note: 'The doctors tried very hard' -> moved heaven and earth (CGL 2024).

formulas.f: Anger cluster: fly off the handle = hit the roof = see red = fly into a passion = foam at the mouth
formulas.note: All of these mean to become very angry.

formulas.f: Trouble cluster: in hot water = in a soup = in a tight corner = in a fix
formulas.note: All of these mean to be in trouble.

formulas.f: Rarely cluster: once in a blue moon; off and on = now and then = occasionally
formulas.note: 'Off and on' = periodically (CGL 2024).

formulas.f: Secret cluster: let the cat out of the bag = spill the beans (reveal); keep one's cards close to one's chest = keep plans hidden
formulas.note: Opposites inside one cluster are a favourite distractor.

formulas.f: Peace cluster: bury the hatchet, hold out an olive branch, pour oil on troubled waters
formulas.note: 'A gesture of peace' = an olive branch (CGL 2022).

formulas.f: Waste cluster: flog a dead horse, carry coals to Newcastle, wild goose chase, cast pearls before swine
formulas.note: All of these mean useless effort; casting pearls before swine means offering good things to those who cannot value them.

formulas.f: Cowardice cluster: lily-livered, yellow-bellied, show the white feather, get cold feet
formulas.note: 'Become yellow bellies' = cowards (CGL 2022).

formulas.f: Deceit cluster: throw dust in one's eyes, pull the wool over one's eyes, draw the longbow, cock and bull story
formulas.note: Draw the longbow = exaggerate (CGL 2025).

formulas.f: Inexperience cluster: green horn, tyro, raw recruit
formulas.note: 'The new electrician is a green horn' = inexperienced (CGL 2021).

formulas.f: Long time: donkey's years, a month of Sundays, for ages
formulas.note: 'For a very long time' = donkey's years (CGL 2022).

formulas.f: Mythology set: Achilles' heel (weakness), Penelope's web (endless task), Sword of Damocles (constant threat), Hobson's choice (no choice), Pandora's box (source of troubles)
formulas.note: Penelope's web was asked in 2024, and the sword of Damocles and Hobson's choice in 2025.

method: 1. Read the idiom, and the sentence if one is given, and ask whether you know it; if you do, pick the figurative meaning at once.
2. If you do not know it, picture the literal image and name the idea in two or three words, such as danger overhead, no real choice or own trap.
3. Strike out the literal option and any option that is opposite in tone.
4. Test the remaining options against every word of the idiom, because the right answer explains all of it.
5. For sentence and fill-in items, plug each option into the sentence; it must make sense and be grammatical.
6. Do not spend more than 25 seconds; if two options still fit, mark one and move on.
7. For revision, learn idioms in families (anger, effort, trouble, deceit, peace, time) with one past-paper sentence each, and revise the fact list every three or four days.
traps: The literal trap: one option always describes the picture, such as fiddling, burying a hatchet, kicking a bucket or a spoon in the mouth.
The opposite-tone trap: 'eat humble pie' is offered with 'celebrate one's success', and 'on the ball' with 'unaware of changes'.
The half-right trap: 'throw one's hat into the ring' is offered with 'bet', and 'hoist with one's own petard' with 'risen through deceit'; only the option that matches every word is right.

The look-alike trap: 'sit on the fence' means undecided but 'mend fences' means make peace; 'bite the bullet' means face bravely but 'bite the dust' means fail; 'hold water' means be valid but 'in hot water' means in trouble.
The similar-image trap: 'keep at arm's length' means avoid friendship, while 'keep at bay' means hold off a threat.
The family confusion trap: 'let the cat out of the bag' means reveal a secret, while 'keep one's cards close to one's chest' means hide one's plans.

The wrong-word trap in Sentence Improvement: 'up his sheath' should be 'sleeve', 'saxophone' should be 'trumpet', 'make it a day' should be 'call it a day', and 'speaks his eye' should be 'speaks his mind'.
The near-synonym trap: 'off and on' means periodically, not constantly or regularly, and 'green horn' means inexperienced, not uneducated.
The proverb trap: options that explain the image ('money grows on shrubs') are wrong; choose the lesson (money is limited and hard-earned).
The old-British-idiom trap: 'cry stinking fish' means belittle one's own work, not complain, and 'keep a good table' means serve good meals, not maintain discipline.
The fill-in grammar trap: 'a/an ___' needs a noun phrase, while 'I can ___' needs a verb phrase such as 'pat myself on the back'.
The Hobson trap: 'hand and glove' means very close partners, not working openly, and 'Hobson's choice' means no choice, not a dilemma between two evils, which is 'between the devil and the deep sea'.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. To kick the bucket. (a) Be happy (b) To be ill (c) To die (d) Be sad (CGL 2023)
examples.how: 1. 'Kick the bucket' is a standard idiom for death. 2. 'Be ill' is a near-miss from the same area, and 'be happy' and 'be sad' are unrelated. 3. The answer is (c), to die.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Cat's paw. (a) A person used as a tool by another (b) The most important attribute (c) To attack someone (d) Move at a fast pace (CGL 2021)
examples.a: (a) A person used as a tool by another
examples.how: 1. The idiom comes from the fable of the monkey that used a cat's paw to pull chestnuts out of a fire. 2. The image is of someone else's hand doing the risky work. 3. The answer is (a).

examples.q: Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom. My uncle lives in New York, so I only see him once in a blue moon. (a) Monthly (b) Weekly (c) Very often (d) Not very often (CGL 2024)
examples.how: 1. 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely. 2. The context agrees, because the uncle lives far away and meetings are rare. 3. 'Monthly' and 'weekly' are too frequent and 'very often' is the opposite, so the answer is (d).

examples.q: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the idiom in the given brackets. His PhD degree seems to be (Penelope's web). (a) An endless task (b) A difficult task (c) An important task (d) A secret task (CGL 2024)
examples.how: 1. In the Odyssey, Penelope wove a shroud by day and undid it by night, so it was never finished. 2. 'A difficult task' is only a half-match, because the key idea is that the task never ends. 3. The answer is (a).

examples.q: Select the most appropriate idiom to fill the blank. I thought Sadhna would always stick by me, but when I got into trouble, she turned out to be a/an ____. (a) white elephant (b) fair-weather friend (c) hard nut to crack (d) open secret (CGL 2024)
examples.how: 1. The clue is that Sadhna stayed in good times but left when trouble came. 2. A fair-weather friend is a friend only when things go well. 3. The other options do not describe a person who deserts, so the answer is (b).

examples.q: Read the sentence and select the most suitable idiom. The renowned publisher decided to withdraw a book from the market. No one was interested in the book as the arguments presented were ____. (a) under the rose (b) high and mighty (c) beside the mark (d) out of the woods (CGL 2024)
examples.how: 1. Readers lost interest because the arguments were irrelevant. 2. 'Beside the mark' means irrelevant or off the point. 3. 'Under the rose' means secretly, 'high and mighty' means arrogant and 'out of the woods' means out of danger, so the answer is (c).

examples.q: Select the correct idiom that can substitute the italicised words. My business partners thought that I would simply accept their cheating, but they will soon realise that I am more powerful than what they expected. (a) casting pearls before swine (b) they caught a tartar (c) damsel in distress (d) cutting a cloth (CGL 2023)
examples.how: 1. The italicised idea is that the opponent turned out to be stronger than expected. 2. 'Catch a Tartar' means to take on someone who proves too strong for you. 3. The answer is (b).

examples.q: Select the sentence that uses the idiom correctly. (a) Ranita was not selected for the job as she got cold feet. (b) Walking bare feet on grass gave him cold feet. (c) After too much cycling Arun got cold feet. (d) One can swim easily with cold feet. (CGL 2022)
examples.how: 1. 'Get cold feet' means to lose nerve before an important act. 2. Options (b), (c) and (d) use cold feet in the literal sense. 3. Only (a) uses the figurative sense, because nervousness cost Ranita the job.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the italicised words. The world needs a global leader who can hold out a gesture of peace. (a) mother wit (b) halcyon days (c) a grass widow (d) an olive branch (CGL 2022)
examples.how: 1. An olive branch is an offer of peace, from the dove that brought an olive leaf to Noah. 2. 'Halcyon days' means peaceful past times, which is a near-miss but not a gesture. 3. The answer is (d).

examples.q: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Hobson's choice. (a) A dilemma between two evils (b) A free and fair decision (c) No real choice at all (d) A selection made under duress (CGL 2025)
examples.how: 1. Thomas Hobson, a stable owner, let customers take the horse nearest the door or none. 2. So Hobson's choice means 'take it or leave it', which is no real choice. 3. A dilemma between two evils is 'between the devil and the deep sea', so the answer is (c).

examples.q: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Hoist with one's own petard. (a) He has benefited by sheer luck (b) He has risen through deceit (c) He has gained unearned praise (d) He is destroyed by his own trap or scheme (CGL 2025)
examples.a: (d) He is destroyed by his own trap or scheme
examples.how: 1. A petard was a small bomb, and to be hoisted by it means to be blown up by one's own bomb, as in Hamlet. 2. The key word is 'own', so the meaning is being hurt by one's own plot. 3. The answer is (d).

examples.q: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: To draw the longbow. (a) To romanticise historical events (b) To fabricate or exaggerate with little credibility (c) To delay justice deliberately (d) To conflate myth with realism (CGL 2025)
examples.a: (b) To fabricate or exaggerate with little credibility
examples.how: 1. Old archers boasted about impossible shots with the longbow. 2. So the idiom means to tell tall stories or exaggerate. 3. Options (a) and (d) are near-misses about history and myth, so the answer is (b).

examples.q: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: To be in high dudgeon. (a) To be in a state of moral superiority (b) To be offended with exaggerated dignity (c) To be excited without restraint (d) To be lost in self-delusion (CGL 2025)
examples.a: (b) To be offended with exaggerated dignity
examples.how: 1. 'Dudgeon' means resentment or indignation, and 'high' intensifies it. 2. Only option (b) mentions being offended. 3. The answer is (b).

examples.q: Select the correct idiom that can substitute the italicised words. Shelley has been contemplating for a few days but still has not decided to quit the job. (a) biting the dust (b) chewing the cud (c) cooling one's heels (d) getting into hot waters (CGL 2023)
examples.how: 1. 'Contemplating' means thinking something over slowly. 2. 'Chew the cud', from cows chewing their food again, means to reflect at length. 3. 'Biting the dust' means failing and 'cooling one's heels' means waiting, so the answer is (b).

examples.q: Complete the dialogue for Person B using the correct idiom. Person A: I am so nervous. I don't think I should make the speech tomorrow. Person B: No. You are just getting _____. You have prepared for this. Options: cold foot / cold feet / cold hand / hot feet (CGL Tier 2, 18 January 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: Person A is nervous before an event. Step 2: The idiom for becoming nervous and wanting to back out is 'get cold feet'. Step 3: Idioms keep their exact words, so 'cold foot', 'cold hand' and 'hot feet' are wrong. The answer is 'cold feet'.

examples.q: Complete the dialogue for Person B using the correct idiom. Person A: We are all going to the club this weekend. Do you want to come? Person B: Thank you for asking. But I don't like clubs. It's ______. Options: my cup of coffee / not my cup of coffee / not my cup of tea / not my cup, not my tea (CGL Tier 2, 20 January 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: Person B dislikes clubs, so the idiom must be negative. Step 2: The fixed idiom is 'not my cup of tea', meaning not something I like. Step 3: Replacing tea with coffee or splitting the phrase breaks the idiom. The answer is 'not my cup of tea'.

examples.q: Select the sentence which gives the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Bite the bullet. Options: The children played in the park on a sunny day. / Despite the pain, Sarah decided to go ahead with the surgery. / The chef prepared a delicious meal for the guests. / Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water. (CGL Tier 2, 26 October 2023)
examples.a: Despite the pain, Sarah decided to go ahead with the surgery.
examples.how: Step 1: 'Bite the bullet' means to face a painful or unpleasant situation bravely. Step 2: Only the sentence about Sarah going ahead with surgery despite the pain shows that. Step 3: The other sentences describe ordinary pleasant actions. The answer is the second option.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate meaning of the highlighted idiom. It was a Catch 22 situation for the manager. Options: Worthy successor to the throne / A difficult situation in which the solution to a problem is impossible / Hailed as the ultimate champion / A positive outcome in a tough situation (CGL Tier 2, 3 March 2023)
examples.a: A difficult situation in which the solution to a problem is impossible
examples.how: Step 1: 'Catch-22' comes from Joseph Heller's novel, where the rule that solves a problem also prevents the solution. Step 2: So it means a dilemma with no way out. Step 3: The other options are positive and unrelated. The answer is the second option.

examples.q: Choose the one which gives the meaning of the given idiom or phrase. To strain at a gnat and swallow a camel. Options: To fuss over trifles while ignoring big issues / To have a very large appetite / To be meticulous in everything / To be extremely physically weak (CGL Tier 2, 19 January 2026)
examples.a: To fuss over trifles while ignoring big issues
examples.how: Step 1: A gnat is a tiny insect and a camel a huge animal. Step 2: The phrase describes someone who is careful about a tiny matter but accepts a huge one without thought. Step 3: 'Meticulous in everything' misses the contrast, and the other options take the words literally. The answer is the first option.

revise: Idioms give about 1.6 questions per shift (1.4 in 2025), and since 2025 the stem has been a bare 'Choose the correct meaning of idiom'.
Kill the literal option first, and then kill the option with the opposite tone.
The right meaning explains every word, especially words like OWN, FAIR-WEATHER and HIGH.

From mythology: Achilles' heel is a weakness, Penelope's web is endless, the sword of Damocles is a constant threat, Hobson's choice is no choice, Pandora's box releases troubles, and a Pyrrhic victory costs too much.
Anger idioms include fly off the handle, hit the roof, see red, in high dudgeon, and gall and wormwood.
Effort idioms include move heaven and earth, leave no stone unturned, tooth and nail, and strain every nerve.
Peace is bury the hatchet or an olive branch, while quarrel is at loggerheads, at daggers drawn, bad blood, or no love lost.
Trouble is in hot water, in a soup, in a tight corner, back against the wall, or on thin ice.
Deceit is draw the longbow, a cock and bull story, or throw dust in the eyes, while honesty is call a spade a spade, above board, or a straight shooter.
Rarity and time idioms include once in a blue moon, off and on, donkey's years, at the eleventh hour, and in the nick of time.
Eat humble pie and eat crow mean humility; win laurels and a feather in one's cap mean fame; play second fiddle means a subordinate role; and not fit to hold a candle to means far inferior.
Wasted effort is carry coals to Newcastle, flog a dead horse, a wild goose chase, or fiddle while Rome burns.
Idioms are fixed: it is sleeve, not sheath; trumpet, not saxophone; call it a day; and speak one's mind.
Phrasal verbs to know are put off (postpone), put up with (tolerate), back out (withdraw), take after (resemble) and give in (surrender).

learn.h: Asked three or more times in SSC papers
points: Face the music - to be scolded or bear the consequences (asked 5 times, including CGL 2011, 2013, 2016).
By fits and starts - irregularly, not continuously. By leaps and bounds / Leaps and bounds - very rapidly.
Bad blood - enmity, angry feeling. At the eleventh hour - at the last moment.
Under a cloud - under suspicion. Put up with - tolerate.
Pros and cons - advantages and disadvantages. A bolt from the blue - a sudden unexpected (usually bad) event. To smell a rat - to suspect a trick.
Blow one's own trumpet - praise oneself.
Turn down - refuse or reject. Take exception to - object to. Stick to one's guns - hold on to one's decision.
Null and void - invalid, having no legal force. For good - permanently. A wild-goose chase - a futile search.
All at sea - puzzled, at a loss. No love lost between - not on good terms. Going places - becoming successful. Hard and fast - strict, fixed.
Make a clean breast of - confess fully. Take after - resemble (a parent). Give the game away - reveal a secret. Cheek by jowl - very close together.
Talk through one's hat - talk nonsense. Get the sack - be dismissed. In the long run - ultimately. Fight tooth and nail - fight with all one's strength.
Ins and outs - full details. In high spirits - cheerful. A close shave - a narrow escape. Eat humble pie - apologise humbly. An open book - someone with no secrets.
Die in harness - die while still working. Cut no ice - have no influence. A dark horse - an unexpected winner. End in smoke - come to nothing.
Have something up one's sleeve - have a secret plan. Take to one's heels - run away. Bone of contention - cause of a dispute. Call it a day - stop working for the day.

Hand in glove - in close (often secret) partnership. Leave in the lurch - abandon someone in difficulty. Take to task - scold severely. Bird's-eye view - an overview. See eye to eye - agree fully. Wet behind the ears - young and inexperienced.
Snake in the grass - a hidden enemy. Make a mountain of a molehill - exaggerate a small problem. Under the weather - unwell. At loggerheads - in strong disagreement. Go Dutch - share the cost.
Rise with the lark - get up very early. Horse sense - common sense. A shot in the arm - an encouraging boost. Catch time by the forelock - seize the opportunity.

Take French leave - be absent without permission. Armchair critic - one who criticises without practical experience. Dog in the manger - a selfish person who neither uses nor lets others use. Chapter and verse - exact details. Give a wide berth - keep away from.
In black and white - in writing. Show a clean pair of heels - run away fast. All moonshine - imaginary, far from reality. Up to the mark - of the required standard.

Cat-nap - a short sleep. Fit like a glove - fit perfectly. Gatecrasher - uninvited guest. For all intents and purposes - practically. Drag one's feet - act reluctantly. Hope against hope - keep hoping when there is little chance.

With one voice - unanimously. At a stone's throw - very near. Scot-free - unpunished. Give oneself airs - behave arrogantly. Drive home - emphasise. A left-handed compliment - an ambiguous compliment. Cut a sorry figure - make a poor impression.

On tenterhooks - in anxious suspense. A house of cards - an insecure plan. Throw cold water on - discourage. Butt in - interrupt. Couch potato - an inactive person who watches TV. Catch a Tartar - meet someone too strong for you. Cap in hand - humbly.

Beyond the pale - unacceptable. Straw in the wind - a sign of what may happen. Curry favour - seek favour by flattery. Put up the shutters - close a business. Draw a blank - get no result. In abeyance - suspended. Cock-and-bull story - an absurd, unbelievable story. A live wire - an energetic person.

Feather in one's cap - an achievement to be proud of. Donkey's years - a very long time. Leave no stone unturned - try every means. Nip in the bud - stop at the start. Put a spoke in one's wheel - hinder. Clip one's wings - reduce one's power. Play fast and loose - behave unreliably. Feather one's nest - enrich oneself dishonestly. Grease the palm - bribe. Turn turtle - overturn.

learn.h: From recent-style practice sets and the capsule
points: Like a cakewalk - an easy task. All eyes - watching eagerly. In weal and woe - in good times and bad. A greenhorn - an inexperienced person. Bag and baggage - with all one's belongings.

A skeleton in the cupboard - an embarrassing secret. Fly into a passion - become suddenly angry. Keep at arm's length - keep at a distance. Bear the palm - be the winner. Bob's your uncle - and it is done easily.
Hit below the belt - act unfairly. In hot water - in trouble. Greek (or Latin and Greek) to me - incomprehensible.
A doubting Thomas - a sceptic who needs proof. A man of straw - a weak person. A mare's nest - a false discovery or hoax. A stalking horse - a pretext. An axe to grind - a selfish motive.

At sixes and sevens - in confusion. Between Scylla and Charybdis / between the devil and the deep sea - between two dangers. Between the cup and the lip - at the point of success (much can go wrong). Baker's dozen - thirteen. Alpha and omega - the beginning and the end. Above board - honest and open.

E|Synonyms.why: Synonyms are one of the steadiest English topics: 320 questions in 147 shifts from 2021 to 2025, about 2.2 a shift (2.12 in 2025). About 56% were plain one-word items and about 37% put the word in a sentence. In 2025 the sentence formats vanished, 24 of 55 items were a new homonym format, and the one-word words got much harder.

lines: Expect about two synonym questions in every shift, and since 2025 one of them is usually a hard one-word synonym and the other a homonym sentence.
A true synonym matches the given word in four ways at once: meaning, part of speech, tone and strength.
Frugal and stingy both mean careful with money, but only frugal is praise, which is why tone decides between near-synonyms.
Before choosing, strike out the ALT options: the Antonym, the Look-alike and the same-Topic word.
When three options belong to one family and the fourth stands apart, the odd one is very often the key, as Tardy was for dilatory.
An unknown word can usually be cracked by its parts, because in-transigent is simply 'not willing to compromise', which is stubborn.
A familiar phrase is a hidden dictionary: a callow youth, a cogent argument, dilatory tactics and an implacable enemy all reveal their meanings.
Prefixes carry the charge of a word: in, im, il, ir, un and a mean not, while bene and eu are good and mal and dys are bad.
Roots such as fid (faith), loqu (speak), plac (calm) and pug (fight) turn frightening words like perfidious, loquacious, implacable and pugnacious into easy ones.
SSC loves the less common sense of a word, so commute was keyed as convert, bare as basic and illuminate as explain.
Confusable pairs such as complaisant and complacent, or credible and credulous, are planted side by side to catch careless readers.
In a sentence format, the sentence decides the sense, so 'the stories were hysterical' means the stories were funny.
In the 2025 homonym format, three option sentences use the word in the same sense and the one sentence in an odd setting is the answer.
You do not need to know a rare homonym word like corbel or paten, only to notice which sentence moves it to a different world.
Spend no more than 30 seconds, and if you can remove two options, guess, because a 50-50 guess earns more than it risks.

expand: A -> Antonym: almost every option set hides one (callow: Experienced)
L -> Look-alike: shares letters or sound (Sagacious: Malicious)
T -> Topic word: from the same area but a different meaning (Threshold: stairs)

chapters.intro: A synonym is a word with the same or nearly the same meaning in a given context, as abandon, quit and forsake are. English has very few perfect synonyms, so SSC asks for the closest option, and the closest option must match the given word in four ways. Many words also have more than one sense, and SSC often keys the less common one.

items.f: Synonym = same meaning + same part of speech + same tone + same strength
items.note: Check all four before you click.

blocks.q:
Select the most appropriate SYNONYM of the given word.
PUERILE
steps: Meaning of PUERILE: childishly silly, immature, not worth taking seriously (like juvenile in its childish sense).
Check part of speech: all options are adjectives, so meaning and tone decide.
'Pure' is a look-alike, and 'powerful' is unrelated.
'Innocent' is a positive word, but puerile is a criticism, so the tone does not match.
'Trivial' (silly, of little importance) carries the same critical sense.
Answer: Trivial
blocks.trick: Puer = boy in Latin: puerile behaviour is boyish, childish and silly.

blocks.body: Near-synonyms are like siblings: they share a family face but have different personalities. Frugal is the sibling who saves wisely, stingy is the one who will not share, and SSC wants you to pick the twin, not just any sibling.
blocks.title: Siblings, not twins

blocks.body: A word can have several senses, and SSC often keys the less common one: commute means convert (as in commuting a sentence), bare means basic, and felicitous means apt.

blocks.q:
Which word is nearest in meaning to 'demonstrating'?
This trend is already booming in China, demonstrating significant potential globally.
steps: Say the meaning in the sentence: the trend 'is demonstrating significant potential' = is clearly showing that it has potential.
All four options mean 'show', so test tone and use: which one fits a trend showing a quality?
'Exhibiting' means showing a quality or sign, as in 'exhibiting potential'; it fits exactly.
'Showcasing' and 'displaying' suggest deliberately putting something on show, and 'revealing' means uncovering something hidden; none fits a trend that simply shows potential.
Answer: Exhibiting
blocks.trick: When all options are near-synonyms, put each into the sentence and keep the one with the natural collocation: exhibit potential.

chapters.intro: Synonyms appear in six different formats, and recognising the format tells you how to attack it. The plain one-word format has run through every year, the sentence formats dominated 2022 to 2024, and the homonym format replaced them in 2025. In every sentence format, the sentence decides which sense of the word is meant.

rows: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word
Synonym of the underlined, bold, highlighted or italicised word in the sentence
Synonym of the bracketed word to fill in the blank
Select the synonym of the word X from the given sentence
reproduce: replicates; encountered: experiencing; consensus: agreement
Select the most appropriate meaning of the word
harangue: a lengthy and aggressive speech; atheist: one who does not believe in God; diffident: shy due to lack of confidence
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word
blocks.title: Formats A to F

blocks.body: In the bracketed-blank format the answer must mean the bracketed word and also fit the blank grammatically, as convalescing becomes recovering and not recovery.

chapters.h: Solving when you know the word
chapters.intro: When you know the word, the danger is not ignorance but haste, because SSC plants options that look right at a glance. Put the meaning into your own words first, so that the options cannot steer you. Then strike out wrong options in a fixed order.

steps: Say the meaning in your own words before looking at the options.
Strike out the antonym, which almost every option set contains.
Strike out look-alikes that share letters or sound.
Strike out words from the same topic but with a different meaning.
From the survivors, choose the one with the same part of speech and tone.
blocks.title: Five-step routine

rows: callow: Experienced; circumspect: Reckless; upbraid: Praise
Sagacious with Precious, Delicious, Malicious; Peruse with Pursue; Consent with Dissent
blocks.title: The ALT traps

blocks.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word given below.
Mitigate
steps: Mitigate means to make something less severe or painful.
Alleviate also means to lessen or ease (a pain or problem).
Aggravate and intensify are opposites (make worse or stronger), and instigate means to provoke or start.
Answer: Alleviate.

blocks.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word:
ASPERITY
steps: Meaning first: asperity is roughness or sharpness of tone or manner (from Latin asper, rough).
Look for a noun with the same negative, rough sense.
Gentleness, patience and warmth are opposite in meaning, which is the antonym trap.
Harshness matches the meaning and the part of speech.
Answer: Harshness.
blocks.trick: asper = rough (as in 'exasperate'), so pick the 'rough' word.

blocks.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word: AWRY
steps: Meaning first: awry means out of the correct position, crooked, or (of plans) gone wrong.
Look for a word with the same 'crooked / not straight' meaning.
Aligned, orderly and symmetrical all mean straight or in order, which is the antonym trap.
Askew means not straight, at an angle.
Answer: Askew.

blocks.q:
Find the word most nearly SIMILAR in meaning to the given word:
Prolific
steps: Say the meaning: prolific = producing a great deal, highly productive.
Remove the antonym trap: barren means producing nothing, the opposite.
Remove the unrelated words: furtive = secretive; amiable = friendly.
Fruitful = producing good results in plenty, the same sense.
Answer: Fruitful.
blocks.trick: A prolific writer is a 'fruitful' one; the antonym 'barren' is planted to catch hurried readers.

chapters.h: Solving when you do not know the word
chapters.intro: Even the hardest word leaves clues in its parts, in phrases you have heard, and in the sound of the word itself. The option set is also a clue, because three options often belong to one family. Combine these clues and you can usually remove two options, which is enough to make a guess worthwhile.

steps: Break the word into prefix, root and suffix and build a rough meaning: in-transigent is not compromising, so stubborn.
Recall a phrase you have heard the word in.
Decide the charge: harsh sounds and negative prefixes often signal negative words such as perfidious, pugnacious and pernicious.
Use elimination: if quick, efficient and prompt form one family, the odd one, tardy, is probably the key.
In sentence formats, replace the word with each option and keep the one that leaves the sense unchanged.
blocks.title: Five clues for an unknown word

blocks.body: Never leave a synonym blank if you can remove two options. With +2 for a right answer and -0.5 for a wrong one, a 50-50 guess has a positive expected value.
blocks.title: Guessing pays

chapters.intro: A prefix at the front of a word often decides whether the word is positive or negative, and in what direction it points. Learning about ten prefix families lets you estimate the meaning of hundreds of words. This is the fastest tool for the hard 2025-style words.

rows: a-, an-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, un-, non-, dis-
amoral, anarchy, inscrutable, implacable, illegible, irrevocable, disparate
mal-, mis-, dys-, and per- in some words
abnegate, abdicate, demolish, derogatory, secede, seclude
circumspect, perimeter, transient, permeate, peruse, diagnose
poly-, multi-; mono-, uni-; omni-, pan-
blocks.title: Ten prefix families

items.f: in-, im-, il-, ir-, un-, a-, non- = not
items.note: implacable means cannot be calmed, inscrutable means cannot be understood, and irrevocable means cannot be reversed.

items.f: circum- (around) + spect (look)
items.note: circumspect means looking around before acting, that is, cautious.

chapters.intro: A root is the core of a word, and the same root appears in whole families of words. Once you know that fid means faith, perfidious (faithless), fidelity and diffident all fall into place. These twelve Latin roots cover many words SSC has asked.

rows: perfidious (faithless), fidelity, diffident (lacking faith in oneself), confide
benevolent, benefactor, benign / malevolent, malicious, malady
pacify, placate, placid, implacable (cannot be calmed)
credible, credulous (too ready to believe), incredible, credence
blocks.title: Twelve Latin roots

blocks.body: Picture a flock of sheep for greg. A gregarious person loves to be in the flock, people congregate like a flock, and an egregious error stands out of (e-) the flock because it is so bad.
blocks.title: The flock root

chapters.intro: The second set mixes Greek roots such as path and chron with Latin roots such as pug and mort. Many 2025 words, including garrulous, nebulous, cadaverous and sagacious, come straight from this list. Learn them in opposite pairs where you can, because SSC often puts the pair in one option set.

rows: apathy (lack of interest), empathy, antipathy (dislike), sympathy
philanthropist, bibliophile / misanthrope (hater of mankind), misogynist
chronic, anachronism (out of its time), chronicle, synchronise
gravity, grave, aggravate / levity (lack of seriousness), alleviate (lighten)
mortal, moribund (dying), mortify / vivacious (lively), vital, revive
blocks.title: Thirteen more roots

blocks.body: A nebula is a cloud in space, so a nebulous plan is as vague and shapeless as a cloud. A cadaver is a corpse, so a cadaverous face is as pale as a dead body.
blocks.title: Two pictures for 2025 words

chapters.intro: The ending of a word usually tells you its part of speech, and the part of speech must match between the word and its synonym. This lets you strike out options in one glance, as with temerity (noun) against three adjectives. A few Greek endings also carry meaning of their own.

blocks.title: Endings that reveal the part of speech

chapters.h: Confusable pairs SSC plants as distractors
chapters.intro: SSC often places a look-alike of the right word among the options, or keys a word whose twin has a very different meaning. These pairs differ by a letter or two but can mean opposite things. Learn them as pairs, because that is how they appear.

blocks.q:
Which word can best replace ingenuity?
The ancient Egyptians demonstrated remarkable ingenuity in their architectural designs.
steps: Ingenuity is the noun of 'ingenious' = clever and inventive (not 'ingenuous' = innocent).
In the sentence it praises the Egyptians' clever, original designs.
Strike out the antonyms: stupidity and ignorance; 'simplicity' is unrelated.
Creativity (inventiveness) matches the meaning and tone.
Answer: Creativity
blocks.trick: Ingenuity, ingenious and engineer share the idea of clever invention.

blocks.body: Enervate looks as if it means energise, but it means the opposite, weaken. Noisome looks as if it means noisy, but it means foul-smelling.
blocks.title: Words that lie about themselves

chapters.intro: Many easy-looking words have a second sense, and SSC likes to key that second sense. If the obvious meaning is missing from the options, look for the less common one before you panic. This table lists every such key in our 2021-2025 data.

rows: convert or change, as in commuting a sentence
basic, as in the bare necessities
react; in 'retaliated the blow' it meant reciprocated
very funny, as in 'the stories were hysterical'
aged, as in 'promises made by the old minister'
check (the dictionary meaning is read carefully, and Pursue was the look-alike trap)
blocks.title: Second-sense keys

blocks.body: When all four options look wrong for the meaning you know, the question is almost certainly testing a second sense. Ask yourself in what other phrase you have seen the word.

chapters.intro: In 2025, 24 of the 55 synonym items were homonym questions. Here a homonym means a word with the same spelling but a different meaning. You are given one sentence and four option sentences that use the same word, and the answer is the sentence where the word has a different sense.

steps: Read the given sentence and name the sense and the setting of the highlighted word (for example, church architecture).
Check each option sentence: three will keep the same sense, even if the place changes.
Pick the one sentence whose sense or setting clashes (engineering, biology, cooking, a tailor, AI, a florist).
Do not be fooled by a change of form: 'compacted the soil' still means pressed together.
blocks.title: Four-step homonym routine

items.b: bishop's staff / curled young fern frond

items: Most 2025 items used a rare church, castle, heraldry or scholarly word, such as fief, pauldron, introit, bailey, codex, rheme, amice, gules, simony, corbel, tripos, sconce, paten, basilica, breviarium or cartouche.
You do not need to know the rare word: identify the setting of the given sentence and pick the option whose setting clashes. {PYQ 2026}

Other true homonyms worth knowing are bank, bark, bat, bear, fair, fine, lead, lie, match, mine, pitch, row, seal, spring, tear, well, rock, second, bow, content, object, present and minute. {PYQ 2026}

blocks.q:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:
The bank approved her loan application without delay.
o: The children played on the grassy bank beside the river.
The bank interest rates were revised this quarter.
She approached the bank manager for financial advice.
The bank's new branch opened in the city centre.
blocks.a: The children played on the grassy bank beside the river.
steps: A homonym has the same spelling but a different meaning.
In the given sentence 'bank' approves a loan, so it means a financial institution.
Check each option: interest rates, a bank manager and a new branch all use the money sense, the same as the given sentence.
Only 'the grassy bank beside the river' uses the other meaning: the sloping land along a river.
Answer: The children played on the grassy bank beside the river.
blocks.trick: Name the setting of the given sentence (money) and pick the option whose setting clashes (a river).

blocks.body: A word used in a new place can keep its old meaning: a crosier displayed in a museum is still a bishop's staff. And SSC keys the odd setting even when the new meaning looks invented, as when 'sconced' (fined) was the key.
blocks.title: Two homonym traps

blocks.q:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:
The dog gave a loud bark when the stranger approached.
o: He bought a new leash for his pet.
The tree's bark was rough and peeling.
The dog began to howl at the moon.
The stranger slowly walked away in fear.
blocks.a: The tree's bark was rough and peeling.
steps: A homonym is a word with the same spelling and sound but a different meaning.
In the given sentence, 'bark' is the loud sound a dog makes.
So we need an option that uses the word 'bark' again, but in another sense.
Options 1, 3 and 4 do not contain 'bark' at all (leash, howl and fear are not homonyms of it).
In option 2, 'bark' is the rough outer covering of a tree, a different meaning.
Answer: The tree's bark was rough and peeling.
blocks.trick: First discard every option that does not even contain the word 'bark'.

blocks.q: Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word: He used a hand file to smooth the metal's rough edges.
o: He used the new file to smooth the wood.
The technician used a special file to shape the plastic.
He had to file his nails before applying the nailpaint.
She put all the important papers in a single file.
blocks.a: She put all the important papers in a single file.
steps: Name the sense in the given sentence: 'file' is a metal tool used to smooth or shape a surface.
(a) and (b): the file smooths wood and shapes plastic, still the same tool, only the material changes.
(c) 'file his nails' is the verb from the same tool sense: to rub smooth.
(d) 'papers in a single file' means a folder or set of documents, an unrelated meaning: this is the homonym.
Answer: She put all the important papers in a single file.
blocks.trick: Ask 'is it still smoothing?' The only sentence where it is not is the answer.

chapters.intro: Words are easier to remember in families than one by one, and SSC often draws the key and the antonym from the same pair of families. Learn each family next to its opposite family. Then any word in a family instantly gives you both its synonyms and its antonyms.

rows: obstinate, obdurate, intransigent, recalcitrant, adamant, headstrong {PYQ 2026}
extol, eulogise, laud, acclaim, glorify, encomium (noun)
upbraid, reprimand, chide, rebuke, admonish, castigate, berate {PYQ 2026}
blocks.title: Ten families and their opposites

blocks.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word given below.
Excoriate
steps: Excoriate literally means to strip off the skin, and figuratively to criticise very severely.
It belongs to the scolding family: upbraid, castigate, berate.
Among the options only 'condemn' expresses strong disapproval.
Praise, encourage and appreciate are all opposite in sense.
Answer: Condemn.
blocks.trick: Three options are positive and one is negative; a harsh-sounding word like excoriate takes the negative one.

blocks.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Adamant
steps: Adamant means firmly refusing to change one's opinion or decision.
It belongs to the 'stubborn' family with obstinate, obdurate and intransigent.
Lax and flexible are opposites (easy-going, yielding); genuine means real, which is unrelated.
Answer: Stubborn
blocks.trick: Adamant comes from adamas, an unbreakable stone: an adamant person will not bend.

blocks.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word:
CANDID
steps: Candid means open, honest and direct in what one says.
Check each option: deceitful (dishonest) and secretive (hiding things) are opposites; ambiguous (unclear) is also against the idea of plain speaking.
Frank means honest and direct, the same meaning, part of speech and tone.
Answer: Frank.
blocks.trick: A candid camera shows things as they are: open and frank.

blocks.q:
Find the word most nearly SIMILAR in meaning to the given word:
Obstreperous
steps: Say the meaning: obstreperous = noisy and difficult to control.
Docile belongs to the 'yielding' family (compliant, submissive), the opposite of obstreperous.
Prudent means careful and ambivalent means having mixed feelings, both unrelated.
Unruly = disorderly and hard to manage, the same sense.
Answer: Unruly.
blocks.trick: Picture an obstreperous child in class: noisy and unruly, never docile.

chapters.intro: The 2025 one-word synonyms were pitched at GRE level, and the same words are likely to return. Each word below is paired with the meaning SSC keyed. Say the pair aloud and link it to a phrase or a root from the earlier chapters.

blocks.body: Group them by charge to remember them: perfidious, invective, upbraid, intransigent and dilatory are negative; cogent, propitious, felicitous and luminous are positive.

chapters.intro: The synonym question has changed shape almost every year, even though the count stayed steady at about two a shift. The plain one-word format has been present throughout, while the sentence formats came and went. For 2026 expect one hard one-word synonym and one homonym or in-sentence item per shift.

items.what: All 43 items were one-word synonyms of common words such as amass, audacity, lacuna, sagacious, taciturn, imbue, perjury and ostentatious.

About half the items were one-word and half were in-sentence, with bracketed blanks (sentimental: mawkish, misleading: mendacious, summarised: recapitulated) and meaning phrases (harangue, diffident).
There were 31 one-word synonyms of GRE-level words and 24 homonym sentences, and the sentence formats disappeared.
About 2 questions a shift: one hard one-word synonym and one homonym or in-sentence item.
