chapters.intro: Stand-alone synonym questions are few in Tier 2: 8 across the eight Tier 2 Paper I English sections on the site (2, 3, 6 and 7 March 2023, 26 October 2023, 18 and 20 January 2025, and 19 January 2026), at most 2 in a paper. But synonyms also appear inside the RC passages, where word-meaning questions made up about 15 of the 97 RC items, and one passage on 7 March 2023 asked four synonyms in a row. Tier 2 formats are more varied than Tier 1: a synonym to fill a blank, the pair of synonyms among underlined words, the meaning of an underlined word in a sentence, and the plain word. The syllabus lists 'Synonyms/Homonyms' together, so see also the note on homonyms and homophones.

blocks.body: Tier 2 plants words that look like the answer. For 'advised medicine' the options were prevented, proscribed, presented and prescribed. 'Proscribed' means forbidden, the opposite of what the doctor did. Read each option slowly when two options differ by one or two letters.

blocks.title: What Tier 2 needs beyond the chapters above
items: In a blank-filling synonym question, the answer must be a synonym of the bracketed word and fit the sentence grammatically.
For the pair of synonyms among underlined words, look for two words that share a secondary meaning: 'threshold' and 'dawn' both mean a beginning.
For an RC synonym, reread the sentence in the passage; the answer is the sense used there ('spotted' as witnessed, not speckled).
Adverb meanings are tested as phrases: 'leisurely' means without haste.
Formal Latin words are common: erroneous (fallacious), unacknowledged (unidentified), fruition (accomplishment), luscious (juicy).

formulas.f: Synonym = same meaning + same part of speech + same tone + same strength
formulas.note: Livid means Furious; Pale is a second dictionary sense of livid but was not the SSC key.

formulas.f: Eliminate the antonym, then the look-alike, then the same-topic word
formulas.note: For Sagacious with Precious, Delicious, Malicious and Judicious, the three look-alikes go and Judicious stays.

formulas.f: Three options from one family means the odd one is likely the key
formulas.note: For Dilatory with Quick, Efficient, Prompt and Tardy, the answer is Tardy.

formulas.f: in-, im-, il-, ir-, un-, a-, non- = not
formulas.note: implacable means cannot be calmed, inscrutable means cannot be understood, and irrevocable means cannot be reversed.

formulas.f: per- = through, or wrongly (perfidy, perjury)
formulas.note: perfidious means treacherous, and perjury means lying under oath.

formulas.f: circum- = around; spect = look
formulas.note: circumspect means looking around before acting, that is, cautious.

formulas.f: bene/eu = good; mal/dys = bad
formulas.note: benevolent means kind, a eulogy is a tribute, and malicious means spiteful.

formulas.f: pac/plac = peace; placate = calm down
formulas.note: implacable means unyielding or relentless.

formulas.f: loqu/garrul = speech, chatter; tacit = silent
formulas.note: garrulous means talkative, and taciturn means reserved.

formulas.f: Underlined word in a sentence = its meaning in that sentence
formulas.note: 'the stories were hysterical' means funny, and 'his modest nature' means shy.

formulas.f: Bracketed blank = synonym of the bracketed word + grammatical fit
formulas.note: In 'made ____ (sentimental) appeals', the answer is mawkish, an adjective before a noun.

formulas.f: Synonym from the sentence = the word in the sentence closest to the given word
formulas.note: For reproduce in 'DNA replicates itself', the answer is Replicates.

formulas.f: Homonym question = pick the sentence whose sense or setting differs
formulas.note: If the given sentence has a compact mirror (small), 'They signed a compact to maintain peace' (agreement) is the homonym.

formulas.f: A change of form is not a change of sense
formulas.note: 'compacted the soil' still means pressed together, while 'sconced' is a different word (fined) and was the key.

formulas.f: Second-meaning keys
formulas.note: commute means convert, bare means basic, illuminate means explain, felicitous means apt, and retaliate means react.

formulas.f: Confusable pairs are planted distractors
formulas.note: complaisant (obliging) vs complacent (smug), eminent vs imminent, and credible vs credulous.

method: 1. Identify the format: given word, underlined in a sentence, bracketed blank, find-in-sentence, meaning phrase, or homonym.
2. Say the word's meaning in your own words, and fix its part of speech and tone.
3. Strike out the antonym, then the look-alikes, then the same-topic words.
4. If the word is unknown, split it into prefix, root and suffix, recall a common phrase, and use the three-of-a-family rule.
5. For sentence formats, substitute each surviving option into the sentence and keep the one that preserves the meaning.
6. For homonym items, name the sense and setting of the given sentence, then pick the option sentence whose sense or setting differs.
7. Spend at most 30 seconds, and with two options left, guess, because the expected value is positive.
facts: Abrogate: repeal, abolish (a law or agreement)
Ambiguous: equivocal, having more than one meaning
Anachronistic: out of its proper time
Commute: convert, change (a sentence); travel daily
Ebullient: cheerful and full of energy
Flout: openly disregard (a rule); SSC keyed 'mock'
Jargon: technical language; SSC keyed slang
Kilter: order, good condition (out of kilter)
Morbid: gloomy, unhealthily interested in death
Peruse: read carefully; SSC keyed check
Pugnacious: quarrelsome, belligerent (SSC also keyed waspish)

Homonym words asked in 2025: fief, mitre, vault, pauldron, introit, digest, tenure, cartouche, bailey, tableau, codex, rheme, compact, breviarium, amice, gules, simony, corbel, tripos, sconce, paten, basilica, stern, crosier
traps: Picking the antonym by reflex: callow is not Experienced, circumspect is not Reckless, luminous is not Dull, upbraid is not Praise, and dilatory is not Prompt.
Falling for look-alike options: Sagacious is placed with Precious, Delicious and Malicious, Peruse with Pursue, Consent with Dissent, and Repulse with Reprove.
Mixing up confusable meanings: complaisant (obliging) is not complacent (smug), eminent is not imminent, and credible is not credulous.
Choosing the common sense of a two-meaning word: SSC keyed commute as Convert, bare as Basic, illuminate as Explain and felicitous as Appropriate.
Ignoring the part of speech: an adjective answered with a noun (Juvenile: childhood) or a verb answered with an adjective (Illuminate: Bright) is wrong.
Ignoring strength: invective is a tirade, not mere criticism, and livid is furious, not merely annoyed.
Picking a same-topic distractor: Threshold is placed with stairs, exit and window, and Cascade with Arcade and Garden.
In sentence items, choosing the word's general meaning when the sentence forces another sense, as 'hysterical' meaning funny.
In bracketed blanks, choosing an option with the right meaning but the wrong grammar for the blank.
In find-in-sentence items, choosing a word from the sentence that is related but not a synonym, such as Equipped for 'Ready'.
In homonym items, choosing a sentence where the word keeps its sense in a new place, since a museum's crosier is still a bishop's staff.
In homonym items, rejecting the odd sentence because its new meaning looks invented, when SSC's key is the odd setting even if the usage is unusual.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. Amass. Options: Gather / Spread / Divide / Scatter. (CGL 2021)
examples.how: Step 1: Amass means to collect a large amount over time, as in 'amass wealth'. Step 2: Spread, divide and scatter all mean the opposite. Step 3: Gather matches the meaning.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. Sagacious. Options: Precious / Delicious / Malicious / Judicious. (CGL 2021)
examples.how: Step 1: Sagacious means wise, with good judgement. Step 2: Precious, delicious and malicious are sound-alike traps ending in -cious. Step 3: Judicious (showing good judgement) is the synonym.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. Commute. Options: Consume / Convert / Condense / Conserve. (CGL 2021)
examples.how: Step 1: Besides travelling daily, commute means to change one thing into another, as in commuting a death sentence to life imprisonment. Step 2: All four options begin with con-, so the look of the word cannot help. Step 3: Meaning decides, and the answer is Convert.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. Lacuna. Options: Misfortune / Languor / Apathy / Hiatus. (CGL 2021)
examples.how: Step 1: A lacuna is a gap or missing part, as in 'a lacuna in the law'. Step 2: A hiatus is also a gap or break. Step 3: Languor (tiredness) is a look-alike, and misfortune and apathy are unrelated.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word. The foreign company is chary of investing in Africa. Options: Keen / Fervent / Confident / Cautious. (CGL 2022)
examples.how: Step 1: Chary means wary or hesitant, so 'chary of investing' means cautious about investing. Step 2: Keen, fervent and confident all show eagerness, the opposite attitude. Step 3: The answer is Cautious.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence. She had the temerity to call her teacher a liar. Options: tedious / impudence / trenchant / taciturn. (CGL 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: Temerity is reckless, usually disrespectful boldness, and it is a noun. Step 2: The only noun among the options is impudence (cheeky disrespect). Step 3: The other three options are adjectives with unrelated meanings.

examples.q: Select the synonym of the word 'reproduce' from the sentence. Many scientific researches have proved that DNA replicates itself in the human body and is an enzyme based catalyst reaction. Options: Replicates / Proved / Researches / Reaction. (CGL 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: This is the find-in-sentence format, so the answer must be a word from the sentence. Step 2: To replicate is to make a copy, that is, to reproduce. Step 3: The other options are simply other words from the sentence.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word in the following sentence to fill in the blank. During Covid times, many organisations made ________ (sentimental) appeals to raise funds for migrant workers. Options: practical / mawkish / cynical / sincere. (CGL 2024)
examples.how: Step 1: The blank needs an adjective meaning sentimental. Step 2: Mawkish means sentimental in an excessive way. Step 3: Practical and cynical are near-opposites, and sincere means honest, which is a different quality.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given word. Pugnacious. Options: Impatient / Waspish / Good-tempered / Arrogant. (CGL 2024)
examples.how: Step 1: Pugnacious comes from Latin pugnare, to fight, and means eager to quarrel. Step 2: Waspish means sharply irritable, the closest option. Step 3: Good-tempered is the antonym, and impatient and arrogant are different faults.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. Kilter. Options: Anarchy / Shambles / Order / Disrepair. (CGL 2024)
examples.how: Step 1: Kilter means good working order, as seen in 'out of kilter' (out of order). Step 2: Anarchy, shambles and disrepair all mean disorder and form one family. Step 3: The odd one out, Order, is the key.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word: DILATORY. Options: Quick / Efficient / Prompt / Tardy. (CGL 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: Dilatory means slow and causing delay, as in 'dilatory tactics'. Step 2: Quick, efficient and prompt form one family of opposites. Step 3: Tardy (late, slow) is the synonym.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word: INTRANSIGENT. Options: Willing / Compliant / Stubborn / Submissive. (CGL 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: Split the word: in- (not) + transigent (ready to compromise) means refusing to compromise. Step 2: Willing, compliant and submissive all mean yielding. Step 3: The answer is Stubborn.

examples.q: Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word: The architect discussed the vault beneath the cathedral. Options: The gymnast performed a perfect vault over the horse. / The treasury vault was secured with biometric locks. / The earthquake cracked the stone vault supporting the nave. / The nobles were interred in the family vault. (CGL 2025)
examples.a: The gymnast performed a perfect vault over the horse.
examples.how: Step 1: In the given sentence a vault is a built arched chamber. Step 2: The treasury strongroom, the arched roof and the burial chamber are all built structures of the same family. Step 3: Only the gymnast's vault is a leap, which is a different meaning.

examples.q: Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word: She placed a compact mirror in her purse. Options: The team formed a compact defensive unit. / He compacted the soil using a roller. / They signed a compact to maintain peace. / The book was written in a compact style. (CGL 2025)
examples.a: They signed a compact to maintain peace.
examples.how: Step 1: In the given sentence compact is an adjective meaning small and closely packed. Step 2: A compact unit, compacted soil and a compact style all keep the idea of packed or condensed. Step 3: The noun 'a compact' means a formal agreement, a different sense, so it is the answer.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate synonym of the word given in brackets to fill in the blank. The doctor has __________ (advised) medicine for the treatment of the disease. Options: prevented / proscribed / presented / prescribed (CGL Tier 2, 3 March 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: A doctor advising medicine is prescribing it. Step 2: 'Proscribed' means forbidden, which looks similar but has the opposite sense. Step 3: 'Prevented' and 'presented' do not mean advised. The answer is 'prescribed'.

examples.q: Identify the pair of synonyms from the underlined words in the given sentence. It was a fairly foul day, as omens could be seen in abundance from the threshold of his border town ever since the dawn struck. Options: fairly, abundance / foul, omens / day, border / threshold, dawn (CGL Tier 2, 3 March 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: Check each pair for a shared meaning. Step 2: 'Threshold' means the point of entering or beginning, and 'dawn' also means the beginning of something. Step 3: None of the other pairs share a meaning. The answer is 'threshold, dawn'.

examples.q: Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined word in a sentence. Even though James won the election, he has not brought any of his campaign promises to fruition. Options: concealment / nourishment / disappointment / accomplishment (CGL Tier 2, 7 March 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: 'Bring to fruition' means to realise or complete a plan. Step 2: The contrast 'Even though he won' shows he has not carried out his promises. Step 3: 'Nourishment' plays on 'fruit', and 'disappointment' is the result, not the meaning. The answer is 'accomplishment'.

examples.q: Choose the appropriate synonym of the given word. Erroneous. Options: Fallacious / Right / Vital / Accurate (CGL Tier 2, 19 January 2026)
examples.how: Step 1: 'Erroneous' means wrong or based on error. Step 2: 'Fallacious' means based on a mistaken belief, so it matches. Step 3: 'Right' and 'Accurate' are antonyms, and 'Vital' is unrelated. The answer is 'Fallacious'.

examples.q: (Passage on a solar explosion, which says that debris was thrown out from the Sun.) Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word from the passage. Debris. Options: Detritus / Rays / Specks / Liquid (CGL Tier 2, 7 March 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: 'Debris' means scattered pieces of waste or remains. Step 2: 'Detritus' has the same meaning. Step 3: 'Specks' are tiny spots, not remains, and 'Rays' and 'Liquid' are unrelated. The answer is 'Detritus'.

revise: Expect about 2 synonym questions a shift, and in the 2025 pattern one is a hard one-word synonym and one a homonym sentence.
Match meaning, part of speech, tone and strength before choosing.
Strike out the antonym first, then the look-alikes, then the same-topic words.
When three options come from one family, the odd one is usually the key.
Know the prefixes: in, im, il, ir, un and a mean not; per means through or wrongly; circum means around; bene and eu mean good; mal means bad.
Know the roots: fid (faith), loqu (speak), plac (calm), mut (change), cred (believe), pug (fight), lumin (light) and nebul (cloud).
Remember the second meanings SSC keyed: commute means convert, bare means basic, illuminate means explain, felicitous means apt, and retaliate means react.
In sentence formats, substitute the option into the sentence, because context decides the sense.
In homonym items, name the setting of the given sentence, and the option set in a different setting is the answer.
Learn the 2025 words cogent, trenchant, invective, perfidious, propitious, garrulous, nebulous, cadaverous, coruscate and circumspect.
Also learn apogee, nonchalant, sentient, complaisant, abnegate, exiguous, callow, intransigent, upbraid, dilatory and implacable.
Keep the confusables apart: complaisant and complacent, eminent and imminent, credible and credulous, ingenious and ingenuous.
Spend a maximum of 30 seconds, and take a 50-50 guess when you have one.

Exaltation - Ecstasy. Nexus - Link. Satisfaction - Contentment. Stagnant - Motionless. Peril - Hazard. Obligatory - Compulsory.

G|Polity.why: Polity averages about 2.6 questions per shift in 2021-2025, rising to 3.4 in 2025. About 35% ask which Article or Part covers Fundamental Rights, DPSP, Duties, the executive or the judiciary, followed by amendments, Acts and bodies, Parliament procedure and Constitution-making. In 2025 SSC added two-statement questions on Centre-State Articles, the GST Council and the new criminal laws.

lines: The Constituent Assembly, created under the 1946 Cabinet Mission Plan, took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to write a Constitution adopted on 26 November 1949 and fully in force on 26 January 1950.
Rajendra Prasad presided over the Assembly, B.R. Ambedkar led the seven-member Drafting Committee, and Nehru's Objectives Resolution grew into the Preamble.
India borrowed wisely, taking rights and courts from the USA, Parliament from Britain, Directive Principles from Ireland and Fundamental Duties from the USSR.
The Preamble declares India a sovereign socialist secular democratic republic, and the 42nd Amendment of 1976 is the only one that ever changed it.
Six groups of Fundamental Rights in Part III (Arts 12-35) shield the citizen, with Art 32 as their heart and soul and Arts 20 and 21 never suspended.
Directive Principles in Part IV (Arts 36-51) guide the State without being enforceable, while the eleven Fundamental Duties of Art 51A guide the citizen.
The President is the constitutional head of the Union, but the Prime Minister and a Council of Ministers answerable to the Lok Sabha actually govern.
Parliament is the President plus a permanent Rajya Sabha of at most 250 and a Lok Sabha of at most 550, and only the Lok Sabha controls a Money Bill.
One integrated judiciary, led by a Supreme Court whose basic structure doctrine from Kesavananda Bharati (1973) limits even Parliament, guards the Constitution.
Every State mirrors the Union with a Governor, a Chief Minister and a legislature, and the 73rd and 74th Amendments of 1992 added panchayats and municipalities below them.
The Seventh Schedule's three lists divide law-making, while residuary power and the last word in a Concurrent conflict stay with the Centre.
Money is shared through Part XII and the Finance Commission (Art 280), and since 2017 through a GST Council where the Centre holds one-third and the States two-thirds of the vote.
In a crisis the Centre takes charge through a National Emergency (Art 352), President's Rule (Art 356) or a Financial Emergency (Art 360).
Art 368 lets Parliament amend the Constitution by special majority, with State ratification for federal provisions, but never its basic structure.
Bodies such as the Election Commission, UPSC and CAG keep the system honest, and since 1 July 2024 the BNS, BNSS and BSA have replaced the colonial criminal codes.

chapters.h: The Constituent Assembly: people, committees and dates
chapters.intro: India's Constitution was written by Indians, in an Assembly that met for almost three years. SSC treats this chapter as a quiz of names and dates: who chaired which committee, which session fell when, and which day is celebrated as what. Learn the story in order and every date falls into place.

items.what: The Nehru Report, an early draft constitution, came from an All Parties Conference in Lucknow led by Motilal Nehru.
After the 1929 Lahore session Congress marked 26 January as Purna Swaraj Day from 1930; this is why the Constitution began on that date.
M.N. Roy first put forward the idea of a constituent assembly for India.
Congress formally demanded a Constituent Assembly.
Nehru declared for Congress that free India's constitution must be framed without outside interference by an Assembly elected on adult franchise.
The August Offer, made during the Second World War, accepted the demand in principle.
Cripps Proposal.
Wavell Plan.
Cabinet Mission (Pethick-Lawrence as chairman, Stafford Cripps, A.V. Alexander). Its scheme created the Assembly, indirectly elected by the provincial assemblies.
The Interim Government took office under Nehru.

items.what: First session (9-23 December 1946); 211 members present on day one. Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary president.
Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President of the Assembly.
Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution; it was adopted on 22 January 1947 and later became the Preamble. {PYQ 2022}
The Assembly adopted the National Flag, designed by Pingali Venkayya.
Midnight session; Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan was among those who spoke.
Drafting Committee set up under B.R. Ambedkar; it met first on 30 August and sat for 141 days.
The Assembly ratified India's Commonwealth membership.
The tenth session of the Assembly was held. {PYQ 2021}
The eleventh and last session.
Constitution adopted. Provisions on citizenship, elections and the provisional Parliament took effect at once. The day is Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas), observed since 2015. {PYQ 2022, 2024}
The Assembly adopted the National Anthem and the National Song, and elected Rajendra Prasad first President of India, unopposed. 284 members signed the Constitution. {PYQ 2021}
The rest of the Constitution came into force; Prasad was sworn in as President and the National Emblem (Sarnath Lion Capital) was adopted. {PYQ 2021}

blocks.title: Two dates for Rajendra Prasad
blocks.body: He was elected President of the Assembly on 11 December 1946. He was elected first President of India, unopposed, on 24 January 1950, and sworn in on 26 January 1950. Do not blur the last two dates.

items: The Drafting Committee had 7 members, with B.R. Ambedkar as chairman. {PYQ 2021}
The other members were N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, K.M. Munshi and Syed Mohammad Saadullah.
N. Madhava Rau replaced B.L. Mitter, and T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan after his death.
S.N. Mukherjee was the chief draftsman.

Ambedkar first entered the Assembly from Bengal (a seat lost to Pakistan at Partition) and was later re-elected from Bombay after M.R. Jayakar resigned.

items: Section 8(1) of the Indian Independence Act 1947 recognised the Assembly and made it a sovereign law-making body as well. {PYQ 2021}

blocks.title: One Assembly, two hats
blocks.body: Picture one body wearing two hats. With Rajendra Prasad in the chair it wrote the Constitution; with G.V. Mavalankar in the chair it passed ordinary laws. The hand-written original was calligraphed by Prem Behari Narain Raizada and illustrated by Nandalal Bose and his Santiniketan team.

chapters.h: Sources of the Constitution and its salient features
chapters.intro: The framers borrowed the best working ideas from other constitutions and from British-era Acts, then adapted them to India. SSC asks 'borrowed from which country' almost every year, so learn each country as a small bundle of features. The salient features explain what kind of state India is: federal in form but with a strong Centre.

blocks.title: Borrowed features, country by country
rows: Federal scheme with provincial autonomy, office of Governor, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions and administrative details {PYQ 2025}

Parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship, cabinet system, bicameral Parliament, law-making procedure, parliamentary privileges, prerogative writs (habeas corpus, mandamus), office of Speaker. Fundamental Rights do not come from Britain. {PYQ 2021}

Fundamental Rights, written Constitution, separation of powers, office of the President, judicial review, independent judiciary, impeachment of the President, removal of judges, Vice-President, idea of a Preamble; PIL also began in the USA {PYQ 2024}
Directive Principles, nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha, method of electing the President {PYQ 2021, 2023, 2024}
Federation with a strong Centre (quasi-federal design), residuary powers with the Centre, Governors appointed by the Centre, advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce, joint sitting of the two Houses
Fundamental Duties and the ideal of social, economic and political justice in the Preamble {PYQ 2023}
Republic, and the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity {PYQ 2024}
Suspension of Fundamental Rights during an Emergency
Procedure for amending the Constitution and election of Rajya Sabha members
'Procedure established by law' (the opposite of the American 'due process of law')

blocks.title: Four hooks that answer most questions
blocks.body: Link each country to one image. Ireland is the 'guiding' country, so it gave the Directive Principles. The USSR is the 'duty' country, so it gave Fundamental Duties. The USA is the 'rights and courts' country, and Britain is the 'Parliament' country.

blocks.title: Company-era Acts, 1773 to 1853
rows: Governor of Bengal became Governor-General (Warren Hastings first), helped by a 4-member council; Bombay and Madras were placed under Bengal; a Supreme Court was set up at Calcutta in 1774 (Elijah Impey first Chief Justice); company servants barred from taking gifts or bribes
Fixed flaws of the 1773 Act; the Governor-General and his council were kept outside the Supreme Court's reach
Board of Control looked after political matters while the Court of Directors kept trade, so control was shared (dual control); company lands were first called British possessions in India
Renewed the company's trade monopoly for another 20 years

Ended the company's trade monopoly with India except tea and the China trade; allowed Christian missionaries; set aside Rs 1 lakh a year for education; asserted the Crown's sovereignty over company territory

Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India (William Bentinck first); Bombay and Madras lost law-making power; the company stopped trading and became purely administrative; a Law Member was added (Macaulay first); a Law Commission was provided for
Legislative work of the Governor-General's council was separated from executive work, with 6 legislative members added; open competition for the civil service began

blocks.title: Crown rule, 1858 to 1947
rows: Company rule ended; the Governor-General became Viceroy (Canning first); a Secretary of State for India with a 15-member council replaced the Board of Control and the Court of Directors

Slowly added Indians to the legislative councils; portfolio system (Canning, 1859) recognised; three Indians nominated to the Viceroy's council in 1862 (Raja of Benares, Maharaja of Patiala, Dinkar Rao); Bombay and Madras got back law-making power; the Viceroy could issue ordinances lasting 6 months
Introduced indirect election in a limited form and let members discuss the budget and put questions

Central council raised from 16 to 60 members; Satyendra Prasad Sinha became the first Indian on the Viceroy's council; separate Muslim electorates, so Minto is called the father of communal electorates

Dyarchy in provinces with transferred subjects (health, education, local government, agriculture) and reserved subjects (police, justice, prisons, land revenue, finance); first bicameral central legislature, with direct elections; High Commissioner for India in London; separate provincial budgets; separate electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; a public service commission followed in 1926 {PYQ 2021, 2023, 2025}
Government of India Act 1935 (in force 1 April 1937)

Provincial autonomy and a federal structure (the all-India federation never came into force); provincial dyarchy ended and dyarchy at the Centre proposed; three lists with 59 Federal, 54 Provincial and 36 Concurrent items; residuary power with the Governor-General; 6 of 11 provinces got two houses; seats reserved for Scheduled Castes, women and labour; only about 14 per cent could vote; Reserve Bank, Federal Court and Federal Public Service Commission created; Sindh and Orissa formed and Burma separated {PYQ 2025}

Ended British rule and gave the Constituent Assembly full sovereign power; partition into two dominions with the right to leave the Commonwealth; Viceroy's post ended and Secretary of State for India abolished; British paramountcy over princely states lapsed and they could join either dominion or stay independent; Mountbatten was the first Governor-General and C. Rajagopalachari the first and last Indian one

nodes: Satyendra Prasad Sinha (first Indian on the Viceroy's council)

blocks.title: Salient features
rows: It covers the Union, the States and many details in one document
Some parts change by simple majority and others need State ratification; K.C. Wheare praised this variety in the amending process {PYQ 2024}
Art 1 calls India a 'Union of States' and the word 'federal' is never used; Indian federalism leans towards the Centre; Wheare called India quasi-federal {PYQ 2025}
The executive is responsible to the Lok Sabha {PYQ 2022}
One Supreme Court sits above all High Courts and lower courts
There is no separate State citizenship as in the USA; dual citizenship is not a feature of the Constitution {PYQ 2024}
Universal adult franchise and secular state
Every adult citizen votes, and the State has no religion
The Centre can take over in a crisis, and the 73rd and 74th Amendments added local government

blocks.title: The 22 Parts at a glance
rows: The Union (Union Executive is Arts 52-78; Parliament Arts 79-122)
The States (State Legislature is Arts 168-212; High Courts Arts 214-231)
Short title, commencement, Hindi text, repeals

blocks.title: Which Parts were added or removed
items: Part VII was deleted by the 7th Amendment (1956).
Parts IVA and XIVA were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). {PYQ 2024}
Part IX was added by the 73rd Amendment and Part IXA by the 74th (both 1992). {PYQ 2021}
Part IXB was added by the 97th Amendment (2011).

blocks.title: Federal and unitary traits side by side
rows: Single Constitution for Centre and States
Flexible amendment for most other parts
Two Houses of Parliament, with States in the Rajya Sabha

items.b: Quasi-federal; also praised the variety of India's amending process {PYQ 2024}

blocks.title: Seventh Schedule lists: then and now
rows: Defence, atomic energy, citizenship, airways, banking, foreign affairs, census, inter-State trade
Public order, local government, health, agriculture, fisheries, betting, land, lotteries, liquor
Marriage and divorce, criminal law and procedure, bankruptcy, labour disputes, electricity, education, weights and measures

blocks.title: Other salient points
items: The Seventh Schedule has three lists: Union, State and Concurrent. {PYQ 2025}
Residuary powers (matters in none of the three lists) lie with the Union legislature. {PYQ 2022}
Written constitutions are compiled in a systematic document, formally made and hard to amend, as in India; the British constitution is unwritten, scattered and easy to amend.
India follows the parliamentary form with three organs (legislature makes laws, executive carries them out, judiciary reviews them) but without a strict separation of powers.
Canada is the source of the quasi-federal design, including the Supreme Court's advisory role.

chapters.h: Preamble, Union and territory, and citizenship
chapters.intro: The Preamble is the Constitution's identity card: it says who made it, what India is and what it promises. Articles 1 to 4 then describe the territory and let Parliament redraw the map, and Articles 5 to 11 decide who is a citizen. India has a single citizenship for the whole country, so nobody is a citizen of a State.

blocks.title: The Preamble in its exact order
steps: Source of authority: WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA
Nature of the State: SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC
JUSTICE: social, economic and political
LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
EQUALITY of status and of opportunity
FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation

blocks.title: Preamble: what SSC asks
items: Liberty has five parts: thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. {PYQ 2023}
Justice is of three kinds: social, economic and political. Equality has two: of status and of opportunity.
'Federal', 'federalism' and 'welfare' are not in the Preamble; 'Federal' is not one of the words before 'Republic'. {PYQ 2021, 2022}
Republic means an elected head of state; the UK, with a monarch, is not a republic. {PYQ 2023}
The 42nd Amendment (1976) changed 'sovereign democratic republic' to 'sovereign socialist secular democratic republic' and 'unity of the nation' to 'unity and integrity of the nation'. {PYQ 2021}
The 42nd Amendment is the only amendment ever made to the Preamble. In November 2024 the Supreme Court dismissed petitions challenging the words 'socialist' and 'secular'.
Liberty, equality and fraternity come from the French Revolution; the ideal of justice comes from the Russian one.
The Preamble was drafted after the rest of the Constitution and reworks Nehru's Objectives Resolution.
The Preamble is not enforceable in court and is neither a source of power nor a limit on the legislature, but it helps interpret the text.

blocks.title: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?

nodes: Preamble is not part of the Constitution
Preamble is part of the Constitution
Part of the Constitution but not enforceable

blocks.title: What each Preamble word means
rows: Supreme over internal and external affairs; no outside power can dictate
Wealth is shared fairly and the State regulates land and industry to reduce inequality; India follows a mixed model between the capitalist USA and the communist USSR
No State religion and equal treatment of all faiths; the Indian model lets the State engage with religion positively
Government by consent of the people; direct (Switzerland) or indirect and representative (India, UK, USA, Canada)
Head of State is elected, not hereditary; the UK, with a monarch, is not a republic {PYQ 2023}

items.b: The identity card of the Constitution
The political horoscope of the Constitution
The soul and the jewel of the Constitution
Like the American Declaration of Independence, but more than a declaration

blocks.title: Union and territory: Arts 1 to 4
rows: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.' Art 1(3): territory means the States, the Union Territories in the First Schedule, and any territory acquired later. {PYQ 2024}
Parliament may admit or establish new States from outside India.

Parliament forms new States and changes areas, boundaries or names by a simple-majority law, on the President's prior recommendation, after taking the State legislature's views, which are not binding. Only Parliament, never a State, can alter a State's boundary or name. {PYQ 2022}
Laws under Arts 2 and 3 that alter the First or Fourth Schedule are not amendments under Art 368, so a simple majority is enough.

blocks.title: Union of States, in more detail
items: India is often called an indestructible union of destructible States: States cannot secede, but Parliament can change their borders.
A federation of the American kind arises from an agreement among units; India's Union came from no such agreement.
Art 2 concerns bringing foreign territory in; Art 3 concerns changes to existing States.

Telangana, the 29th State, was formed on 2 June 2014 under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, an Art 3 law; Chhattisgarh came much earlier, on 1 November 2000, under the Madhya Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2000. {PYQ 2026}
The 5th Amendment lets the President set a time limit for the State legislature to give its views on an Art 3 Bill.
Ceding Indian territory to another country needs an Art 368 amendment (Berubari case, 1960).
The 100th Amendment (2015) gave effect to the swap of enclaves with Bangladesh, India passing 111 and receiving 51.

blocks.title: Princely states and the road to linguistic States

items.what: 562 of 565 princely states signed the Instrument of Accession; the holdouts were Jammu and Kashmir, Junagadh and Hyderabad.
Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession for Jammu and Kashmir after a tribal invasion backed by Pakistan.
Junagadh joined after a plebiscite; Hyderabad was integrated by the military action called Operation Polo in September 1948.
The Dhar Commission (S.K. Dhar) favoured administrative convenience over language; the JVP Committee (Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya) also rejected a linguistic basis for now.
States were sorted into Part A, B, C and D.
Andhra State became the first linguistic state after Potti Sriramulu died on a fast unto death; the Fazl Ali Commission was appointed the same year with Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru.

The States Reorganisation Act, with the 7th Amendment, created 14 States and 6 UTs and ended the four-fold classification. It did not accept 'one language, one State' as a rule, and refused a separate Sikh State and tribal States carved out of Bihar and Assam. {PYQ 2021}

blocks.title: States in order of creation
rows: Meghalaya was a sub-State within Assam from 1970 (22nd Amendment)
Associate State under Art 2A (35th Amendment, 1974), full State by the 36th; 22nd State
From Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar

blocks.title: Union Territories in order
rows: 20 Dec 1961, after India's Operation Vijay against Portuguese rule (12th Amendment)
31 Oct 2019, when Jammu and Kashmir was split into two UTs; J&K's legislative council was abolished
Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (merged)

blocks.title: UT provisions
items: Art 239: UTs are administered by the President through administrators.
Art 239A (14th Amendment, 1962) allowed a legislature or council of ministers for some UTs, first Puducherry.
Art 239AA (69th Amendment, 1991) made Delhi the National Capital Territory with an Assembly whose power over land, police and public order is restricted.

blocks.title: Citizenship at the start, Arts 5 to 10
rows: Together they deal with citizenship at commencement; Art 11 lets Parliament regulate citizenship by law, which it did in the Citizenship Act 1955 (first passed in 1955). {PYQ 2021, 2022, 2023}
A citizen on 26 Jan 1950 if born in India, or a parent was born in India, or ordinarily resident for at least 5 years before that date
Migrants from Pakistan who came before 19 July 1948 became citizens; later arrivals had to register
Those who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 lost citizenship unless they returned on a resettlement or permanent-return permit
People of Indian origin living abroad can register at an Indian mission
Voluntarily taking a foreign citizenship ends Indian citizenship
Citizens continue to be citizens, subject to laws made by Parliament

blocks.title: Acquiring citizenship under the 1955 Act
rows: Born in India before 1 July 1987: citizen. From 1 July 1987: a parent must be a citizen. For births on or after 3 December 2004 (the 2003 amendment): both parents citizens, or one a citizen and the other not an illegal migrant
Born abroad, with an Indian parent, and registered at the Indian consulate within a year
Persons of Indian origin, spouses and minor children of citizens, after 7 years' residence
12 years' residence (11 of the last 14 plus the year before applying) and knowledge of a language in the Eighth Schedule
Government specifies who becomes a citizen when territory joins India

items.title: Five ways to acquire
points: By birth in India.
By descent from an Indian parent.
By registration.
By naturalisation.
By incorporation of territory into India.

items.title: Three ways to lose
points: Renunciation, when a citizen gives it up voluntarily.
Termination, when a citizen voluntarily takes another country's citizenship.
Deprivation, when the government takes it away, for example for fraud.

blocks.title: Loss, recent changes and comparison
items: The Citizenship Amendment Act 2003 bars illegal migrants from registration or naturalisation and laid the base for the National Register of Citizens.

Deprivation covers fraud or false documents, disloyalty to the Constitution, trading with or helping the enemy in war, 7 years' continuous residence abroad, and a 2-year sentence within 5 years of registration.
The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 covers Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered before 31 December 2014.
Its Sec 6B cuts the naturalisation wait to 6 years for those six named communities.
Sec 6A, from the 1985 Assam Accord, sets 25 March 1971 as the Assam cut-off; those who entered before 1966 are citizens.
In India both natural-born and naturalised citizens can become President; in the USA only natural-born citizens can.

items.a: Dual citizenship in the US sense
items.b: Citizenship of the country together with that of a constituent State; India has none, since it has single citizenship. {PYQ 2023}
Not dual citizenship; the scheme began in 2005 by amending the Citizenship Act and merged with the PIO scheme in 2015.

items.title: Can
points: Enter India on a lifelong multiple-entry visa.
Get NRI-like facilities in finance and education.
Buy and sell immovable property except agricultural land, plantation property and farmhouses.
Practise certain professions.

items.title: Cannot
points: Vote.
Hold government posts.
Own agricultural property.
Get an Indian passport, since the holder is a foreign citizen.

chapters.intro: Fundamental Rights are the citizen's shield against the State, borrowed from the USA and enforceable in court. Art 12 defines 'State', and Art 13 makes any law that violates these rights void, which is the root of judicial review. SSC asks article numbers, the six groups, the writs, the right to property and Art 21 cases almost every year.

blocks.title: Big picture
items: Fundamental Rights sit in Part III (Arts 12-35) and can be enforced in court, so they are called the Magna Carta of India. {PYQ 2022, 2023}
Part III lists 6 groups of rights; there were 7 until the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property. {PYQ 2023}
They are borrowed from the USA and are not derived from the British Constitution. {PYQ 2024}
Property is now a constitutional legal right under Art 300A: no one can be deprived of it except by authority of law. {PYQ 2022, 2023, 2025}
The right to vote is not a Fundamental Right; it is a constitutional and statutory right. {PYQ 2022}
Rights only for citizens: Arts 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30. The rest also protect foreigners.
Fundamental Rights are not absolute. They can be curbed within limits and, except Arts 20 and 21, suspended in an Emergency.

blocks.title: The six groups in Article order
blocks.note: Read it as 'Every Free Even Religious Citizen Complains': the groups come in exactly this Article order.

blocks.title: Arts 12-13: State and void laws
items: Art 12: 'State' covers the Government and Parliament, the State governments and legislatures, and all local and other authorities under Government control. The BCCI was held not to be 'State'.
Art 13(1): pre-1950 laws that clash with a right are void. Doctrine of eclipse: such a law is only inoperative to that extent and revives if the clash is removed. {PYQ 2026}
Art 13(2): later laws that clash with a right are void. Art 13(3): 'law' includes ordinances, rules, bye-laws and notifications.
Art 13(4): amendments made under Art 368 are outside Art 13.
Doctrine of severability: only the invalid part of a law is struck down and the valid part is kept.
Doctrine of waiver means voluntarily giving up a known legal right.
Marbury v. Madison (USA, 1803) first set out judicial review.

blocks.title: Right to Equality: how many
items: The Right to Equality covers Arts 14 to 18, which is 5 rights. {PYQ 2021, 2022}

In Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (November 2022) a five-judge Constitution Bench upheld the 103rd Amendment's 10% EWS reservation by a 3-2 majority, holding that it does not violate the basic structure. {T2 2022}

blocks.title: Equality: Arts 14-18
rows: Equality before law and equal protection of laws {PYQ 2026}
Reasonable classification is allowed (State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, 1952) {PYQ 2025}
No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
16(4A) reservation in promotion (77th). Persons with disabilities also have this right (State of Kerala v. Leesamma Joseph, 2021) {PYQ 2023}
Untouchability (Offences) Act of 1955, renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976
Military and academic distinctions are allowed

blocks.title: Equality before law versus equal protection (Art 14)

items.title: Equality before law
points: A negative concept from British law.
Says no one is above the ordinary law.

items.title: Equal protection of laws
points: A positive concept from the USA.
Says like persons must be treated alike.

blocks.title: Reservation clauses and cases
rows: Special provision for SCs, STs and backward classes; came with the 1st Amendment after the Champakam Dorairajan case
103rd Amendment (2019): up to 10% for economically weaker sections
Parliament may fix residence requirements for certain posts
77th Amendment: reservation in promotion with consequential seniority for SCs and STs
81st Amendment: unfilled reserved posts can be carried forward
Religious institutions may reserve posts for their own faith
Second one (1979), recommended 27% for OBCs; V.P. Singh implemented it in 1990
Upheld 27% OBC reservation, capped total reservation at 50% and excluded the creamy layer

blocks.title: Arts 17-18 and the property freedom
items: Art 17 binds private persons as well as the State, and 'untouchability' is not defined.
Art 18: no titles except military and academic. Citizens cannot accept foreign titles, and office-holders need the President's consent for gifts or titles. {PYQ 2026}
Civilian awards are not titles (Balaji Raghavan, 1996).
The 44th Amendment removed the right to property from Art 19(1)(f); the 97th added co-operatives to 19(1)(c).

blocks.title: Freedom: Arts 19-22
rows: Speech and expression (includes press), assembly without arms, associations, unions and co-operatives (97th), movement, residence, profession. Art 19(2) allows reasonable limits for public order, decency or morality, sovereignty and integrity, defamation and contempt of court {PYQ 2022}
Protection in respect of conviction for offences
No ex post facto criminal law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination {PYQ 2022}
Life and personal liberty; the foremost right among the freedoms
Maneka Gandhi 1978 (fair procedure), Puttaswamy 2017 (privacy), K.A. Najeeb 2021 (speedy trial) {PYQ 2022, 2023}
Free and compulsory education for ages 6-14
Added by the 86th Amendment 2002; RTE Act 2009, in force 1 April 2010 {PYQ 2021, 2022, 2025}
Grounds of arrest, a lawyer of choice, production before a magistrate within 24 hours; rules for preventive detention {PYQ 2023}

blocks.title: Arts 20 and 22 in detail
items: Art 20(1): no penalty heavier than the law in force at the time of the offence. 20(2): no double jeopardy.
Art 20(3): no forced self-incrimination, though blood samples or thumb impressions can be taken.
Arts 14, 19 and 21 are together called the golden triangle.
Preventive detention aims to stop a future offence; punitive detention follows a crime.
Art 22: an arrested person has the right to a lawyer and must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (travel time excluded). Enemy aliens and preventive detainees do not get these.
Preventive detention beyond 3 months needs an Advisory Board. Grounds must be told to the detainee, but facts against public interest may be withheld. Parliament sets the maximum period.

blocks.title: Judgments on freedom of speech
rows: Press freedom is part of Art 19(1)(a)
Right to information as part of speech
Right to information falls under Art 19(1)(a)
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
Section 66A of the IT Act struck down
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)
Access to the internet is protected

items.what: A.K. Gopalan: narrow reading; 'procedure established by law' did not need to be fair.
Maneka Gandhi: overruled that view; procedure must be just, fair and reasonable, and the right to travel abroad is part of liberty.
Hussainara Khatoon v. Bihar: speedy trial; the first reported PIL case.
Olga Tellis: livelihood is part of the right to life.
M.C. Mehta: pollution-free environment; absolute liability for hazardous industries.
Mohini Jain and Unnikrishnan: education up to 14 as part of Art 21.
P. Rathinam: read a right to die into Art 21 and struck down Sec 309 IPC on attempted suicide.
Gian Kaur: overruled Rathinam.
Aruna Shanbaug: passive euthanasia allowed under safeguards.
Puttaswamy: privacy is a fundamental right.
Common Cause: living will and passive euthanasia valid; Joseph Shine struck down adultery (Sec 497); Navtej Johar read down Sec 377.
K.A. Najeeb v. Union of India: prolonged jail without trial violates Art 21 (speedy trial). {PYQ 2023}

blocks.title: Extra Art 21 rights
items: Rights also read into Art 21 include shelter, sleep, health, freedom from noise pollution and against public hanging.

blocks.title: Exploitation, religion, culture: Arts 23-30
rows: Bans traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour; the State may impose compulsory service for public purposes {PYQ 2023}
No child below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work {PYQ 2024}
Includes propagation (Sikhs may carry kirpans); subject to public order, morality and health {PYQ 2022}
Religious groups may set up institutions, manage affairs, own property and administer it by law
No tax to promote a religion
No religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions
Arts 25 to 28 together form the Right to Freedom of Religion {PYQ 2022, 2023, 2024}
Cultural and educational rights: protects language, script and culture
Open to any section of citizens
For religious and linguistic minorities; 'minority' is not defined {PYQ 2022}

blocks.title: Laws and limits for Arts 23-26
items: Related laws for Art 23: Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976, Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act 1956 and Minimum Wages Act 1948.
Art 24 is backed by the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986; children may still help in safe work outside school hours.
The State may regulate secular activity linked to religion (Art 25).

blocks.title: Property protection: Arts 31, 31A, 31B, 31C
rows: Property as a Fundamental Right; removed by the 44th (1978), now Art 300A
1st Amendment 1951: land reform laws such as zamindari abolition cannot be attacked under Arts 14 and 19 {PYQ 2021}
1st Amendment 1951: laws in the Ninth Schedule are shielded from judicial review
25th Amendment 1971: laws to implement Art 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged under Arts 14 and 19; the second part barring court review was struck down in Kesavananda

blocks.title: Art 32: constitutional remedies
items: Art 32 is the right to constitutional remedies; Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. {PYQ 2025, 2026}

Art 32 has four clauses: right to approach the Court, power to issue directions and writs, Parliament may empower other courts, and the remedy cannot be suspended except as the Constitution allows (Arts 358-359).
Art 226 gives the High Court a writ power similar to Art 32. {PYQ 2024} {T2 2022}
The Supreme Court (Art 32) and the High Courts (Art 226) can issue five kinds of writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. {T2 2022}

blocks.title: The five writs
rows: To produce a detained person before the court and free them if detention is unlawful; the arrested person must be presented before the court {PYQ 2022}
To order a public authority to do its legal duty
To stop a lower court acting beyond its jurisdiction while the case is still pending {PYQ 2024}
To quash an order a lower court has already passed without jurisdiction
To ask a person by what right they hold a public office; stops illegal holding of office

blocks.title: Writs: against whom and how far
rows: Lawful detention or contempt orders; detention outside the court's jurisdiction
Private individuals, the President, Governors, or where the duty is optional
Judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, and administrative bodies since 1991
Holder of a substantive public office; any citizen can file

blocks.title: Supreme Court versus High Court on writs
rows: Writs only to enforce Fundamental Rights; Art 32 is itself a Fundamental Right
Writs for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose'
No, since Art 32 is itself a right
Yes, since it is a discretionary power
Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, so wider

blocks.title: Emergency and Arts 33-35
items: Arts 20 and 21 can never be suspended, even in a National Emergency, since the 44th Amendment.
Art 19 is suspended automatically when an Emergency is declared on grounds of war or external aggression (Art 358).
Art 33 (changed by the 50th Amendment, 1984) lets Parliament restrict the rights of armed forces, police and intelligence agencies.
Art 34 covers restrictions during martial law, an idea taken from Britain.
Art 35 gives Parliament the power to legislate to give effect to rights. Parliament alone can legislate under Arts 16(3), 17, 23, 32(3), 33 and 34.

chapters.h: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties (Parts IV and IVA)
chapters.intro: Directive Principles are the State's to-do list and Fundamental Duties are the citizen's to-do list; neither can be enforced in court. DPSPs came from Ireland, trace back to the Karachi Resolution of 1931, and were called a 'novel feature' by Ambedkar. SSC asks the article for each DPSP, the list of duties and what is not a duty every year.

items.title: Fundamental Rights
points: Justiciable: courts enforce them. {PYQ 2025}
Negative: they stop the State from acting.
Aim at political democracy.
Automatically enforceable; a court can strike down a law that violates them.
Oriented to the individual.

items.title: Directive Principles
points: Non-justiciable under Art 37, but fundamental in governance. {PYQ 2024, 2025}
Positive: they tell the State what to do.
Aim at social and economic democracy with moral and political sanction.
Need legislation; courts cannot strike down a law for ignoring them.
Oriented to society's welfare, not to individuals. {PYQ 2024}

blocks.title: DPSP basics
items: Directive Principles are in Part IV, Arts 36 to 51, and are non-justiciable. {PYQ 2023, 2024}
The Directive Principles carry the idea of a welfare state: they aim at social and economic democracy, while Fundamental Rights secure political democracy. {T2 2022}
The idea came from the Irish Constitution. {PYQ 2021, 2023, 2024}
Their origin can be traced to the Karachi Resolution of 1931. {PYQ 2023}
The 42nd Amendment added four DPSPs: 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A. {PYQ 2023, 2024}
Art 36 defines 'State' as in Art 12. Art 37 says DPSPs are not enforceable but are fundamental to governance, and the State must apply them when making laws.

items.note: Ambedkar compared them to the Instrument of Instructions of the 1935 Act. {PYQ 2023, 2024}

blocks.title: Directive Principles, Article by Article
rows: Secure a social order for the welfare of the people; 38(2), added by the 44th, asks it to reduce inequality in income, status, facilities and opportunities {PYQ 2024}
Give citizens an adequate means of livelihood
Distribute ownership and control of material resources to serve the common good {PYQ 2024}
Ensure equal pay for equal work
Provide equal justice and free legal aid (42nd)
Secure the right to work, education and public assistance in old age, sickness and disablement; basis for senior citizen policies {PYQ 2024}

Provide just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief. In K. Umadevi v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2022) the Supreme Court granted maternity benefit for a third child under the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017
Secure a living wage and promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas {PYQ 2024}
Organise village panchayats and give them powers to work as units of self-government {PYQ 2023, 2024}
Promote the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections {PYQ 2024}
Raise nutrition and public health, and prohibit intoxicating drinks and harmful drugs
Organise agriculture and animal husbandry, and ban slaughter of cows, calves and useful cattle
Provide early childhood care and education below 6 (recast by the 86th)
Protect the environment, forests and wildlife (42nd) {PYQ 2024}
Separate the judiciary from the executive {PYQ 2022, 2025}
Promote international peace and security, respect international law and settle disputes by arbitration

blocks.title: DPSPs added by the 42nd Amendment

lines.t: Equal justice and free legal aid

blocks.note: Later changes: the 44th added 38(2), the 86th recast Art 45, and the 97th added 43B.

blocks.title: Grouping is unofficial
blocks.body: The Constitution does not use the labels socialist, Gandhian or liberal. They are teaching devices, so an article can sit in two of them.

blocks.title: What critics called the Directive Principles

items.b: A manifesto of aims and aspirations
A cheque payable by the bank when it suits
Moral precepts for the authorities of the State
A novel feature, like the Instrument of Instructions of the 1935 Act {PYQ 2024}

items.what: Champakam Dorairajan: Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs, and rights can be amended. {T2 2024}
Golaknath: Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. {T2 2024}
24th Amendment restored Parliament's power to abridge rights, and an amendment is not 'law' under Art 13; the 25th inserted Art 31C. {PYQ 2021}
Kesavananda Bharati (13 judges): Parliament may amend rights but not the basic structure; the clause of 31C barring review fell. {PYQ 2022, 2025}
Minerva Mills: the Constitution rests on a balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs; that harmony is part of the basic structure.

blocks.title: Basic structure list
items: Elements often listed in the basic structure: separation of powers, unity and integrity of the nation, Fundamental Rights, judicial review, supremacy of the Constitution and the parliamentary system.

blocks.title: Fundamental Duties: the essentials
items: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Art 51A. {PYQ 2022, 2024}
They were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) under PM Indira Gandhi. {PYQ 2022, 2023}
The idea was taken from the USSR. {PYQ 2023}
The 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th duty, so there are 11 in all. {PYQ 2021, 2022}
They were kept out of Part III because Part III is justiciable. {PYQ 2023}
The Justice Verma Committee (1999) found legal provisions already enforcing some duties. {PYQ 2024}
Not duties: paying income tax, voting, respecting elders, mandatory national service of 5 years, prohibiting trade in rare species. {PYQ 2022, 2024}

items.note: The Committee proposed 8 duties; the Amendment inserted 10. {PYQ 2021, 2022, 2023}

blocks.title: The 11 Fundamental Duties of Art 51A
rows: Abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem; misusing the Flag breaks this duty {PYQ 2022, 2024}
Cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle
Uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India {PYQ 2022}
Defend the country and render national service when called
Promote harmony and brotherhood, and renounce practices derogatory to women {PYQ 2024}
Value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture {PYQ 2023}
Protect and improve the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures {PYQ 2024}
Develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform {PYQ 2023}
Safeguard public property and abjure violence {PYQ 2022, 2024}
Strive for excellence in all spheres
As a parent or guardian, provide education opportunities to a child aged 6-14 (86th, 2002) {PYQ 2022, 2024}

blocks.title: These are NOT Fundamental Duties
blocks.body: Paying income tax, voting, respecting elders, mandatory national service of 5 years and prohibiting trade in rare or endangered species are not duties in Art 51A. Only defending the country and rendering national service when called is.

blocks.title: Duties: background
items: The Swaran Singh Committee suggested 8 duties, with penalties for not following them, no court challenge to those penalties and a duty to pay taxes. These were not taken up, and the 42nd Amendment added 10 duties. {T2 2023}
H.R. Gokhale, then Law Minister, said the duties were meant to check anti-national activity seen before the 1975 Emergency.
The duties partly resemble the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
The Constitution Review Commission of 2002 (chaired by M.N. Venkatachaliah) urged effective implementation.

blocks.title: Laws that reflect a duty
rows: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971
Protection of Civil Rights Act (the 1955 untouchability law, renamed in 1976)
Wildlife Protection Act 1972; Forest Conservation Act 1980

blocks.title: Duties in one breath
blocks.body: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added 10 duties under Indira Gandhi on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice, borrowing the idea from the USSR; the 86th (2002) added the 11th. They bind only citizens and are not enforceable in court. {PYQ 2026}

chapters.h: Union Executive: President, Vice-President and Prime Minister (Arts 52-78)
chapters.intro: The President is the constitutional head in whose name the Union acts (Arts 52 and 53), but real power lies with the Council of Ministers led by the Prime Minister. Think of the President as the captain on paper and the Prime Minister as the one steering the ship. SSC asks each Article with its actor and its number: age, term, oath, majority.

items: Part V (Arts 52-78) is the Union Executive. Its full scope: Executive (52-78), Parliament (79-122), the President's legislative power (123), Union Judiciary (124-147) and CAG (148-151). {PYQ 2024}
Executive power of the Union is vested in the President and is exercised in that name. {PYQ 2022}
The President is the constitutional head; the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers actually run the government. {PYQ 2022}
Art 53 makes the President supreme commander of the armed forces.
Art 63: there shall be a Vice-President. The Vice-President's election also comes under Part V. {PYQ 2024}
Art 77: all executive action is taken in the President's name, and this Article covers the conduct of business of the Government of India. {PYQ 2024}
blocks.title: Part V and who really governs
Article walk for 52 to 62
blocks.body: Read Arts 52 to 62 as one story: President (52), executive power (53), election (54), manner (55), term (56), re-election (57), qualifications (58), conditions of office (59), oath (60), impeachment (61) and time to fill a vacancy (62).

blocks.title: President and Vice-President side by side

items.title: President
points: Elected by elected MPs and elected MLAs of all States, Delhi and Puducherry; nominated members and MLCs do not vote (Arts 54-55). {PYQ 2024}
Proportional representation by single transferable vote, secret ballot; 50 proposers, 50 seconders, Rs 15,000 security deposit. {PYQ 2025}
Age 35, qualified for the Lok Sabha, no office of profit (Art 58). {PYQ 2025, 2026}
Term 5 years (Art 56); re-election allowed any number of times (Art 57). {PYQ 2024}
Oath before the Chief Justice of India (Art 60); if the CJI is unavailable, the senior-most Supreme Court judge. {PYQ 2026}
Election disputes go only to the Supreme Court (Art 71).

items.title: Vice-President
points: Elected by all MPs, elected and nominated; MLAs and MLCs have no role (Art 66).
Age 35, qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha, not the Lok Sabha. {PYQ 2022}
Term 5 years (Art 67). {PYQ 2022}
Oath before the President (Art 69). {PYQ 2024}
Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Art 64) and acts as President in a vacancy (Art 65).

nodes: oath before Chief Justice of India (Art 60)

items.note: The VP oath is administered by the President. {PYQ 2024}

nodes: chairs NITI Aayog, Inter-State Council, National Disaster Management Authority
items.note: The ex-officio Chairman of NITI Aayog is the Prime Minister. {PYQ 2022}

blocks.title: How vote values are worked out
rows: State population (1971 census) divided by the number of elected MLAs, then divided by 1000
Total value of all MLA votes divided by the number of elected MPs
Valid votes polled divided by (vacancies plus 1), plus 1; for the single post of President this is just over half

items: Art 58: no office of profit, but the offices of President, Vice-President, PM, Governor and Ministers are exempt.
Art 59: no seat in Parliament or a State legislature (vacate on taking office); emoluments set by Parliament cannot be cut during the term.
Rent-free official residence is a right of the President, not a restriction on the office. {PYQ 2024}
A naturalised citizen can also hold the office.
The President may resign by writing to the Vice-President.
Immunity (Art 361): no criminal proceedings during the term; civil suits need two months' notice.
blocks.title: Conditions of the President's office (Arts 58-59, 361)
How a President is impeached (Art 61)
steps: The only ground is 'violation of the Constitution' (Art 61).
Notice of 14 days, signed by one-fourth of the members of the House that starts it; either House may start.
That House passes it by two-thirds of its total membership.
The other House investigates and also passes it by two-thirds of total membership.
The President stands removed; elected and nominated MPs vote, MLAs do not (the idea is borrowed from the USA).
A vacancy must be filled within 6 months (Art 62).

items: Art 71(1): every dispute about the election of the President or Vice-President goes only to the Supreme Court, and its decision is final.
Art 71(2): if the election is declared void, acts already done by the person in office remain valid.
Art 71(3): Parliament regulates these elections by law. Art 71(4): an election cannot be challenged merely because the electoral college was incomplete (for example, vacancies).
blocks.title: Election disputes (Art 71)

items: Art 62: election within 6 months of a vacancy from death, resignation or removal, and before expiry if the term ends normally.

Meanwhile the Vice-President acts as President (Art 65), then the Chief Justice, then the senior-most Supreme Court judge, under the Presidents (Discharge of Functions) Act 1969. Art 70 lets Parliament arrange other contingencies.
Presidents who died in office: Zakir Husain (the first) and Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed. The only Vice-President to die in office was Krishan Kant.
Justice M. Hidayatullah acted as President in 1969, the case that made the CJI-as-acting-President rule real.
blocks.title: Vacancies and acting President

nodes: Giri resigns to contest the election
Chief Justice M. Hidayatullah acts (20 July to 24 August 1969)
items.note: Giri was later elected President and served 1969-74.

blocks.title: President's powers
rows: Art 72: pardon, commutation, remission, respite and reprieve, including death sentences and court-martial {PYQ 2023, 2025}
Art 123: only when Parliament is not in session; lapses unless approved within 6 weeks of reassembly {PYQ 2024}
Art 143: the President may seek its advisory opinion, which is not binding {PYQ 2022}
Art 124(2): appoints Supreme Court judges; also appoints High Court judges and transfers them between High Courts {PYQ 2023, 2024}
Absolute, suspensive and pocket veto (Zail Singh, Indian Post Office Bill 1986); no qualified veto; a Money Bill cannot be returned {PYQ 2026}
Art 74: binding since the 42nd Amendment; the 44th lets the President return it once for reconsideration

items: Art 72 gives five forms of clemency: pardon (wipes out sentence and conviction), commutation (changes the type of punishment), remission (reduces the length), respite (lesser sentence for a special reason such as pregnancy) and reprieve (temporary stay of execution). {PYQ 2025}
The Governor has a parallel pardoning power under Art 161, but it does not cover a death sentence or court-martial. {PYQ 2025}

Maru Ram v Union of India (1980): the pardon power under Art 72 and Art 161 must be used on the advice of the Council of Ministers and is open to limited judicial review for malafide, arbitrariness or irrelevant considerations.
Kehar Singh v Union of India (1989): the courts can review the exercise of the power only on narrow grounds such as arbitrariness or discrimination.
blocks.title: Pardon power and the courts

items: Art 75: the President appoints the Prime Minister, and other ministers on the PM's advice. {PYQ 2024}
Art 75(3): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, not to any Upper House. {PYQ 2025}
Art 75(5): a non-member minister must enter Parliament within 6 months.
The 91st Amendment (2003) caps the Council of Ministers at 15% of the Lok Sabha's strength. Art 75(1B): a member disqualified for defection cannot be made a minister. {PYQ 2022}

Art 75(2): ministers hold office during the President's pleasure. Art 75(4): the President administers the oaths of office and secrecy. Art 75(6): salaries fixed by Parliament, and until then as in the Second Schedule.
Art 74(2): a court cannot inquire into what advice, if any, the ministers gave the President.
Art 77: all executive action is expressed in the President's name, and the President makes the rules for business and allocation of work among ministers. {PYQ 2024}

Art 78(a) to (c): the PM must pass on all decisions of the Council on administration and proposed legislation, give any information the President asks for, and place before the Council a decision taken by one minister if the President wants it considered.
blocks.title: Council of Ministers: Arts 74 to 78
Types of Ministers (not defined in the Constitution)
rows: Heads a major ministry such as Defence, Home, Finance; attends Cabinet meetings
Runs a smaller ministry alone; does not attend Cabinet unless invited
Assists a Cabinet Minister as attached to a ministry
Assists Cabinet Ministers and Ministers of State

items: The real executive power sits with the Council of Ministers with the PM as its head. {PYQ 2022}
The PM runs the government at the national level together with the Council of Ministers. {PYQ 2022}
The PM chairs the NITI Aayog (as ex-officio Chairman), the Inter-State Council and the National Disaster Management Authority. {PYQ 2022}
If the PM dies or resigns, the whole Council falls and the President invites the leader who commands a Lok Sabha majority. If any other minister goes, only that post falls vacant.

PM's functions: advises the President on summoning, proroguing and dissolving the Lok Sabha; announces policy in the House; recommends ministers; allocates and reshuffles portfolios; can ask a minister to resign; presides over the Council and coordinates ministries.
Nehru called the PM the linchpin of government, since the PM links the Council with the President under Art 78. Ambedkar said collective responsibility works only through the PM.
blocks.title: Prime Minister: role and chairs
Prime Ministers: records and trivia
rows: Acting PM twice, 13 days each time; the shortest tenure {PYQ 2024}
Shortest tenure among Chandra Shekhar (7 months), V.P. Singh (11 months), Deve Gowda (10 months) and Gujral (11 months) {PYQ 2023}
Never faced Parliament as PM; 170 days
First government lasted only 13 days in 1996, the shortest government
First PM to resign (1979); oldest PM at appointment
Indira Gandhi, Deve Gowda, I.K. Gujral, Manmohan Singh
Rajya Sabha members who became PM; Deve Gowda had never held a Union Cabinet post
Began a third straight term in June 2024

blocks.title: Presidents of India with terms
rows: Elected by the Assembly on 24 January 1950 and sworn in on 26 January 1950; longest serving, two full terms
First Muslim President; first to die in office; shortest tenure of an elected President
First acting President to be elected later
Died in office; proclaimed the 1975 Emergency
First Sikh President; pocket veto on the Post Office Bill 1986
Earlier Union Finance Minister and Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission {PYQ 2022}
15th President; first tribal and second woman President

items: Radhakrishnan and Hamid Ansari each served two full terms; Ansari was the longest-serving VP and served under three different Presidents.
Radhakrishnan, Zakir Husain, V.V. Giri, R. Venkataraman, Shankar Dayal Sharma and K.R. Narayanan all moved from the Vice-Presidency to the Presidency.
blocks.title: Vice-Presidents worth knowing

items: Nominations: 20 proposers and 20 seconders, all MPs; security deposit Rs 15,000; single transferable vote by secret ballot (Art 66).
MLAs and members of State Legislative Councils take no part in the Vice-President's election.

Removal (Art 67b): a resolution can start only in the Rajya Sabha, with 14 days' notice; it needs a majority of the total membership of the Rajya Sabha and simple-majority agreement of the Lok Sabha. The Constitution names no ground. The President has no part in removing the VP. {PYQ 2022}
A Vice-President who resigns writes to the President, and continues in office until a successor takes charge.
Art 68: an election due to term expiry must be finished before the term ends; a vacancy from death, resignation or removal is filled as soon as possible (no 6 month rule, unlike the President).
The VP must be qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha but cannot hold a seat in either House of Parliament or in a State Legislature.
blocks.title: Vice-President: election and removal

items: Attorney General (Art 76): appointed by the President, must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge, holds office at the President's pleasure, and may speak but not vote in either House (Art 88). Not a full-time government counsel, so may practise privately. M.C. Setalvad was the first; R. Venkataramani is the present AG.

Solicitor General: the second law officer, assists the AG, and is a statutory rather than constitutional post. Appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (chaired by the PM), not directly by the President; Tushar Mehta holds the post at present. {PYQ 2025}
Advocate General (Art 165): appointed by the Governor, must be qualified for High Court judgeship, advises the State Government and holds office at the Governor's pleasure. {T2 2022}
blocks.title: Law officers compared

items: Art 244(1): the President declares Scheduled Areas.
Art 143 lets the President ask the Supreme Court for advice; a High Court gives no such advisory opinion to the President.
blocks.title: Other Articles to note

chapters.intro: Parliament is the President plus the Rajya Sabha plus the Lok Sabha (Art 79); bicameralism at the Centre first came with the GoI Act 1919. The Lok Sabha controls money and the government, while the Rajya Sabha is permanent and speaks for the States. Most questions test numbers, the Money Bill rules and the names of devices.

items: Parliament is the President plus the Rajya Sabha plus the Lok Sabha (Art 79), the national legislature and the legislative organ of the Union. {PYQ 2022, 2024}
Art 79 provides for a bicameral Parliament, and Arts 79-122 deal with Parliament and its proceedings. {PYQ 2023, 2024}
The bicameral idea comes from the British Constitution; bicameralism at the Centre first came with the GoI Act 1919. {PYQ 2021}
A bill becomes an Act when both Houses pass it and the President assents. {PYQ 2021}
blocks.title: Parliament in the Constitution

items.title: Rajya Sabha (Art 80)
points: Art 80 gives the composition; the Fourth Schedule allocates seats to States and UTs. {PYQ 2024}
Maximum 250: 238 elected by State and UT legislatures plus 12 nominated for literature, science, art and social service; present strength 245 (233 elected plus 12 nominated). {PYQ 2024}
Nominees need special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art or social service; eloquence is not a condition. {PYQ 2022}
Permanent House, not open to dissolution: members serve 6 years and one-third retire every second year (Art 83). {PYQ 2025}
Minimum age 30 (Art 84); elected indirectly by single transferable vote; seats follow population, so representation is unequal.
Constituted on 3 April 1952 and first sat on 13 May 1952.

items.title: Lok Sabha (Art 81)
points: Maximum 550 elected: 530 from States and 20 from UTs; present 543 constituencies. {PYQ 2022}
Anglo-Indian nomination (Art 331) ended with the 104th Amendment in January 2020. {PYQ 2025}
Term 5 years, extendable one year at a time in a National Emergency; minimum age 25 (Art 84).
The 106th Amendment (2023) reserves one-third of seats for women after the first delimitation following the next census.
Constituted 17 April 1952 and first sat on 13 May 1952.

blocks.title: Where the Parliament features came from

items: Hindi names Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha were adopted in 1954.
The new Parliament building (2023) uses the peacock for the Lok Sabha and the lotus for the Rajya Sabha as themes. The Lok Sabha has a green carpet and the Rajya Sabha a red one.
The 12th Lok Sabha had the shortest life, 13 months 4 days (10 March 1998 to 26 April 1999).

The Lok Sabha can be dissolved by the President on the advice of the PM. Its term was raised to 6 years by the 42nd Amendment and restored to 5 by the 44th. Elections must be held within 6 months of an Emergency ending.
Delimitation redraws constituencies according to population after a Census (Art 82). Commissions were set up four times: 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002.

The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze seat allocation on the 1971 Census until 2000; the 84th (2001) extended the freeze until the first Census after 2026; the 87th (2003) allowed delimitation on the 2001 Census figures.
Art 84: a candidate for the Rajya Sabha from a State need not be an elector in that State (dispensed with in 2003).
blocks.title: Life of the Houses and delimitation
State-wise seats (Rajya Sabha / Lok Sabha / Assembly)
Union Territories: seats
rows: Andaman and Nicobar, Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Ladakh
Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu

blocks.title: Only three UTs have Assemblies
blocks.body: Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir. The State rows add up to 233 Rajya Sabha seats plus 12 nominated for the present strength of 245, and the Lok Sabha total of 543.

blocks.title: Sessions and their endings
