rows: Budget (Feb to April/May), Monsoon (July to Aug/Sept), Winter (Nov/Dec); gap between sittings never above 6 months (Art 85)
Temporary break inside a sitting or session
Ends the sitting without fixing a return date; usually just before prorogation
Ends the life of the Lok Sabha (Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved)
President, on the advice of the PM

blocks.title: Presiding officers of Parliament
rows: The Vice-President, ex-officio, not a member of the House
Elected by the Rajya Sabha from its members; removed by effective majority (majority of total members less vacancies); resigns to the Chairman
Named by the Chairman to preside when both are absent (a rule, not in the Constitution)

Elected by the Lok Sabha by simple majority; date fixed by the President (for the Deputy Speaker's election, by the Speaker); ex-officio head of the Indian Parliamentary Group, which was set up in 1949 {PYQ 2022}
Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker and vice versa; removal by effective majority after 14 days' notice; Speaker stays in office until the new House meets even after dissolution
Cannot preside but can speak and vote in the first instance; no casting vote
Chairman or Speaker votes only to break a tie
When Speaker and Deputy are absent, a member of this panel presides
Fixed by Parliament and charged on the Consolidated Fund
Each House has its own; staff regulated by Parliament in consultation with the presiding officer
Senior-most member appointed by the President to swear in new members until the House elects its Speaker

items: The Deputy Speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker. No Deputy Speaker has been elected since 2019.
The Speaker chairs the Business Advisory Committee, the Rules Committee and the General Purposes Committee. Whenever the Deputy Speaker is a member of a committee, he becomes its chairman.
Firsts: G.V. Mavalankar first Speaker; M.A. Ayyangar first Deputy Speaker; Balram Jakhar longest-serving Speaker; G.M.C. Balayogi first to die in office; Meira Kumar first woman Speaker.
Om Birla is Speaker of the 18th Lok Sabha, re-elected in June 2024.

The President appoints the Pro tem Speaker and administers the oath to him or her; the Pro tem Speaker then swears in the newly elected members and presides until the House elects its Speaker. {PYQ 2026}
The Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act was passed in 1977.
blocks.title: Speakers: rules and firsts

nodes: chaired the Constituent Assembly's Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly
items.note: He was Chairman of that Committee. {PYQ 2021}

blocks.title: Rules and devices
rows: The gap between two sessions cannot exceed 6 months
The President gives a special address at the first session
Quorum is one-tenth of total members; the presiding officer has a casting vote {PYQ 2022}
Privileges; business in Hindi or English (Art 120); courts cannot question proceedings (Art 122). {PYQ 2022}

First hour of a sitting: starred questions get oral answers with supplementaries, unstarred get written answers. Ordinary questions need at least 10 clear days' notice; a short notice question is asked with less notice than that
Indian innovation of 1962, not in the rules; follows Question Hour
Lok Sabha only, 50 members, not in the Constitution; needs no reasons; if passed the ministry resigns {PYQ 2021}
Calling attention, half-an-hour discussion, short-duration discussion, censure motion; 'full-day discussion' is not a device {PYQ 2024}
Policy cut (Re 1), economy cut, token cut (Rs 100)

items.title: Censure motion
points: Must state reasons
Can be moved against an individual minister, a group or the whole Council
Aimed at particular policies or actions
If passed, no resignation is required

items.title: No-confidence motion
points: No reasons need be given {PYQ 2021}
Can be moved only against the whole Council
Tests whether the Lok Sabha still backs the ministry
If passed, the ministry must resign

items: Daily routine: Question Hour 11 am to 12 noon, then Zero Hour.
Closure motion: moved to cut short debate on a matter. Calling attention: draws a minister's notice to an urgent public matter. Point of order: raised when rules are broken and is not debated.
Private members (those who are not ministers) can also ask questions and bring bills.

Art 86: the President may address either House or both together and send messages about pending bills. Art 87: special address at the first session after each general election and the first of each year, followed by the Motion of Thanks.
Art 88: ministers and the Attorney General can speak in either House but vote only in their own; the AG belongs to neither.
Art 118: each House makes its own rules of procedure. Art 121: no debate on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge, except an impeachment motion.
Art 120: English use was to end after 15 years unless Parliament decides otherwise; the presiding officer may allow a member to speak in the mother tongue.
Delegated legislation is made by executive authorities under a parent Act, and courts can strike it down if it exceeds that Act.
blocks.title: Devices and small Articles 86 to 121
Disqualification and seats (Arts 101 to 104)
rows: No dual membership of both Houses, or of Parliament and a State Legislature; a member resigns to the Speaker or Chairman; the House may declare a seat vacant if the member is absent for 60 days without leave
Disqualified for: office of profit, unsound mind declared by a court, undischarged insolvent, not a citizen or voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship

Defection: voting against the party whip or abstaining without permission (not condoned within 15 days), voluntarily giving up party membership, an independent joining a party, or a nominated member joining a party after 6 months
President decides disqualification questions after obtaining the Election Commission's opinion; for defection the presiding officer decides
Sitting or voting while disqualified, or before oath: fine of Rs 500 per day
Courts can review the Speaker's decision on defection

items: Under the Representation of the People Act 1951, a conviction with imprisonment of two years or more disqualifies a member.
Merger exception: the 91st Amendment protects members only when two-thirds of a legislature party merges with another party; the earlier one-third split rule was removed.
blocks.title: Disqualification: other points

items: Art 105: freedom of speech in Parliament; no member is liable in court for a speech or vote; proceedings cannot be questioned.
Members are free from civil arrest during a session and for 40 days before and after; this does not protect against criminal arrest or preventive detention.
Presidential immunity from criminal proceedings comes from Art 361, not Art 105.
Art 106: salaries and allowances of members are fixed by Parliament by law.
blocks.title: Privileges (Art 105)

items: Bill types: ordinary, money, financial and constitution amendment.
Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill, but not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill. {PYQ 2025}
A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, with the President's recommendation. {PYQ 2022} {T2 2022}

Only taxes, borrowing, the Consolidated Fund and related matters can be in it (Art 110); a bill that imposes a new tax is a Money Bill. A bill is not a Money Bill merely because it imposes fines or fees, or deals with taxes levied by local bodies.
The Lok Sabha Speaker decides whether a bill is a Money Bill, and the decision is final, though open to limited judicial review (Puttaswamy, the Aadhaar case, 2018). {PYQ 2025}

After it passes the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days (Art 109); it cannot reject or amend it, and the same holds for Legislative Councils in States. {PYQ 2021, 2025}
The President can assent or withhold but cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
blocks.title: Money Bill: the full path
The State trap
blocks.body: In a State, a Money Bill needs the Governor's prior recommendation and the Legislative Council also gets only 14 days. There is no joint sitting on a Money Bill or a Constitution Amendment Bill.

items: In a State Assembly, a Money Bill can be introduced only with the prior permission of the Governor. {PYQ 2024}
Art 117: a Financial Bill starts only in the Lok Sabha with the President's recommendation; otherwise it follows ordinary bill procedure.
blocks.title: Money Bills in the States

items: Art 107: any bill except a Money Bill may start in either House. A bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses at dissolution; a bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha also lapses; a bill pending only in the Rajya Sabha does not lapse.
Adjournment or prorogation does not make a pending bill lapse.

Art 108 deadlock arises when the other House rejects a bill, disagrees finally on amendments, or holds it more than 6 months. The joint sitting is chaired by the Speaker, then the Deputy Speaker, then the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The bill passes by a simple majority of members present and voting; Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills are excluded.
The Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is final but is open to limited judicial review (Puttaswamy, the Aadhaar case, 2018).
A bill is not a Money Bill merely because it imposes fines or fees, or deals with taxes levied by local bodies.
blocks.title: Bills: what lapses and what a deadlock is
Vetoes of the President (Art 111)
rows: President withholds assent and the bill dies
Rajendra Prasad, PEPSU Appropriation Bill 1954; R. Venkataraman, MPs' salary bill 1991
Bill returned once; if passed again, assent is compulsory; not for Money Bills
No time limit for action, so the bill is left pending
Zail Singh, Indian Post Office Bill 1986

items: The Indian pocket veto is deeper than the American one, because the Constitution fixes no time limit for the President. The US President must act within 10 days.
No veto exists against a Constitution Amendment Bill (24th Amendment, 1971).
The word Budget is not in the Constitution; Art 112 calls it the Annual Financial Statement.
The Railway Budget was separated from the General Budget in 1924 on the Acworth Committee's advice, and merged again in 2017 when Arun Jaitley presented the first combined Union Budget.
blocks.title: Veto and Budget trivia
Funds of India
rows: All revenues, loans raised and repayments received; largest fund; nothing can be withdrawn without an Appropriation Act
Money held as banker or trustee: provident funds, small savings, deposits; no parliamentary approval needed to withdraw
For urgent unforeseen spending; held by the President and operated by the Finance Secretary; Parliament approves after the event

blocks.title: Budget grants and motions
rows: Only the Lok Sabha votes; the Rajya Sabha can only discuss; presented on the President's recommendation
Authorises withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund after grants are voted; no amendment can change the amount
Sanctioned amount is found too small
For a new service not planned in the budget
Money already spent beyond what was granted
Advance permission to spend on essential items until the full budget passes; concerns spending only
Lump sum for a large, uncertain need whose details cannot be given; a blank cheque to the executive
For a special purpose not part of the regular budget

items: Arts 112-117 budget: 112 Annual Financial Statement, 113 demands for grants, 114 Appropriation Bill, 116 vote on account, 117 financial bills.
Charged expenditure is not voted: salaries of the President, judges and CAG, and pensions of Supreme Court staff (Art 146), which are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. {PYQ 2023}
Stages of a budget: presentation, general discussion, scrutiny by departmental committees, voting on demands for grants, Appropriation Bill, then Finance Bill.
blocks.title: Budget stages and charged items

items: Art 123: an ordinance has the same force as an Act; the President's ordinance power is the most important legislative power of the President. It must be laid before both Houses and lapses at 6 weeks from reassembly unless approved. Its maximum life is therefore about 6 months and 6 weeks. {PYQ 2024}
The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time.

R.C. Cooper v Union of India (1970): the President's satisfaction can be questioned in court on grounds of malafide. D.C. Wadhwa v State of Bihar (1986): repeated re-promulgation of ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution.
An ordinance cannot deal with a subject outside Parliament's legislative power. The Governor's parallel power is Art 213.
The Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 was amended by the 2020 ordinance. {PYQ 2024}
blocks.title: Ordinances (Art 123)
Parliamentary committees
rows: Examines CAG audit reports; CAG is its guide and friend
Roots in 1921; present form 1950 on John Mathai's advice
Chairman from Lok Sabha; examines reports of public enterprises

items: A minister cannot be a member of the Public Accounts Committee. {PYQ 2023}
The three financial committees are elected each year by proportional representation and single transferable vote; members serve one year; a minister cannot be a member.
Committees are of two kinds: standing (permanent) and ad hoc (temporary). The Constitution mentions them without laying down their term or functions; the House rules do.
The Public Accounts Committee has 22 members (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha), has been chaired by an opposition member since 1967, and no minister can be a member.

The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, is elected, and is the largest committee; the Committee on Public Undertakings has 22, and there are 24 Department-Related Standing Committees.
The Estimates Committee was first set up in 1950 on the recommendation of Finance Minister John Mathai; it traces its roots to the Standing Financial Committee of 1921. {T2 2022}
blocks.title: Committee features

chapters.h: Judiciary: Supreme Court and High Courts
chapters.intro: India has one integrated and independent judiciary: the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the States and subordinate courts below. The Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950, replacing the Federal Court of 1937. SSC swaps Article numbers, judge counts and retirement ages in options, so learn the Article tables and the removal and collegium steps.

blocks.title: Supreme Court at a glance
items: India has one integrated, independent judiciary, an idea borrowed from the USA: Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the States, subordinate courts below. The independence of the judiciary is a US feature.
The Supreme Court took over from the Federal Court (set up in 1937 under the 1935 Act) and from the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. It was inaugurated and first sat on 28 January 1950.
Originally it had the Chief Justice and 7 judges (8 in all). Strength is now the CJI plus 33 judges under the 2019 Act. {PYQ 2024}
In August 2026 Parliament passed a Bill raising the sanctioned strength from 34 to 38 including the CJI.
Its seat is Delhi (Art 130). A bench of five or more judges is a Constitution Bench.
The High Court and Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Amendment Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 30 November 2021. {PYQ 2024}
Judicial review means courts can test the validity of legislative and executive action against the Constitution. {PYQ 2023}

blocks.title: Supreme Court Articles in order
rows: Writs to enforce Fundamental Rights; Art 226 gives the High Courts a similar writ power {PYQ 2024}

Establishment; 124(2) President appoints the judges; 124(4) removal; 124(2A) Parliament decides how a judge's age is determined (15th Amendment); 124(7) a retired judge cannot practise before any court in India {PYQ 2024, 2026}
Salaries and allowances are fixed by Parliament
President appoints an acting Chief Justice when the post is vacant or the CJI cannot act
Ad hoc judges (a High Court judge borrowed with the President's consent when a quorum is missing) / retired judges may be asked to sit
Seat is Delhi; it can sit elsewhere if the CJI recommends and the President approves
Original and exclusive jurisdiction: Centre vs States and State vs State (not given to High Courts); Parliament can take water disputes out under Art 262 {PYQ 2022, 2025}
Appellate jurisdiction (133 civil and 134 criminal appeals from High Courts) and special leave to appeal; Art 136 does not cover armed forces tribunals or court-martial
It can use the Federal Court's powers under pre-Constitution law
Review of its own judgments and orders {PYQ 2023}
Parliament can enlarge its jurisdiction and confer ancillary powers {PYQ 2023}
Parliament can let it issue writs for purposes other than Fundamental Rights
Transfer of cases between High Courts or to itself (42nd Amendment) {PYQ 2025}
Its law binds all courts; power to do complete justice

All authorities must aid it; it makes its own rules with the President's approval; the CJI appoints its staff; its expenses and staff pensions are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India; Art 147 explains how to read the Constitution alongside the 1935 and 1947 Acts {PYQ 2023}
Parliament may set up additional courts for better administration of Union laws {PYQ 2023}

blocks.title: Judges cases and the collegium
rows: The CJI's recommendation was not binding on the President, so the executive had the upper hand
'Consultation' was read as concurrence; the CJI plus two senior-most judges decide and their advice binds the President. The collegium was born
Collegium enlarged to the CJI plus four senior-most judges; its recommendation binds the President
Fourth Judges case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association, 2015)
99th Amendment (2014) and the NJAC Act struck down; collegium system restored

blocks.title: Appointment, qualification and retirement
items: Judges are appointed by the President under the collegium system; the President also transfers judges from one High Court to another. {PYQ 2023}
Supreme Court qualifications: 5 years as a High Court judge, or 10 years as a High Court advocate, or a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion. No minimum age is prescribed. {T2 2024}
Supreme Court judges retire at 65.
Art 131A (added by the 42nd) gave the Supreme Court exclusive power over the validity of central laws, and the 43rd Amendment (1977) repealed it.

blocks.title: Removing a judge
steps: Grounds: only proved misbehaviour or incapacity (Art 124(4)).
A motion needs the signatures of 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members before the inquiry begins.
Inquiry under the Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968.
Each House passes an address by a special majority: majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting.
The President orders removal.

items: A Supreme Court judge can be removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. {PYQ 2022}

Justice V. Ramaswami was the first judge against whom removal proceedings were started (motion admitted 1991, voted in Parliament in May 1993); proceedings were also started against Justice Soumitra Sen (2011).
blocks.title: Removal in practice
Special powers and remedies
items: Art 143: on a pre-Constitution treaty dispute the Court must answer the President; on other questions of public importance it may decline. Either way the opinion does not bind the President.

Art 142 has been used for 'complete justice'. Judicial activism examples: Union Carbide (1989), Vishaka (1997) and the Ayodhya verdict (2019). The phrase 'judicial activism' is credited to the American historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr.
A curative petition is the last remedy after a review is dismissed; it began with Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002).
The Supreme Court's FASTER system (2021) sends orders electronically to prisons. {PYQ 2023}

items.note: Learn this as the top case. {PYQ 2022}

nodes: Executive upper hand; also began the loosening of locus standi
Collegium of CJI plus four senior-most judges
Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer
Guidelines on sexual harassment at work

blocks.title: Firsts and office holders
items: H.J. Kania was the first Chief Justice; Y.V. Chandrachud served the longest and K.N. Singh the shortest.
Fatima Beevi (1989) was the first woman Supreme Court judge.
B.R. Gavai was the 52nd CJI, earlier a Bombay High Court judge. Surya Kant is the 53rd CJI since 24 November 2025 and retires on 9 February 2027.
B.V. Nagarathna is next in line to be the first woman CJI (expected September 2027).
Justice Anna Chandy was the first woman High Court judge (Kerala) and Justice Leila Seth the first woman High Court Chief Justice (Himachal Pradesh).

items.title: Supreme Court
points: Judges retire at 65.
Gives advisory opinions to the President (Art 143). {PYQ 2026}
Original jurisdiction in federal disputes (Art 131). {PYQ 2026}
Writs only for Fundamental Rights under Art 32.

items.title: High Courts (Arts 214-231)
points: Arts 214 to 231 in Part VI deal with High Courts. {PYQ 2024}
Judges are appointed under Art 217 and retire at 62 (the 15th Amendment of 1963 raised it from 60).
They never give advisory opinions to the President. {PYQ 2022}
Art 226 gives wider writs and Art 227 superintendence over lower courts.
Under Art 222 the President transfers judges after consulting the CJI, and Art 231 allows a common High Court for two or more States.

blocks.title: High Court Articles
rows: Every High Court is a court of record; it has a Chief Justice and other judges as the President decides
Judges are appointed by the President after consulting the CJI, the Governor and the High Court's Chief Justice
Qualification: 10 years as a High Court advocate or 10 years in judicial office; there is no 'distinguished jurist' route
If a judge's age is in doubt, the President decides after consulting the CJI (15th Amendment)
The Supreme Court removal procedure applies to High Court judges too
Oath is taken before the Governor; a former High Court judge cannot practise except in the Supreme Court and other High Courts
Salary is paid from the State's Consolidated Fund, but pension comes from the Consolidated Fund of India
President transfers judges from one High Court to another after consulting the CJI {PYQ 2023}
Acting Chief Justice; additional judges for up to 2 years when arrears pile up, and acting judges; retired judges may be asked to sit
Jurisdiction: original (revenue and election petitions of MPs and MLAs), appellate and writ
A High Court can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other legal right, and may refuse; it also supervises all subordinate courts {PYQ 2024}
The Chief Justice appoints the court's officers and staff
230: Parliament can extend a High Court to a Union Territory; 231: common High Court; 232 on Federal Court cases was repealed by the 7th Amendment

blocks.title: High Courts: number, seats and history
items: India has 25 High Courts, the latest being Andhra Pradesh's separate High Court (Amaravati) from 1 January 2019. {PYQ 2024}

Art 214 is the Article that establishes High Courts: it says there shall be a High Court for each State. Art 216 then deals with their composition and Art 231 with a common High Court for two or more States. {PYQ 2026}
Calcutta (1862) is the oldest, with Bombay and Madras also set up in 1862.
Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura got their High Courts in 2013.
The Delhi High Court had jurisdiction over Himachal Pradesh until 1971. {PYQ 2023}
Common High Courts (Art 231): Maharashtra and Goa (Mumbai) and Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (Guwahati).

Seats: Allahabad HC at Prayagraj (bench at Lucknow); Kerala at Ernakulam; Gujarat at Ahmedabad; Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur; Rajasthan at Jodhpur; Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur; Uttarakhand at Nainital; Odisha at Cuttack.

blocks.title: Union Territories and their High Courts (Art 230)
rows: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu

blocks.title: Subordinate courts
items: Art 233: the Governor appoints district judges after consulting the High Court; an outsider needs 7 years as an advocate or pleader. Art 233A (20th Amendment, 1966) validated earlier irregular appointments.
Art 234: other judicial service posts are filled by the Governor after consulting the State PSC and High Court.
Art 235 gives the High Court control over subordinate courts; Arts 233-237 cover subordinate courts. A death sentence from a Sessions Judge must be confirmed by the High Court. {PYQ 2026}
Art 241 lets Parliament create a High Court for a Union Territory.

blocks.title: Other courts and remedies
rows: Family Courts Act 1984; for marriage and family disputes, with settlement first; meant for cities above 10 lakh people; appeals go to the High Court before a bench of at least two judges
Handle small money, rent and contract claims under the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act 1887; orders are final but open to High Court revision

Legal Services Authorities Act 1987, functioning from 9 November 1995; settles pending or pre-litigation disputes; no court fee, and any fee already paid is refunded; the award is treated as a civil court decree, is binding and cannot be appealed; divorce and non-compoundable offences are excluded; the Permanent Lok Adalat handles public utility cases up to Rs 1 crore
Civil Judge (Junior Division), the lowest civil court for small-value cases
Passed in 1971 to define and limit the powers of courts in punishing contempt {PYQ 2021}
Resolving disputes outside court using digital tools and ADR methods such as negotiation, mediation and arbitration {PYQ 2024}

items.title: Public Interest Litigation
points: The concept of PIL originated in the USA. {PYQ 2024}
Started in India in the 1980s by Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer.
It relaxes locus standi, the right to approach a court, so a public-spirited person can sue for the poor even if not personally affected.
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) began this loosening.
Can be filed in the Supreme Court (Art 32) or a High Court (Art 226).

items.title: Tribunals (Part XIVA)
points: Added by the 42nd Amendment (1976); quasi-judicial bodies.
Art 323A: Parliament can set up administrative tribunals for recruitment and service disputes of public servants.
Art 323B: Parliament or State legislatures can set up tribunals for tax, foreign exchange, labour, land reform, elections and rent.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997): tribunal decisions remain open to High Court review; tribunals do not replace High Courts.

blocks.title: Landmark cases in order
rows: Early narrow readings of liberty and the amending power
Preamble not part of the Constitution
Golaknath held Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights
Free and fair elections as basic structure
Balance of FRs and DPSPs is basic structure
Maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman
50% cap on reservation and creamy layer
Guidelines against sexual harassment at work
Art 370 case Dec 2023, Electoral bonds Feb 2024
State of Kerala v. Leesamma Joseph (28 June 2021)
Persons with disabilities have a right to reservation in promotion under Art 16(4) {PYQ 2023}
Laxmibai Chandaragi v. State of Karnataka (2021)
Consent of family is not needed once two adults decide to marry {PYQ 2023}

blocks.title: Numbers SSC swaps
blocks.body: Supreme Court judges retire at 65 but High Court judges at 62. Only the Supreme Court gives advisory opinions (Art 143); a High Court never does. Original jurisdiction under Art 131 belongs to the Supreme Court, not the High Courts. Art 217 has no distinguished jurist route, but Art 124 does.

blocks.title: Small facts
items: Maharashtra ranked first among 18 large and mid-sized States in justice delivery in the second India Justice Report. {PYQ 2023}

chapters.intro: Each State copies the Union's design on a smaller scale: the Governor mirrors the President, the Chief Minister the Prime Minister and the Legislature Parliament. SSC asks where the State version differs, such as the Governor's oath and narrower pardon power, plus State Article numbers, Legislative Councils and special-status areas.

items.title: President (Union)
points: Elected by an electoral college.
Oath before the Chief Justice of India.
Art 72 pardon covers death sentences and court-martial.
Ordinances under Art 123.

items.title: Governor (State)
points: Appointed by the President (Art 155) and holds office at the President's pleasure (Art 156); term 5 years; minimum age 35 (Art 157).
Oath before the Chief Justice of the High Court (Art 159). {PYQ 2023}
Art 161 pardon cannot pardon a death sentence or touch court-martial. {PYQ 2025}
Ordinances under Art 213; assent, withhold or reserve bills for the President under Art 200; discretion under Art 163.
Nominates members to the Legislative Council (Art 171).

blocks.title: State executive Articles
rows: Defines 'State' for Part VI; originally it excluded Jammu and Kashmir {PYQ 2023}
One Governor per State, though one person can serve two or more States (7th Amendment); the State's executive power is vested in the Governor {PYQ 2023}
President appoints the Governor; he holds office at the President's pleasure. 156(2): he resigns by writing to the President

Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or of a legislature of a First Schedule State; he gets a rent-free official residence and his emoluments cannot be lowered during his term; if he serves several States they are shared as the President orders {PYQ 2024}
Oath before the Chief Justice of the High Court
President can make arrangements for the Governor's functions in unforeseen situations
Governor's pardoning power, narrower than the President's {PYQ 2025}
Advice of ministers is not strictly binding in areas of the Governor's discretion, and his decision on whether a matter is in his discretion is final

Governor appoints the CM and appoints other ministers on the CM's advice; a minister who is not a member of the Legislature for 6 consecutive months ceases to be a minister. Council of ministers is responsible only to the Legislative Assembly, not the Council; size at least 12 and at most 15% of the Assembly (91st) {PYQ 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025}
Advocate General, the highest law officer of the State, advises the State Government {PYQ 2024}
Conduct of business of the State Government {PYQ 2024}
CM must communicate all Cabinet decisions to the Governor {PYQ 2023}

blocks.title: Governor: facts and traps
items: Sarojini Naidu (Uttar Pradesh) was the first woman Governor. {PYQ 2023}
The Governor unfurls the flag in the State capital on Republic Day. {PYQ 2024}
The 7th Amendment (1956) allowed one person to be Governor of two or more States; it also reorganised States on linguistic lines. {PYQ 2023}
The Sarkaria Commission recommended that the appointment of Governor should be non-partisan. {PYQ 2022}
The Governor's discretionary report can lead to President's Rule under Art 356(1). {PYQ 2025}
In a hung Assembly the Governor uses situational discretion, normally inviting the leader most likely to command a majority.
Vinai Kumar Saxena was appointed Lieutenant Governor of Delhi in May 2022. {PYQ 2024}

blocks.title: State Legislature Articles
rows: State Legislature (Part VI); Art 168: the Governor plus the Assembly, and the Council where it exists {PYQ 2024}
Parliament creates or abolishes a Council by ordinary law after the Assembly passes a resolution by special majority; this is not an amendment under Art 368
Assembly of 60 to 500 members, with exceptions such as Goa, Sikkim, Mizoram and Puducherry
Council at most one-third of the Assembly and at least 40 members
Assembly lasts 5 years from its first sitting; the Council is permanent, with one-third retiring every 2 years
Membership needs Indian citizenship and age 25 for the Assembly, 30 for the Council
Governor summons the House; gap between sessions not above 6 months; Governor can prorogue and dissolve the Assembly
Governor's address and messages; special address at the first session after each general election and the first of each year
Ministers and the Advocate General can speak in either House but vote only in their own House
Speaker and Deputy Speaker are elected by the Assembly and removed by a resolution of the majority of all members; they do not preside over their own removal debate
The same rules for the Council's Chairman and Deputy Chairman
Decisions by majority present and voting; presiding officer votes only to break a tie; quorum one-tenth of members
Seat vacated by dual membership, resignation or disqualification; grounds match Parliament's (office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency, anti-defection law) {PYQ 2026}
Penalty for sitting and voting before oath or while disqualified

Appropriation, supplementary grants, vote on account and Financial Bills, with the Governor's recommendation in place of the President's; a Money Bill in a State Assembly needs the Governor's prior permission {PYQ 2024}

blocks.title: Councils and Assemblies: numbers
items: The upper House of a State Legislature is the Vidhan Parishad (Legislative Council). {PYQ 2024}
Six States have both Houses: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.
West Bengal's Assembly passed a resolution to create a Legislative Council in 2021. {PYQ 2023}
Telangana's Assembly has 119 elected members and one nominated member. {PYQ 2023}
Sikkim has the smallest Legislative Assembly, with 32 members.
Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils can only recommend changes to a Money Bill (within 14 days for the Rajya Sabha). {PYQ 2025}

blocks.title: Governor and a bill (Art 200)
rows: Legislature reconsiders; if passed again, assent must be given
Governor sends it to the President, in cases such as those touching the Constitution or High Court powers (Art 201)

blocks.title: Supreme Court on delay (2025)
blocks.body: In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor of Tamil Nadu (April 2025) the Supreme Court held that indefinite delay by a Governor on bills is illegal and set time limits, including three months for the President on a bill reserved under Art 201. A later advisory opinion on a Presidential Reference (November 2025) said courts cannot impose fixed timelines, though indefinite inaction can still be challenged.

blocks.title: Union Territories and Article 370
items: Union Territories are in Part VIII (Arts 239-242), and Art 239AA (69th Amendment, 1991) gives Delhi an Assembly as the National Capital Territory.
Only Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir have Legislative Assemblies among the Union Territories.
N. Rangasamy became Chief Minister of Puducherry in May 2021; he founded the All India NR Congress. {PYQ 2024}
Art 370 on Jammu and Kashmir was made inoperative in August 2019 by a Presidential Order under Art 370(3) read with Art 367. {PYQ 2025}

blocks.title: Fifth and Sixth Schedules
blocks.body: The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas of only four States: Tripura, Assam, Meghalaya and Mizoram (remember 'TAMM'), not Nagaland or Arunachal Pradesh. They get autonomous district councils that can make laws on listed subjects. The Fifth Schedule covers Scheduled Areas in most other States, and the PESA Act 1996 extends panchayats to them.

blocks.title: Map the Union to the State
items: Shortcut: to find the State twin of a Union Article, add 89 for Arts 73 to 111 (Art 79 becomes 168, Art 111 becomes 200) and add 90 for Arts 112 to 123 (Art 112 budget becomes 202, Art 123 ordinance becomes 213).

Replacements: President -> Governor, Parliament -> State Legislature, Prime Minister -> Chief Minister, Attorney General -> Advocate General, Consolidated Fund of India -> Consolidated Fund of the State.

Part VI (Arts 152 to 237) has six chapters: general (152), State executive (153-167), State legislature (168-212), Governor's legislative power (213), High Courts (214-231) and subordinate courts (233-237).

blocks.title: Small facts often asked
items: The Sixth Schedule is not applicable to Nagaland or Arunachal Pradesh. {PYQ 2025}
Manipur is commonly cited as the first place in independent India to hold elections on universal adult franchise.
Art 341(1): the President, after consulting the Governor, notifies which castes, races or tribes count as Scheduled Castes in a State or Union Territory.

chapters.intro: Local government began as a Directive Principle (Art 40) and became constitutional in 1992 through two twin amendments. The 73rd built village democracy and the 74th built urban democracy, and both follow the same pattern of Part, Schedule and subject count. SSC asks the amendment numbers, the Parts, the Election and Finance Commission rules, and who recommended what, so learn the committees in order.

items.title: 73rd Amendment: Panchayats
points: Passed in 1992 under PM P.V. Narasimha Rao, in force 24 April 1993; it gave panchayats constitutional status. {PYQ 2021, 2022, 2026}
Part IX, Arts 243-243O. {PYQ 2024}
Eleventh Schedule with 29 subjects.
Gram Sabha is the foundation of the system. {PYQ 2021}
Three tiers (gram panchayat, panchayat samiti, zila parishad); the middle tier is optional where the population is up to 20 lakh.
24 April is observed as National Panchayati Raj Day.

items.title: 74th Amendment: Municipalities
points: Passed in 1992, in force 1 June 1993; it gave municipal governments constitutional status. {PYQ 2021, 2022}
Part IXA, Arts 243P-243ZG. {PYQ 2021}
Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects.
Nagar Panchayat for an area in transition, Municipal Council for a smaller urban area, Municipal Corporation for a large city.

blocks.title: Rules common to both
items: Both bodies have a 5-year term, and elections must be held within 6 months of an early dissolution. {PYQ 2022}
One-third of seats are reserved for women, and many States give 50%.
The State Election Commission (Art 243K) conducts the elections and its Commissioner is appointed by the Governor. {PYQ 2022}
The State Finance Commission (Art 243I) is set up every 5 years by the State government. {PYQ 2022}
Part IX covers all States except Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram and some hill areas; Nagaland has no Panchayati Raj institutions at all. {PYQ 2024}
Art 40 (Directive Principle): the State shall organise village panchayats and give them the powers of units of self-government. {PYQ 2023, 2024}
Art 43 (Directive Principle): the State shall promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas. {PYQ 2024}

items.what: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee: three tiers, namely gram panchayat, panchayat samiti and zila parishad.
Rajasthan started the system at Nagaur; Andhra Pradesh followed on 11 October 1959.
K. Santhanam Committee studied panchayat finances.
Ashok Mehta Committee: two tiers, with the Zila Parishad as the main unit and a Mandal Panchayat below it.
G.V.K. Rao Committee: the Zila Parishad should be the nodal agency for development and rural administration.
L.M. Singhvi Committee: first to ask for constitutional status, financial autonomy and Nyaya Panchayats for village clusters; it called the Gram Sabha the base of direct democracy.
Gadgil Committee (Congress panchayati raj policy group): directly elected members at all levels, a fixed 5-year term and reservation for SCs, STs and women.
P.K. Thungon Committee: constitutional recognition of local bodies. {PYQ 2024}
73rd and 74th Amendments give panchayats and municipalities constitutional status.

nodes: Gram Sabha as base of direct democracy

items.note: Thungon is the 1989 committee SSC asked about. {PYQ 2024}

blocks.title: Panchayat Articles (Part IX)
rows: Definitions, including Gram Sabha (all registered voters of a village); the Gram Sabha has the powers the State law gives it {PYQ 2021}
Panchayats at village, intermediate and district level; the middle tier can be skipped where the population is up to 20 lakh
All seats are filled by direct election; the village chairperson is chosen as State law says, and the chairpersons at the upper two levels are chosen indirectly
Seats reserved for SCs and STs by population share, and one-third for women
Five-year term; if dissolved early, elections within 6 months, and the new body serves only the remaining term {PYQ 2022}
Disqualification is set by State law; the minimum age to contest is 21
State law decides the powers of panchayats and their power to levy taxes, tolls and fees
State Finance Commission reviews finances, every 5 years; the Legislature decides how accounts are audited {PYQ 2022}
State Election Commission conducts panchayat elections; its Commissioner is removable like a High Court judge {PYQ 2022}
Part IX applies to Union Territories with changes

Part IX does not apply to Scheduled and tribal areas, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, the hill areas of Manipur that have district councils, and the Darjeeling hill areas; Parliament can extend it with changes
Courts cannot interfere in the delimitation of constituencies or seat allotment in panchayat elections

blocks.title: Panchayat extras
items: The PESA Act 1996 extends Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas. It reserves at least half the seats for STs, reserves every chairperson post for STs, and gives the Gram Sabha a voice in matters like minor minerals.

Gram Nyayalayas: created by the Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008 and functioning from 2 October 2009; a judicial officer (Nyayadhikari) tries civil and criminal cases in rural areas, with criminal appeals to the Sessions Court and civil appeals to the District Court.
Nyaya Panchayats are traditional village bodies set up under State laws to settle minor civil and petty criminal disputes informally.

items.what: First municipal corporation set up at Madras; Bombay and Calcutta followed in 1726.
Lord Mayo's resolution began financial decentralisation.
Ripon's resolution is called the Magna Carta of local self-government, and Ripon is called the father of local self-government in India.
74th Amendment adds Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule.

blocks.title: Urban bodies and planning committees
items: Kinds of urban local body: Municipal Corporation, Municipality, Notified Area Committee (discontinued after 1992), Cantonment Board (Cantonments Act 2006, under the Defence Ministry), Township, Town Area Committee, Port Trust and Special Purpose Agency.
Art 243ZD: each district has a District Planning Committee, where four-fifths of members are elected by the district panchayat and municipalities from among themselves.
Art 243ZE: a Metropolitan Planning Committee has two-thirds elected members.

blocks.title: Co-operative societies (Part IXB)
items: The 97th Amendment (2011) added Part IXB, Arts 243ZH to 243ZT, made forming co-operatives a right under Art 19(1)(c) and added Art 43B.

Art 243ZI asks States to make co-operative laws based on voluntary formation, democratic member control, member economic participation and autonomous functioning; compulsory State supervision is not one of these principles. {PYQ 2026}
Under Art 243ZT a State co-operative law that clashes with the amendment stays in force for only one year.
On 20 July 2021 the Supreme Court struck down parts of Part IXB because co-operatives are a State subject. {PYQ 2023}
The Constitution (112th Amendment) Bill 2009 proposed 50% reservation for women in urban local bodies. {PYQ 2021}

blocks.title: Twin pattern
blocks.body: 73rd means Panchayats, Part IX, Eleventh Schedule, 29 subjects. 74th means Municipalities, Part IXA, Twelfth Schedule, 18 subjects. Both were passed in 1992 and came into force in 1993.

chapters.intro: This became SSC's favourite area in 2025, asked through two-statement questions. Learn it as three relationships: who makes laws, who gives orders, and who collects and shares money. The Constitution never uses the word 'federal', and its federalism leans towards the Centre. For each Article remember the actor and the limit, because a wrong statement usually swaps one of them.

blocks.title: Seventh Schedule: who makes which laws
rows: Defence, foreign affairs, banking, railways (97 entries originally); 'taxes on services' was added by the 88th Amendment {PYQ 2021}
Police, public order, public health, agriculture (66 entries originally)
Criminal law, marriage, education, forests (47 entries originally); both Centre and States may legislate
If the Union List and State List clash, the Union List prevails {PYQ 2023}
Residuary powers, for subjects in none of the three lists, belong to Parliament {PYQ 2022, 2023}
Concurrent conflict: Union law prevails, unless a State law was reserved for and assented to by the President; Parliament can still override it later {PYQ 2023, 2025}

blocks.title: Concurrent List trap
blocks.body: In a clash on a Concurrent subject the State law does not win by default. Union law prevails; only a State law reserved for the President and assented to holds in that State, and Parliament can later nullify it by passing another law on the subject.

blocks.title: Legislative and administrative relations, Article by Article
rows: Parliament may set up additional courts for laws on the Union List {PYQ 2023}
Rajya Sabha resolution (two-thirds present and voting) lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject in the national interest, for 1 year at a time {PYQ 2025, 2026}
Parliament legislates on State subjects during a National Emergency
If a State law clashes with a law Parliament made under Art 249 or 250, the Union law prevails and the State law is inoperative to the extent of the clash
Two or more States consent, and Parliament legislates for them {PYQ 2023}
Missing prior recommendation or sanction (of President or Governor) does not void a law if the required assent is given later
States must comply with Union laws and the Union may give directions
State executive power must not impede or prejudice the Union's; the Union may direct States, for example on railways protection and national communications {PYQ 2024}
A State may, with the Union's consent, entrust its functions to Union officers {PYQ 2025}
The Union may take on functions in territories outside India by agreement
Public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and every State are recognised throughout India (full faith and credit)
Parliament may provide for tribunals on inter-State water disputes and bar the Supreme Court's jurisdiction {PYQ 2025}
Inter-State Council framework for Union-State coordination {PYQ 2025}
Parliament may restrict freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse in the public interest
Parliament may create new All India Services after a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds present and voting {PYQ 2025}

blocks.title: Ways Parliament can legislate on a State subject
rows: Law lapses 6 months after the Emergency ends
Law continues until repealed or amended
Permanent; only Parliament can repeal it {PYQ 2023}
Special majority; lasts 1 year plus 6 months after expiry {PYQ 2025}

blocks.title: Two councils that are often confused

items.title: Inter-State Council (Art 263)
points: Set up by Presidential order in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice. {PYQ 2025}
Chaired by the PM; members are all Chief Ministers, CMs of UTs with Legislatures, Administrators of other UTs and 6 Union Cabinet ministers named by the PM. {PYQ 2025}
Recommendatory only: it cannot enforce or adjudicate. {PYQ 2025}

items.title: Zonal Councils
points: Statutory, created by the States Reorganisation Act 1956. {PYQ 2025}
Five councils: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western and Southern.
The Union Home Minister is ex-officio chairman; the Chief Ministers of the zone's States are vice-chairmen by rotation for one year. {PYQ 2025}
The North Eastern Council is a separate body, created by an Act of Parliament in 1971.

items.what: The States Reorganisation Act created the Zonal Councils. {PYQ 2025}
Tamil Nadu set up the Rajamannar Committee on State autonomy.
The 42nd Amendment moved education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice to the Concurrent List. {PYQ 2025}
The Sarkaria Commission was appointed by the Centre.
Sarkaria reported, recommending non-partisan Governors and a permanent Inter-State Council. {PYQ 2022, 2025}
The Inter-State Council was set up by Presidential order under Art 263. {PYQ 2025, 2026}
The Punchhi Commission was constituted. {PYQ 2025}

blocks.title: Commissions on Centre-State relations
rows: Article 356 only as a last resort; Governors should be neutral, non-partisan and not active in State politics, and should not be removed before their term except in rare, compelling cases; keep All India Services; fair sharing of resources; consult States before legislating on Concurrent List subjects; set up Inter-State Council under Art 263 (done in 1990) {PYQ 2022, 2025}
Fixed tenure for Governors, who should act impartially; a bill reserved for the President should be decided within six months

items.note: Order to remember: Sarkaria report, then ISC, then Punchhi. {PYQ 2025}

nodes: reserved bills decided within six months

blocks.title: Money rules (Part XII)
rows: No tax without law; Consolidated Fund and Public Accounts; Contingency Fund
Stamp duties levied by the Union but collected and kept by States
Taxes levied and collected by the Union but assigned to States; GST on inter-State supply
Taxes shared between the Union and States, including GST after the 101st Amendment {PYQ 2025}
Parliament may levy a surcharge on certain Union taxes for the Union's own purposes
Profession tax ceiling raised from Rs 250 to Rs 2,500 by the 60th Amendment {PYQ 2021}
States cannot tax sales in inter-State trade or imports and exports
Union borrowing; State borrowing within India only, and a State owing the Centre money needs its consent
Government of India and States can sue and be sued (each is a legal entity); Art 300A makes property a constitutional legal right, not a Fundamental Right {PYQ 2022, 2025}

blocks.title: GST Council and Finance Commission
rows: 101st Amendment 2016, launched 1 July 2017; it created the GST Council. {PYQ 2021, 2024}
Both Parliament and State legislatures can make GST laws, but only Parliament for inter-State supply (IGST). {PYQ 2025}
Chair is the Union Finance Minister; members are the Union MoS Finance and State finance ministers. {PYQ 2025}
Centre holds 1/3 of weighted votes and all States together 2/3; decisions need 3/4, so neither side can pass one alone. {PYQ 2025}
Chairman plus 4 members, every 5 years; quasi-judicial; recommends to the President how taxes are shared between Centre and States. {PYQ 2023, 2025, 2026}
15th (N.K. Singh) set the States' share at 41%. The 16th (Arvind Panagariya, 2026-31) reported on 1 February 2026 and kept the States' share of the divisible pool at 41%.

blocks.title: Art 246A trap
blocks.body: Some sources say Art 246A lets States legislate on inter-State supply of goods and services. It does not: both Parliament and States make GST laws, but only Parliament legislates on inter-State supply. Also, Council recommendations are not binding.

blocks.title: Federal flavour and planning link
items: The Constitution does not use the word 'federal'; Indian federalism leans towards the Centre.
The National Development Council (1952) is extra-constitutional, chaired by the PM, and was set up to involve States in planning.

chapters.h: Emergency provisions and the amendment procedure
chapters.intro: Part XVIII (Arts 352-360) lets the Union take charge in a crisis, and Part XX (Art 368) lets Parliament change the Constitution. Both are hedged with majorities and time limits, which is exactly what SSC tests. The basic structure doctrine is the final brake on Parliament's amending power.

blocks.title: Three emergencies
rows: War, external aggression or armed rebellion ('armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance' by the 44th Amendment); only on the Cabinet's written advice
Each House within 1 month by special majority
6 months at a time; revoked by a Lok Sabha resolution by simple majority; used in 1962, 1971 and 1975 {PYQ 2025}
Failure of constitutional machinery in a State, or failure to follow Union directions; the Governor's report is not mandatory
6 months at a time, maximum 3 years; first used in Punjab (1951); the most controversial Article {PYQ 2024, 2025}
Never used; the President can order salary cuts for all officials, including Supreme Court and High Court judges {PYQ 2025}

blocks.title: Steps of four
blocks.note: The Articles climb in steps of four from the nation to a State to money. Approval also climbs: 1 month for National, 2 months for the other two.

items.title: Article 358
points: Suspends the freedoms of Article 19 automatically.
Only in an Emergency declared for war or external aggression, not for armed rebellion.
Lasts as long as the Emergency.

items.title: Article 359
points: President by order suspends the right to move courts to enforce Fundamental Rights that he names.
Can cover any Fundamental Right except Arts 20 and 21, which can never be suspended, even in a war Emergency. {PYQ 2024}
Suspension applies during the period of the order.

blocks.title: Effects and legal points
items: Art 355 makes it the Union's duty to protect States, and Arts 358-359 set out the effects on Fundamental Rights.
Art 353: the Union can give directions to States on any matter, and Parliament can legislate on State List subjects; these laws cease to work 6 months after the Emergency ends.
Art 354: the President can change how tax revenue is shared between the Union and States during the Emergency.
Art 83(2): the Lok Sabha's life may be extended one year at a time, but not beyond 6 months after the Emergency ends.
Only the Union Council of Ministers headed by the PM advises the President, and both the PM and a CM can advise dissolution of their Lower Houses. {PYQ 2025}
Emergency provisions were borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany and the Government of India Act 1935.
The Union government has named 25 June as Samvidhan Hatya Diwas, recalling the 1975 Emergency.

items.title: Effects
points: The President takes over the Governor's functions and Parliament takes over the State Legislature's, which is suspended or dissolved.
The State ministry is dismissed.
Fundamental Rights are not affected.

items.title: Record
points: First used in Punjab in 1951.
Manipur has had it most often (11 times), Uttar Pradesh 10 times.
Chhattisgarh and Telangana have never had it.
The Emergency can be renewed every 6 months, subject to a total of 3 years.
Ambedkar said it should be a last resort.

items.what: Berubari Union case (Supreme Court).
Kesavananda Bharati: Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution but not its basic structure. {PYQ 2022, 2025}
The 38th Amendment tried to bar judicial review of an Emergency proclamation.
Minerva Mills held that a proclamation can be reviewed by the courts.
S.R. Bommai made Art 356 subject to judicial review. {PYQ 2025}

blocks.title: Three ways to change the Constitution
steps: Simple majority, outside Art 368: new States (Art 3), Second Schedule, quorum, citizenship.
Special majority under Art 368: majority of total membership and two-thirds present and voting in each House.
Special majority plus ratification by half the State legislatures for federal provisions, such as election of the President, the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Seventh Schedule and GST.
The bill may start in either House but never in a State legislature, and there is no joint sitting on it.
The President must give assent (24th Amendment).

blocks.title: Which majority for which change
rows: New States and change of boundaries or names; Council creation or abolition; Second, Fifth and Sixth Schedules; quorum; official language; elections to Parliament and State legislatures; delimitation; Union Territories; salaries of MPs
Fundamental Rights, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties, and other provisions not in the other two groups
Special majority plus ratification by at least half the State legislatures
Election of the President; Supreme Court and High Courts; Art 368 itself; any Seventh Schedule list; Centre-State law-making powers; representation of States in Parliament

blocks.title: Art 368 points
items: Art 368 lays down the amendment procedure. {PYQ 2022, 2026}
K.C. Wheare praised the variety in India's amending process as wise but rarely found. {PYQ 2024}
The 24th Amendment: Parliament can abridge Fundamental Rights, and an amendment under Art 368 is not a 'law' under Art 13, and the President must give assent. {PYQ 2021}
A Constitution amendment bill can be brought by a minister or a private member and needs no prior recommendation of the President.

blocks.title: Renovate, do not demolish
blocks.body: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) let Parliament amend any part of the Constitution but not its basic structure: the house can be renovated but its foundation cannot be dug out. The foundation includes supremacy of the Constitution, judicial review, federalism, secularism, free and fair elections, separation of powers, the parliamentary system and rule of law.

chapters.intro: Amendments are asked as number, year and content, so learn them as triples and link each to the Article it created. The 42nd is the big one, called the 'mini-constitution', and the 44th partly undid it after the Emergency. The recent ones (101st onwards) are asked most in 2024-2026.

blocks.title: 1951 to 1978
rows: Ninth Schedule, Art 15(4), new limits on Art 19, and protection for zamindari abolition laws {PYQ 2021}
States reorganised on linguistic lines; one Governor may serve two or more States (Art 153) {PYQ 2021}
Dadra and Nagar Haveli; Goa, Daman and Diu; Nagaland
High Court judges' retirement age raised from 60 to 62
Sindhi added to the Eighth Schedule
Parliament can amend any part including Fundamental Rights; amendment is not 'law' under Art 13; President must assent {PYQ 2021}
Privy purses and privileges of former princes abolished {PYQ 2021}
Art 312A: Parliament can change service conditions of certain officers
Lok Sabha seats raised; Sikkim a full State
Art 297: territorial waters, continental shelf and EEZ vested in the Union {PYQ 2021}
Retirement age of State and Joint PSC members raised to 62
The mini-constitution: added Socialist, Secular and Integrity, Fundamental Duties, four DPSPs and Arts 131A and 139A (details below) {PYQ 2025}

Removed property from the Fundamental Rights (now Art 300A), brought in 'armed rebellion' in place of 'internal disturbance', required emergency approval within 1 month and protected Arts 20 and 21 from suspension {PYQ 2022, 2023}

blocks.title: The 42nd Amendment (1976) in detail
items: It is called the mini-constitution because it changed so much, and it came under PM Indira Gandhi. {PYQ 2025}
It changed the Preamble to 'sovereign socialist secular democratic republic' and 'unity and integrity of the nation'. {PYQ 2021}
It inserted Part IVA with Art 51A, the Fundamental Duties. {PYQ 2023, 2024}
It added four Directive Principles: 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A. {PYQ 2023}
It moved five subjects to the Concurrent List, including education. {PYQ 2025}
It added Arts 131A and 139A; under Art 139A the Supreme Court can transfer cases between High Courts or to itself. {PYQ 2025}
It made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding on the President; the 44th let the President send it back once. {T2 2024}

blocks.title: 1985 to 2015
rows: Profession tax ceiling raised from Rs 250 to Rs 2,500 {PYQ 2021}
Special Officer for SC/ST became a joint national commission
Delhi became the National Capital Territory
Panchayats (Part IX, Gram Sabha as foundation) and municipalities (Part IXA) {PYQ 2021, 2022}
Art 21A, new Art 45, and the 11th duty 51A(k) {PYQ 2021, 2022, 2023, 2025}
'Taxes on services' in the Union List (Art 268A) {PYQ 2021}
15% cap on ministers and tighter anti-defection law
Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali added, making 22 languages
Art 15(5), reservation in educational admissions including private unaided institutions
Co-operative societies: Art 19(1)(c), Art 43B, Part IXB (partly struck down in 2021)
NJAC (struck down 2015); India-Bangladesh land boundary agreement, assent by Pranab Mukherjee {PYQ 2021}

blocks.title: 2016 onwards
rows: Constitutional status for the National Commission for Backward Classes (Art 338B) {PYQ 2021}
SC/ST seat reservation extended to 2030 (10 more years); Anglo-Indian nomination to the Lok Sabha and Assemblies ended {PYQ 2025}
States regained the power to list SEBCs
Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam: one-third seats for women in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Delhi

blocks.title: Amendment to the Article or Part it created

nodes: Property is only a legal right

blocks.title: Pending or failed bills
rows: 50% reservation for women in urban local bodies; introduced in the Lok Sabha on 24 November 2009, not passed {PYQ 2021}
Simultaneous elections; sent to a Joint Committee
Removal of a PM, CM or minister held in custody for 30 days on serious charges; sent to a Joint Committee
To operationalise women's reservation; failed in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026 (298 for, 230 against), short of two-thirds

blocks.title: How amendments are made
items: Art 368 sets the procedure. A special majority (majority of total membership and two-thirds present and voting) is needed. {PYQ 2021, 2022}
Federal provisions also need ratification by half the States.
Some changes, such as forming new States, need only a simple majority and lie outside Art 368.

blocks.title: No 'shorter Governor term' amendment
blocks.body: The 41st Amendment (1976) raised the retirement age of Public Service Commission members to 62. It did not cut the Governor's term from 5 to 4 years, which is a false statement (asked in 2025).

blocks.title: Link number to Article
blocks.body: Tie amendments to the Articles they created: 42nd to Part IVA, 86th to 21A and 51A(k), 101st to 246A and 279A, 102nd to 338B, and 104th to the end of Art 331 nominations. One link answers two kinds of question.

chapters.h: Constitutional and statutory bodies, languages and Schedules
chapters.intro: Bodies are asked as Article, appointing authority and tenure. A constitutional body is named in the Constitution; a statutory body is created by an Act; an executive body is created by a Cabinet resolution. Sort each body into the right box first, and most trap options disappear.

blocks.title: Three kinds of body: sort first

items.title: Constitutional
points: Named in the Constitution with an Article: Election Commission, UPSC, State PSCs, Finance Commission, CAG, Attorney General, National Commissions for SC, ST and BC.

items.title: Statutory
points: Created by an Act of Parliament: NHRC, CVC, CBI (DSPE Act 1946), Lokpal (Act of 2013), NDMA, National Commission for Women, UGC, NIA.

items.title: Executive
points: Created by a Cabinet or Home Ministry resolution: NITI Aayog, Planning Commission (old), National Development Council (1952), Law Commission.

blocks.title: Constitutional bodies
rows: Set up on 25 January 1950 (National Voters' Day); multi-member first in October 1989, permanently since 1993. The CEC is removed like a Supreme Court judge. Sukumar Sen was the first CEC; Gyanesh Kumar is CEC since February 2025 {PYQ 2021, 2022, 2024}
Members are appointed and removed only by the President and serve 6 years or till 65. The first PSC came in 1926 on the Lee Commission's advice {PYQ 2024}
Members serve 6 years or till 62, appointed by the Governor and removed by the President {PYQ 2023}

A single-member body heading the Indian Audit and Accounts Department, serving 6 years or till 65 and removed like a Supreme Court judge. Its Union reports go to the President (Art 151); called the guardian of the public purse {PYQ 2022, 2023, 2024}
Constitutional law officers; the Solicitor General is statutory. The Advocate General is the highest law officer of the State {PYQ 2024}
Chairman plus 4 members; recommends to the President; advisory {PYQ 2023, 2025}
National Commissions for SCs, STs, BCs
Protect the interests of these groups {PYQ 2021}
Reports on safeguards for linguistic minorities

blocks.title: Election Commission: appointment, rolls and laws
items: The CEC and Election Commissioners are appointed by the President on the advice of a selection committee of the PM, the Leader of Opposition and a Union Cabinet minister (Act of 2023).
Tenure of the CEC is 6 years or up to age 65, whichever comes first. {PYQ 2024}
Election Commissioners other than the CEC are removed by the President only on the CEC's advice.
Art 325 provides a single electoral roll with no exclusion on religion, race, caste or sex, and Art 326 gives adult suffrage at 18.
The 61st Amendment (1988) cut the voting age from 21 to 18, and photo voter identity cards began in 1993.
The None of the Above (NOTA) option was introduced in 2013 after the Supreme Court's PUCL judgment of September 2013, and was first used in that year's Assembly elections. {T2 2022}
Art 327 lets Parliament make election laws, Art 328 lets State legislatures do so, and Art 329 bars courts from interfering in electoral matters.
The 19th Amendment (1966) ended election tribunals.
The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor and conducts panchayat elections. {PYQ 2022, 2023}
The Election Laws (Amendment) Act 2021 created four qualifying dates a year (1 January, 1 April, 1 July, 1 October) and allowed voluntary Aadhaar linking. {PYQ 2024}
Parties are registered and recognised by the Election Commission, which also allots symbols (not the President); India has a multi-party system with national and State parties. {PYQ 2024}
A national party needs 6% of votes in four or more States plus four Lok Sabha seats, or 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least three States.
A State party needs 6% of votes plus two Assembly seats, or 3% of Assembly seats (minimum three).

blocks.title: Services and Public Service Commissions
rows: Definition of State for services; recruitment and conditions of service; tenure of persons serving the Union or a State (pleasure of the President or Governor)
Safeguards against dismissal, removal or reduction in rank of civil servants
All India Services: Parliament can create one after a Rajya Sabha resolution of national interest; 312A (28th Amendment, 1972) lets Parliament change service conditions of certain officers {PYQ 2025}
Public Service Commissions; independent bodies called watchdogs of the merit system; half of the members must have held government office for 10 years {PYQ 2024}
Appointment and term; removal and suspension; service rules for members and staff
The President removes a member for insolvency, paid work outside the office, or infirmity of mind or body; for misbehaviour it must follow a Supreme Court inquiry

blocks.title: Public Service Commissions: State and Joint
items: A State PSC has the same structure as UPSC, with members serving 6 years or until 62 (41st Amendment), appointed by the Governor and removed by the President. {PYQ 2023}
A Joint PSC for several States is statutory.
Art 320 lists the functions of UPSC. {PYQ 2024}

blocks.title: Finance Commission (Art 280)
items: Formed every 5 years with a Chairman plus 4 members, who can be reappointed; called the balancing wheel of fiscal federalism. {PYQ 2023, 2025}
It is quasi-judicial and recommends how taxes are shared between the Centre and States. {PYQ 2025}
Recommendations go to the President and are advisory, not binding (Art 281). {PYQ 2023, 2025}
First FC (1951) K.C. Neogy; 14th Y.V. Reddy; 15th N.K. Singh; 16th Arvind Panagariya, who set a 41% vertical share for 2026-31.
The State Finance Commission is set up every 5 years by the State government (Governor). {PYQ 2022}

blocks.title: Commissions for SC, ST and BC
items: National Commission for SCs (Art 338) and STs (Art 338A): each has a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and 3 members serving 3 years, with civil court powers.
A Special Officer became a joint commission by the 65th Amendment (1990) and it was split into two by the 89th (2003).

National Commission for Backward Classes (Art 338B): began as a statutory body in 1993 following the Mandal ruling of 1992; the 102nd Amendment (2018) gave it constitutional status. It has a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and 3 members with 3-year terms. {PYQ 2021}

blocks.title: CAG and law officers
items: CAG (Arts 148-151): the office dates from 1860, and V. Narahari Rao was the first CAG. {PYQ 2024} {T2 2022}
Ambedkar called the CAG the most important officer under the Constitution. It heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department as a single-member body. {PYQ 2022, 2023}

The CAG audits all receipts and expenditure of the Union and of every State (and of Union Territories with a legislature), as provided by Art 149 and the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act 1971. {T2 2022}
It guides the Public Accounts Committee, compiles the States' accounts (not the Centre's), cannot be reappointed, and takes no further government office after retirement.
Art 279 makes the CAG the authority that certifies the net proceeds of a tax. Reports go to the President (Union) or Governor (State). K. Sanjay Murthy is the current CAG.
Attorney General (Art 76): the highest law officer of India; must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge; appointed by the President; M.C. Setalvad was the first.
The Solicitor General helps the Attorney General but is not a constitutional post.
Advocate General (Art 165): appointed by the Governor; must be qualified to be a High Court judge; advises the State Government and is the highest law officer of the State. {PYQ 2024}

blocks.title: Statutory and executive bodies in detail
rows: Protection of Human Rights Act 1993; chair is a former CJI or Supreme Court judge with 5 members; appointed by the President on the advice of a committee (PM, Lok Sabha Speaker, Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman, Home Minister and the two Leaders of Opposition); term 3 years or till 70; members can be reappointed but cannot hold other government jobs; a District Magistrate is not a member; called watchdog of human rights; V. Ramasubramanian is chairperson {PYQ 2024}

Chair is a former Chief Justice or High Court judge with members; appointed by the Governor after a committee of the CM, Speaker, State Home Minister and Opposition leaders; removed by the President; 3 years or till 70
Right to Information Act 2005; 5-year term or till 65 in the original scheme (the 2019 amendment lets the Centre decide terms); appointed the same way as NHRC {PYQ 2021}

Set up in 1964 by an executive resolution on the Santhanam Committee's advice; made statutory in 2003; three-member body; 4-year term or till 65; appointed by a committee of the PM, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition; removed by the President

Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013; the word was coined by L.M. Singhvi in 1963; ombudsman idea taken from Sweden; chair plus up to 8 members, half judicial and half drawn from SC, ST, OBC, minorities and women; term 5 years or till 70; preliminary inquiry within 90 days; Pinaki Chandra Ghose first chair, Ajay Manikrao Khanwilkar current
State body under each State's own law; Maharashtra was the first State to have one (1971); recommendations are not binding; tenure 5 years or till 65
Set up on 31 January 1992 under the NCW Act 1990; Vijaya Rahatkar is chairperson
Statutory since 1956; coordinates and keeps standards in higher education and gives grants; headquartered in New Delhi

NIA Act 2008, after the Mumbai attacks; under the Home Ministry, headed by a Director General; investigates terrorism, hijacking, atomic offences and large-scale fake currency; can probe cases abroad if the Centre directs; Special Courts try cases and appeals go to the High Court
Created in 1963 by a Home Ministry resolution on the Santhanam Committee's advice; draws its powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946
Executive body; the first was formed in 1834 under Macaulay, and the first after independence was in 1955 under M.C. Setalvad

Formed on 1 January 2015 by Cabinet resolution; the Prime Minister is ex-officio chairperson; its Governing Council has all Chief Ministers and Lieutenant Governors of UTs; it follows a bottom-up approach and publishes the SDG India Index, Multidimensional Poverty Index and India Innovation Index; Suman Bery is Vice Chairman and B.V.R. Subrahmanyam CEO {PYQ 2022}

blocks.title: Planning bodies
items: The Advisory Planning Board of 1946 under K.C. Neogy came first; the Planning Commission followed on 15 March 1950 by Cabinet resolution, with Nehru as first chairman and Gulzarilal Nanda as first Deputy Chairman.
Pranab Mukherjee was Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission before becoming President. {PYQ 2022}
The National Development Council (1952) is extra-constitutional, chaired by the PM, and was set up to involve States in planning.
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015; the PM is its ex-officio chairperson. {PYQ 2022}

blocks.title: E-governance models
items: The five models are G2C, G2B, G2E, G2G and C2G.
State projects: Gyandoot (Madhya Pradesh), Bhoomi (Karnataka land records), FRIENDS (Kerala), Disha (Haryana).

blocks.title: Body to founder, committee and year

nodes: Home Ministry resolution 1963, DSPE Act 1946 powers
Nehru and Nanda, 1950, replaced by NITI Aayog 2015

blocks.title: Official language articles (Part XVII, Arts 343-351)
rows: Business in Parliament in Hindi or English {PYQ 2022}
Hindi in Devanagari script is the Union's official language; English was to continue for 15 years from 1950 and later by law; the Official Languages Act 1963 kept English {PYQ 2025}

chapters.h: Important Acts and the new criminal laws
chapters.intro: Statute questions are simple year-matching, so learn the Acts in themed groups. The big change is the three new criminal laws, in force from 1 July 2024, which replaced colonial-era codes to modernise and decolonise criminal justice. SSC asked these in 2025 as detail questions on bail, evidence and new crimes, and asked many Act years in 2021 and 2024.

blocks.title: Three new criminal laws: enacted December 2023, in force 1 July 2024
rows: Substantive criminal law: what is a crime and its punishment. Introduced to modernise and decolonise criminal justice {PYQ 2025}
Procedure: arrest, investigation, bail and trial

items.title: BNS
points: Defines organised crime and petty organised crime, such as theft or snatching by a gang. {PYQ 2025}
Defines terrorist act and mob lynching.
Adds community service as a punishment for petty offences.
Drops sedition and adds an offence against the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.

items.title: BNSS
points: Zero FIR and e-FIR; e-summons.
Video recording of searches, seizures and statements, and electronic recording of witness testimony, for faster trials. {PYQ 2025}
Forensic investigation for offences punishable with 7 years or more.
Police custody up to 15 days, which can be taken in parts; the Magistrate grants default bail after 60 days (below 10 years) or 90 days (death, life or 10 years or more). {PYQ 2025}

items.title: BSA
points: Electronic and digital records are documents and can be primary evidence. {PYQ 2025}
Aligned with the IT Act 2000. {PYQ 2025}
A certificate or valid digital signature establishes authenticity. {PYQ 2025}

blocks.title: Section-wise pointers in the new laws
rows: 358 sections against 511 in the IPC; gender includes transgender; sedition replaced by Section 152 (acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity); adultery and the old Section 377 are not carried over; false promise of marriage and mob lynching are separate offences
Section 106(1): causing death by negligence, up to 5 years; Section 106(2): hit and run where the driver flees without reporting, up to 10 years and fine; a child means below 18 {T2 2025}

170 sections; electronic evidence is on par with paper as primary evidence; a confession to police is admissible only if made before a Magistrate; secondary evidence such as photocopies is allowed only if the original is lost or unavailable; oral evidence may be given electronically {PYQ 2025}

chapters.intro: Polity gave 24 questions in the eight Tier 2 Paper I papers on the site (seven official papers from 2 March 2023 to 20 January 2025, plus the CGL 2025 paper of 19 January 2026), which is 3 per paper (range 2 to 4). The Article-number question is still the commonest single type, but Tier 2 wraps many facts into two- or three-statement items and into List I and List II matches. Landmark cases, committee names and first-time dates also recur, and the CGL 2025 paper asked a Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita punishment.

blocks.title: Four cases that swap places
blocks.body: Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles. Golak Nath (1967): Parliament cannot take away or abridge Fundamental Rights, even to implement Directive Principles. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament can amend any part but not the basic structure. Minerva Mills (1980): balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself basic structure. Read the quoted words in the question and match them to the case, not to the most famous name.

items: Art 254(1): on a Concurrent List subject a conflicting State law is void to the extent of repugnancy; Art 254(2): a State law reserved for and given the President's assent prevails in that State. {T2 2025}

Art 15(2): no citizen may be barred on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth from shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of entertainment, wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and public resorts. {T2 2022}

Supreme Court judge (Art 124(3)): a citizen who has been a High Court judge for 5 years, or a High Court advocate for 10 years, or is a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion. There is no 'Supreme Court advocate for 10 years' route.

A retired President receives a pension of half the salary (Rs 2.5 lakh a month), secretarial staff with office expenses up to Rs 1 lakh a year, and free travel in the highest class with one companion. {T2 2022}
