blocks.title: Any percentage question in four moves
steps: Find the base: the starting value, or the quantity after 'of' or 'than'.
Write each percentage as a fraction or a multiplier (25% → 1/4, +20% → × 6/5).
Multiply along the chain; to go backwards, divide by the multiplier.
Answer the exact question asked: the amount, the change, or the change as a % of which base.

blocks.body: Taking 100 as the starting value is the easiest trick in this topic. With 100 as the start, every final number is directly the percentage of the start.

chapters.intro: Per cent means per hundred, so x% is the fraction x/100. Converting between fractions, decimals and percentages is the most basic skill in the topic. One small trick, that x% of y equals y% of x, often turns an awkward calculation into an easy one.

rows: Move the decimal point two places right
x% of y = y% of x

items.title: Percentage points
points: The plain difference between two percentages.
A rate moving from 10% to 12% rises by 2 percentage points.

items.title: Per cent change
points: The difference measured on the old rate.
The same move from 10% to 12% is a rise of 20%.

blocks.title: Points versus per cent
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 380 190" role="img" aria-label="Bars of 10 and 12 percent"><line class="ln" x1="40" y1="160" x2="330" y2="160"/><rect class="bar" x="60" y="60" width="50" height="100"/><rect class="bar" x="150" y="60" width="50" height="100"/><rect class="bar2" x="150" y="40" width="50" height="20"/><line class="lt" x1="110" y1="60" x2="212" y2="60"/><line class="ac" x1="215" y1="40" x2="215" y2="60"/><text class="tb sm" x="225" y="46" text-anchor="start">+2 percentage points</text><text class="tx sm" x="225" y="66" text-anchor="start">= 2/10 of the old rate</text><text class="tx sm" x="225" y="86" text-anchor="start">= a 20% rise</text><text class="tx sm" x="85" y="178" text-anchor="middle">old rate 10%</text><text class="tx sm" x="175" y="178" text-anchor="middle">new rate 12%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The extra piece is 2 points tall, but measured against the old 10 it is a 20% rise.

blocks.q: 0.5 is what percentage of 20?
steps: 'What percentage of 20' means 20 is the base, so we divide by 20.
To turn a fraction or decimal into a percentage, multiply by 100: 0.025 × 100 = 2.5%.
200/100 = 2, so the value is 2.5 × 2 = 5.

blocks.q: Shiva’s monthly salary is Rs.75,000. He spends Rs.12,000 on household items, Rs.14,000 on LIC and mutual funds, Rs.15,000 on his children’s education, and keeps Rs.10,000 for miscellaneous expenses. His savings are Rs.21,000 per month and he donates the rest of the amount to an orphanage. The percentage of his income that he donates is:
steps: Add every use of the money except the donation: 12,000 + 14,000 + 15,000 + 10,000 = ₹51,000 spent.
The rest is donated: 75,000 − 72,000 = ₹3,000.
As a percentage of income: 3,000/75,000 × 100 = 4%.
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 520 128" role="img" aria-label="Salary bar split into six parts"><text class="tb sm" x="260" y="18" text-anchor="middle">Salary ₹75,000 (all figures in thousands)</text><rect class="fa ln" x="20" y="30" width="76.8" height="30"/><text class="tx sm" x="58.4" y="50" text-anchor="middle">12</text><text class="tm sm" x="58.4" y="76" text-anchor="middle">home</text><rect class="fa2 ln" x="96.8" y="30" width="89.6" height="30"/><text class="tx sm" x="141.6" y="50" text-anchor="middle">14</text><text class="tm sm" x="141.6" y="76" text-anchor="middle">LIC/MF</text><rect class="fa ln" x="186.4" y="30" width="96" height="30"/><text class="tx sm" x="234.4" y="50" text-anchor="middle">15</text><text class="tm sm" x="234.4" y="76" text-anchor="middle">school</text><rect class="fa2 ln" x="282.4" y="30" width="64" height="30"/><text class="tx sm" x="314.4" y="50" text-anchor="middle">10</text><text class="tm sm" x="314.4" y="76" text-anchor="middle">misc</text><rect class="fa ln" x="346.4" y="30" width="134.4" height="30"/><text class="tx sm" x="413.6" y="50" text-anchor="middle">21</text><text class="tm sm" x="413.6" y="76" text-anchor="middle">savings</text><rect class="bar2" x="480.8" y="30" width="19.2" height="30"/><text class="tx sm" x="490.4" y="76" text-anchor="middle">3</text><text class="tm sm" x="490.4" y="92" text-anchor="middle">donated</text><text class="tb sm" x="260" y="118" text-anchor="middle">75 − (12 + 14 + 15 + 10 + 21) = 75 − 72 = 3, and 3/75 = 4%</text></svg>

blocks.body: For 'what % of B is A', write A/B, cancel it down to a fraction you know, then read off the percentage: 3/75 = 1/25 = 4%, 12/96 = 1/8 = 12.5%. Multiply by 100 only if no known fraction appears.
blocks.title: Cancel first, then read

chapters.intro: Most calculation questions in this topic become one-step once you know the common fractions as percentages. 12.5% of 560 is simply one-eighth of 560. Learn the list below the way you learnt your tables, and read it both ways.

blocks.body: 12.5% of 560 + 66.67% of 240 is just 560/8 + 2/3 × 240 = 70 + 160 = 230. Read every awkward percentage as a fraction first.

blocks.title: Eighths as percentages
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 330 200" role="img" aria-label="Circle cut into 8 slices with 3 shaded"><path class="fa" d="M100 100 L100.0 20.0 A80 80 0 0 1 156.6 156.6 Z"/><circle class="ln" cx="100" cy="100" r="80"/><line class="ln" x1="100" y1="20" x2="100" y2="180"/><line class="ln" x1="156.6" y1="43.4" x2="43.4" y2="156.6"/><line class="ln" x1="180" y1="100" x2="20" y2="100"/><line class="ln" x1="156.6" y1="156.6" x2="43.4" y2="43.4"/><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="75" text-anchor="start">3 of 8 equal slices</text><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="100" text-anchor="start">= 3/8</text><text class="tb lg" x="200" y="128" text-anchor="start">= 37.5%</text><text class="tm sm" x="200" y="155" text-anchor="start">one slice = 12.5%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: One eighth is 12.5%, so any number of eighths is a multiple of 12.5%.

blocks.q: Evaluate: 80% of 350 − 37½% of 160 + 11% of 500
steps: Turn each percentage into a fraction: 80% = 4/5, 37½% = 3/8, 11% stays as 11/100.
Combine in order: 280 − 60 + 55 = 275.

blocks.q: Which of the following is the least? 12% of 625 15% of 555 10% of 720 9% of 845
steps: The smallest value is 72, so 10% of 720 is the least.
blocks.trick: 12% of 625 = 1/8 of 600 at sight (75); 10% of 720 is plainly 72; 9% of 845 is above 9% of 800 = 72; 15% of 555 is far above. So 72 wins.

blocks.q: Out of an earning of Rs.720, Pankaj spends 65%. How much does he save?
steps: He spends 65%, so he saves 100% − 65% = 35%.

blocks.body: Split an awkward percentage into known fractions: 37½% = 25% + 12½% = 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8, and 35% = 25% + 10% = 1/4 + 1/10. Choose the split that makes the number divide evenly.
blocks.title: Split into friendly fractions

chapters.intro: Percentage change is always measured against the original value. The cleanest way to apply a change is to multiply by a factor: a rise of r% multiplies by (1 + r/100), and a fall of r% multiplies by (1 - r/100). Going backwards from a changed value means dividing by that factor, never subtracting the percentage.

items.f: % change = (new - old) ÷ old × 100
items.note: The base is always the original value.

items.f: Original = final × 100 ÷ (100 ± r)
items.note: Use it to undo a change; after a 12% rise, original = value × 100/112.

blocks.q: An article is marked at ₹2,000. A shopkeeper offers a discount of 25% on the article. What is the selling price of the article after the discount?
steps: A 25% discount means the price is multiplied by (100 − 25)/100 = 3/4.
Answer: ₹1,500

blocks.body: A number raised by r% and then lowered by r% ends up r²/100 % below where it started. A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall leaves you 1% down, not back at the start.

blocks.title: Undo a change by dividing
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 162" role="img" aria-label="Arrow from 100 to 125 and back"><rect class="fl ln" x="30" y="40" width="70" height="50"/><rect class="fl ln" x="300" y="40" width="70" height="50"/><text class="tb lg" x="65" y="72" text-anchor="middle">100</text><text class="tb lg" x="335" y="72" text-anchor="middle">125</text><text class="tm sm" x="65" y="32" text-anchor="middle">old</text><text class="tm sm" x="335" y="32" text-anchor="middle">new</text><line class="arr" x1="104" y1="55" x2="296" y2="55"/><path class="arr" d="M289.0 51.0 L296 55 L289.0 59.0"/><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="47" text-anchor="middle">× 5/4 (a rise of 25%)</text><line class="arr" x1="296" y1="78" x2="104" y2="78"/><path class="arr" d="M111.0 82.0 L104 78 L111.0 74.0"/><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="96" text-anchor="middle">÷ 5/4, that is × 4/5 (undo)</text><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="130" text-anchor="middle">Wrong: 125 − 25% of 125 = 93.75, not 100</text><text class="tm sm" x="200" y="150" text-anchor="middle">The 25 was out of 100; out of 125 it is only 20%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Going forward multiplies by 5/4; going back divides by 5/4. Subtracting 25% again overshoots.

blocks.q: Number p is 15% more than 150. If k is 15% less than p, then k is equal to:
steps: 15% more than 150 means multiply by 1.15: p = 150 × 1.15 = 172.5.
15% less than p means multiply by 0.85: k = 172.5 × 0.85.
blocks.trick: An equal rise and fall of 15% loses 15²/100 = 2.25%: k = 150 × 0.9775 = 146.625.

blocks.q: P and Q are two fixed points 10 cm apart, and R is a point on PQ such that PR = 6 cm. By what percentage is the length of QR decreased when the length of PR is increased by 5%?
steps: PQ = 10 cm and PR = 6 cm, so QR = 10 − 6 = 4 cm.
PR rises by 5%: new PR = 6 × 1.05 = 6.3 cm.
P and Q are fixed, so new QR = 10 − 6.3 = 3.7 cm.
QR fell by 4 − 3.7 = 0.3 cm, measured on the old QR of 4 cm: 0.3/4 × 100 = 7.5%.
blocks.trick: The 0.3 cm that PR gains is exactly what QR loses; 0.3 out of 4 = 7.5%.
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 360 134" role="img" aria-label="Segment PQ of 10 cm with R moving from 6 to 6.3 cm"><text class="tb sm" x="30" y="30" text-anchor="middle">P</text><text class="tb sm" x="210" y="30" text-anchor="middle">R</text><text class="tb sm" x="330" y="30" text-anchor="middle">Q</text><line class="ln" x1="30" y1="40" x2="330" y2="40"/><circle class="dot" cx="30" cy="40" r="3.5"/><circle class="dota" cx="210" cy="40" r="3.5"/><circle class="dot" cx="330" cy="40" r="3.5"/><text class="tx sm" x="120" y="57" text-anchor="middle">6 cm</text><text class="tx sm" x="270" y="57" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text class="tb sm" x="30" y="80" text-anchor="middle">P</text><text class="tb sm" x="219" y="80" text-anchor="middle">R</text><text class="tb sm" x="330" y="80" text-anchor="middle">Q</text><line class="ac" x1="30" y1="90" x2="219" y2="90"/><line class="ac2" x1="219" y1="90" x2="330" y2="90"/><circle class="dot" cx="30" cy="90" r="3.5"/><circle class="dota" cx="219" cy="90" r="3.5"/><circle class="dot" cx="330" cy="90" r="3.5"/><text class="tx sm" x="124.5" y="107" text-anchor="middle">6.3 cm</text><text class="tx sm" x="274.5" y="107" text-anchor="middle">3.7 cm</text><text class="tb sm" x="180" y="126" text-anchor="middle">QR: 4 → 3.7, a fall of 0.3 on 4 = 7.5%</text></svg>

blocks.q: There is a constant growth rate (in %) every year in the production of a company, as seen in the table: 2018 – 9,000 units, 2019 – 10,800 units, 2020 – X units. Find the value of X.
steps: The growth rate is constant, so first find it from 2018 to 2019.
The same 20% applies from 2019 to 2020: X = 10,800 × 1.2 = 12,960.

blocks.body: Keep multipliers as fractions (+20% = 6/5, −15% = 17/20, +12.5% = 9/8) and cancel before you multiply. It is faster and safer than long decimal multiplication. {PYQ 2026}
blocks.title: Fractions beat decimals

chapters.h: Comparisons: more than and less than
chapters.intro: The word 'than' tells you the base. If A is 25% more than B, the 25% is measured on B, but when you turn the comparison around, the base becomes A, which is larger, so the percentage shrinks to 20%. Learn the common reversal pairs so you can answer these at sight.

items.f: A is r% more than B, so B is 100r ÷ (100 + r) % less than A
A is r% less than B, so B is 100r ÷ (100 - r) % more than A
items.note: Reverse a 'less than' comparison; Sam 19% less than Peter makes Peter 23.46% more than Sam.

items: For chains, multiply the factors: if A = 1.25B and B = 1.2C, then A = 1.5C and A : C = 3 : 2.
'A is 110% of B' means A is 10% more than B, not 110% more.
If two numbers are x% and y% more than a third number, they are in the ratio (100 + x) : (100 + y).

blocks.title: Same gap, different base
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 380 156" role="img" aria-label="A is five blocks, B is four blocks"><text class="tb sm" x="45" y="45" text-anchor="end">A</text><text class="tb sm" x="45" y="100" text-anchor="end">B</text><rect class="fa ln" x="60" y="25" width="50" height="30"/><rect class="fa ln" x="110" y="25" width="50" height="30"/><rect class="fa ln" x="160" y="25" width="50" height="30"/><rect class="fa ln" x="210" y="25" width="50" height="30"/><rect class="fa2 ln" x="260" y="25" width="50" height="30"/><rect class="fa ln" x="60" y="80" width="50" height="30"/><rect class="fa ln" x="110" y="80" width="50" height="30"/><rect class="fa ln" x="160" y="80" width="50" height="30"/><rect class="fa ln" x="210" y="80" width="50" height="30"/><text class="tx sm" x="320" y="45" text-anchor="start">125</text><text class="tx sm" x="270" y="100" text-anchor="start">100</text><line class="lt" x1="260" y1="55" x2="260" y2="80"/><text class="tx sm" x="190" y="130" text-anchor="middle">extra = 1 block: 1 of B's 4 blocks = 25% more</text><text class="tb sm" x="190" y="147" text-anchor="middle">the same block is 1 of A's 5 blocks = 20% less</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The gap is one block either way; only the base (the word after 'than') changes the percentage.

blocks.q: If, in a competitive exam, the marks obtained by Sam are 19% less than those of Peter, then the marks obtained by Peter are how much percentage more than the marks obtained by Sam? (Correct to two decimal places)
steps: Take Peter's marks as 100. Sam has 19% less, so Sam has 81.
Peter is more than Sam by 100 − 81 = 19 marks.
'More than Sam' means Sam is the base: 19/81 × 100 = 23.456...%.
Correct to two decimal places, this is 23.46%.

blocks.q: Three numbers are such that the second is 150% of the first, and the third is 80% of the second. What is the ratio of the first to the third?
steps: Take the first number as 100.
The second is 150% of the first: 150/100 × 100 = 150.
The third is 80% of the second: 80/100 × 150 = 120.
First : third = 100 : 120 = 5 : 6.
blocks.trick: Multiply the factors: third = 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2 × first, so the ratio is 1 : 1.2 = 5 : 6.

blocks.q: In a constituency, 45% of the total number of voters are males and the rest are females. If 60% of the males are illiterate and 60% of the females are literate, then by what per cent is the number of illiterate females more than that of literate males? (Rounded off to 2 decimal places)
steps: Take 100 voters: 45 males and 55 females.
60% of males are illiterate, so 40% are literate: literate males = 40% of 45 = 18.
60% of females are literate, so 40% are illiterate: illiterate females = 40% of 55 = 22.
Illiterate females are more than literate males by 22 − 18 = 4.
The base is literate males ('more than that of literate males'): 4/18 × 100 = 22.22%.
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 380 182" role="img" aria-label="Voters split by sex and literacy"><rect class="fa ln" x="40" y="30" width="135" height="48"/><rect class="fl ln" x="40" y="78" width="135" height="72"/><rect class="fl ln" x="175" y="30" width="165" height="72"/><rect class="fa2 ln" x="175" y="102" width="165" height="48"/><text class="tb sm" x="107.5" y="22" text-anchor="middle">Male 45</text><text class="tb sm" x="257.5" y="22" text-anchor="middle">Female 55</text><text class="tx sm" x="107.5" y="58" text-anchor="middle">literate 18</text><text class="tx sm" x="107.5" y="118" text-anchor="middle">illiterate 27</text><text class="tx sm" x="257.5" y="70" text-anchor="middle">literate 33</text><text class="tx sm" x="257.5" y="130" text-anchor="middle">illiterate 22</text><text class="tb sm" x="190" y="172" text-anchor="middle">illiterate females 22 vs literate males 18: 4/18 = 22.22% more</text></svg>

blocks.body: Write the percentage as a fraction 1/n. If A is 1/n more than B, then B is 1/(n + 1) less than A. If A is 1/n less than B, then B is 1/(n − 1) more. So 25% (1/4) more reverses to 1/5 = 20% less, and 19% less (19/100) reverses to 19/81 more.
blocks.title: The n ± 1 rule

chapters.intro: When changes follow one another, each new percentage is taken on the already changed value, so the changes multiply rather than add. For two changes there is a neat formula; for three or more, simply multiply the factors. The order of the changes never matters, only the multipliers do.

items.f: Two changes a% and b%: net = a + b + ab/100
items.note: Write a decrease as a negative number.

items.f: Three or more changes: multiply (1 + a/100)(1 + b/100)(1 + c/100)
Area with length +a% and breadth +b%: +(a + b + ab/100)%
items.note: A square whose side rises r% gains (2r + r²/100)% in area.

items.f: Cube with side +r%: volume changes by (1 + r/100)³ - 1

items: If the second rise is twice the first, solve (1 + x)(1 + 2x) = final ÷ initial; ₹1000 becoming ₹2295 gives x = 35%, so the second rise is 70%.

blocks.body: Adding the percentages directly is the classic mistake: +12%, +23% and -34% do not make +1%, they make about -9%.

blocks.title: Why a + b + ab/100
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 370 205" role="img" aria-label="Square grown by 20 percent one way and 10 percent the other"><text class="tb sm" x="150" y="24" text-anchor="middle">length +20%, breadth +10%</text><rect class="fl ln" x="40" y="40" width="140" height="140"/><rect class="fa ln" x="180" y="40" width="28" height="140"/><rect class="fa ln" x="40" y="180" width="140" height="14"/><rect class="fa2 ln" x="180" y="180" width="28" height="14"/><text class="tx sm" x="110" y="115" text-anchor="middle">100</text><text class="tx sm" x="194" y="115" text-anchor="middle">20</text><text class="tx sm" x="110" y="191" text-anchor="middle">10</text><text class="tx sm" x="194" y="191" text-anchor="middle">2</text><text class="tx sm" x="222" y="70" text-anchor="start">area was 100</text><text class="tx sm" x="222" y="95" text-anchor="start">+20 (length strip)</text><text class="tx sm" x="222" y="120" text-anchor="start">+10 (breadth strip)</text><text class="tm sm" x="222" y="145" text-anchor="start">+2 (corner = 20 × 10/100)</text><text class="tb sm" x="222" y="175" text-anchor="start">= 132, so +32%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The two strips give a + b; the small corner is the change on the change, ab/100.

blocks.q: An investor, invested ₹2,00,000 in shares. The shares rose by 18% on the first day, fell by 15% on the second day, and then fell by 3% on the third day. What is the net percentage increase or decrease in the value of the investor's shares? (Rounded up to one decimal place)
steps: Turn each day into a multiplier: +18% → 1.18, −15% → 0.85, −3% → 0.97.
First two days: 1.18 × 0.85 = 1.003.
The shares are now 97.291% of the start, a fall of 100 − 97.291 = 2.709%.
Rounded to one decimal place, this is a decrease of 2.7%. (The ₹2,00,000 is not needed.)

blocks.q: Ravi's salary was increased by 50%. After some time, his new salary was also increased by 50%. Find his gain percentage of salary.
steps: Take the salary as 100.
After the first 50% rise it is 150.
The second 50% is taken on 150: 50% of 150 = 75, so the salary becomes 225.
Gain = 225 − 100 = 125 on a start of 100, which is 125%.

blocks.q: A number is decreased by 20% to get another number. The number so obtained is increased by 200% to get a third number. The difference of the third number and the original number is what percentage more or less than the difference of second and the third number?
steps: Take the original number as 100.
Decreased by 20%: the second number is 80.
Increased by 200% means adding twice itself, so the third number is 80 + 160 = 240 (that is, 3 times 80).
Third − original = 240 − 100 = 140.
Third − second = 240 − 80 = 160.
140 is less than 160 by 20. Measured on 160: 20/160 × 100 = 12.5% less.
blocks.trick: An increase of 200% multiplies by 3, not by 2. That single fact removes most wrong options.

blocks.body: For two changes, a + b + ab/100 is quicker than multiplying. For three, apply it to the first two and then again with the third. Keep the sign: a fall is negative, and the ab/100 term is negative when one change is a fall.
blocks.title: Two at a time

chapters.intro: Expenditure equals price multiplied by consumption. If spending must stay fixed while the price rises, consumption has to fall by exactly enough to cancel the price multiplier. That required cut is always smaller than the price rise, because it is measured on the old consumption.

items.f: Expenditure = Price × Consumption
items.note: Every question in this chapter starts here.

items.f: Price up r%, spending fixed: consumption down 100r ÷ (100 + r) %
Price down r%, spending fixed: consumption up 100r ÷ (100 - r) %
Price cut r% on amount M buys q more: new price = (rM/100) ÷ q, and old price = new price × 100 ÷ (100 - r)
items.note: The money saved buys the extra quantity.

steps: A 20% price cut lets a person buy 50 kg more rice for ₹450.
The money saved is 20% of ₹450 = ₹90.
This ₹90 buys the extra 50 kg at the new price, so the new price is ₹1.80 per kg.
The original price is 1.80 × 100/80 = ₹2.25 per kg.
blocks.title: Buying more after a price cut

items: When both price and consumption change, combine them with the successive rule: tomatoes up 300% (× 4) and consumption down 70% (× 0.3) give × 1.2, a 20% rise in spending.
The same logic covers a wage bill: 20% more employees and 18% less wage per head give 1.2 × 0.82 = 0.984, so the total falls 1.6%.

blocks.title: Spending is an area
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 380 206" role="img" aria-label="Two rectangles of equal area"><rect class="fa ln" x="30" y="40" width="100" height="100"/><text class="tx sm" x="80" y="34" text-anchor="middle">price 100</text><text class="tx sm" x="80" y="95" text-anchor="middle">spend 100 × 100</text><text class="tx sm" x="80" y="158" text-anchor="middle">use 100</text><rect class="fa2 ln" x="200" y="60" width="125" height="80"/><rect class="lt" x="200" y="40" width="100" height="100"/><text class="tx sm" x="250" y="34" text-anchor="middle">price 125</text><text class="tx sm" x="262.5" y="105" text-anchor="middle">125 × 80</text><text class="tx sm" x="262.5" y="158" text-anchor="middle">use 80</text><text class="tx sm" x="190" y="182" text-anchor="middle">same area (spending): price × 5/4 needs use × 4/5</text><text class="tb sm" x="190" y="199" text-anchor="middle">so use falls 1/5 = 20%, not 25%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Price is the width and consumption the height; to keep the area, a wider box must get shorter.

blocks.q: Every month, a man consumes 20 kg of rice and 8 kg of wheat. The price of rice is 20% of the price of wheat, resulting in a total expenditure of ₹300 per month for rice and wheat combined. If the price of wheat is increased by 20%, what percentage reduction in rice consumption is needed to maintain the same expenditure of ₹300? (Given that price of rice and consumption of wheat is constant.)
steps: Let the price of wheat be ₹w a kg. Rice costs 20% of that, so ₹0.2w a kg.
Monthly spending: 20 kg of rice × 0.2w + 8 kg of wheat × w = 4w + 8w = 12w.
12w = 300, so w = ₹25 (wheat) and rice = ₹5 a kg.
So rice costs 20 × 5 = ₹100 a month and wheat 8 × 25 = ₹200.
Wheat rises 20% to ₹30, so wheat now costs 8 × 30 = ₹240 (its quantity is fixed).
To keep ₹300, rice may cost only 300 − 240 = ₹60, which buys 60 ÷ 5 = 12 kg.
Rice falls from 20 kg to 12 kg: a cut of 8/20 × 100 = 40%.
blocks.trick: Wheat's bill rises by 20% of 200 = ₹40; rice's ₹100 bill must absorb it: 40/100 = 40%.

blocks.q: The cost of tomatoes per kg is increased by 300%. A housewife reduces her consumption of tomatoes by 70%. By what percentage does her expenditure on tomatoes increase or decrease?
steps: An increase of 300% adds three times the price, so the new price is 4 times the old (multiplier 4).
A 70% cut in consumption leaves 30% of it (multiplier 0.3).
Expenditure = price × consumption, so it is multiplied by 4 × 0.3 = 1.2.
The expenditure rises by 20%.
blocks.trick: Trap: a 300% rise is × 4, not × 3. With × 3 you would get 3 × 0.3 = 0.9, a 10% fall, which is wrong.

blocks.q: The price of a commodity increases by 20%. By what percentage should a consumer reduce their consumption so that the expenditure on the commodity remains unchanged?
steps: Expenditure = price × consumption, so if spending is fixed, consumption must change by the inverse factor.
A 20% rise multiplies the price by 6/5.
Consumption must be multiplied by 5/6, which is a cut of 1/6.
1/6 = 16.66%. Check: 6/5 × 5/6 = 1, so spending is unchanged.
Answer: 16.66%.

blocks.body: Flip the multiplier. If the price is multiplied by p/q and spending stays fixed, consumption is multiplied by q/p. Price +25% = 5/4, so use × 4/5, a 1/5 = 20% cut. Price −20% = 4/5, so use × 5/4, a 25% rise. {PYQ 2026}
blocks.title: Flip the fraction

chapters.intro: Income is always split into expenditure and savings. Take income as 100, or use the actual amounts, and track each part separately, because each part can change by a different percentage. The percentage change in savings must be measured on the old savings, not on income.

items.f: Income = Expenditure + Savings
items.note: Track each part on its own.

items.f: Savings % change = (change in income - change in expenditure) ÷ old savings × 100
Weighted change of a total = Σ(share × change)
items.note: Use it for a budget whose parts change differently.

rows: Rent 30%, then 60% of the rest, then 40% of what is left

blocks.body: Savings are a small base, so a modest change in income makes a large percentage change in savings. Always divide by the old savings.

blocks.q: The monthly income of a person was ₹15,400 and his monthly expenditure was ₹7,200. His income increased by 20% and his expenditure increased by 5%. Find the percentage increase in his savings.
steps: Savings = income − expenditure, so old savings = 15400 − 7200 = 8200.
New income = 15400 × 1.2 = 18480; new expenditure = 7200 × 1.05 = 7560.
New savings = 18480 − 7560 = 10920, a rise of 2720.
Percentage increase = 2720/8200 × 100 ≈ 33.17% (always divide by the old savings).
Answer: 33.17%

blocks.title: Income = spending + savings
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 380 214" role="img" aria-label="Stacked bars for income before and after"><line class="ln" x1="40" y1="190" x2="360" y2="190"/><rect class="bar" x="60" y="94" width="70" height="96"/><rect class="bar2" x="60" y="70" width="70" height="24"/><rect class="bar" x="200" y="84.4" width="70" height="105.6"/><rect class="bar2" x="200" y="46" width="70" height="38.4"/><text class="tx sm" x="95" y="145" text-anchor="middle">spend 80</text><text class="tx sm" x="95" y="86" text-anchor="middle">save 20</text><text class="tx sm" x="235" y="140" text-anchor="middle">spend 88</text><text class="tx sm" x="235" y="69" text-anchor="middle">save 32</text><text class="tb sm" x="95" y="64" text-anchor="middle">income 100</text><text class="tb sm" x="235" y="40" text-anchor="middle">income 120</text><text class="tm sm" x="95" y="206" text-anchor="middle">before</text><text class="tm sm" x="235" y="206" text-anchor="middle">after</text><text class="tx sm" x="284" y="90" text-anchor="start">savings</text><text class="tx sm" x="284" y="108" text-anchor="start">20 → 32</text><text class="tx sm" x="284" y="126" text-anchor="start">+12 on 20</text><text class="tb sm" x="284" y="146" text-anchor="start">= +60%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Income up 20%, spending up 10%: savings grow from 20 to 32, a 60% rise measured on the old 20.

blocks.q: A woman spends 2/3 of her income. If her income increases by 18% and the expenditure increases by 24%, then the percentage increase in her savings will be:
steps: She spends 2/3 of her income, so take income = 3 units, expenditure = 2 units and savings = 1 unit.
New income = 3 × 1.18 = 3.54 units.
New expenditure = 2 × 1.24 = 2.48 units.
New savings = 3.54 − 2.48 = 1.06 units.
Savings rise from 1 to 1.06, an increase of 6%.

blocks.q: The monthly income of a person was Rs.80,000 and his monthly expenditure was Rs.45,000. Next year, his income increased by 16% and his expenditure increased by 8%. Find the percentage increase in his savings (correct to 2 decimal places).
steps: Expenditure rises 8%: 8% of 45,000 = ₹3,600.
blocks.trick: Change in savings = change in income − change in spending; there is no need to find the new totals.

blocks.q: A family income is ₹35,000 in a month. The family spends the income on various expenditures, viz., food, health, education, entertainment, and rent. After incurring all the expenditures, 8% is saved every month. The expenditure on health is 50% more than that of food. While food is three times of the expenditure on entertainment, the expenditure on health is half of the expenditure on education. The expenditure on rent is one-third of the combined expenditure on food, health and education. How much expenditure (in ₹) is incurred on education?
steps: 8% is saved, so total spending = 92% of 35,000 = ₹32,200.
Let entertainment = e. Food is three times that: 3e.
Health is 50% more than food: 1.5 × 3e = 4.5e.
Health is half of education, so education = 2 × 4.5e = 9e.
Rent is one-third of food + health + education: (3e + 4.5e + 9e)/3 = 16.5e/3 = 5.5e.

blocks.body: For a person who spends E out of income I (savings S = I − E), the savings change % = (I × income change − E × spending change) ÷ S. With I = 100, E = 80, S = 20, income +15% and spending +5%: (1500 − 400)/20 = 55%. {PYQ 2026}
blocks.title: One-line savings formula

chapters.intro: Population growth works like compound interest: each year's rise is taken on the previous year's figure. A decline or a machine's depreciation uses the same formula with a minus sign. To find a past value, divide by the growth factor instead of subtracting.

items.f: After n years: P(1 + r/100)ⁿ, or P(1 - r/100)ⁿ for a decline
items.note: Machine depreciation uses the minus sign.

items.f: n years ago: present ÷ (1 + r/100)ⁿ
Different rates each year: multiply the factors

items: If 20% of a population die and then 30% of the rest leave, 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.56 of the original remains.
A town that rose 12% and then fell 8% to 64,400 started at 64,400 ÷ 1.0304 = 62,500.

blocks.body: Do not apply each year's rate to the original population; each rate acts on the previous year's figure.

blocks.title: Growth is compound
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 228" role="img" aria-label="Bars 1000, 1100, 1210, 1331"><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="18" text-anchor="middle">10% a year on a growing base: +100, then +110, then +121</text><line class="ln" x1="30" y1="205" x2="370" y2="205"/><rect class="bar" x="50" y="85" width="50" height="120"/><text class="tx sm" x="75" y="78" text-anchor="middle">1000</text><text class="tm sm" x="75" y="221" text-anchor="middle">year 0</text><rect class="bar" x="130" y="85" width="50" height="120"/><rect class="bar2" x="130" y="73" width="50" height="12"/><text class="tx sm" x="155" y="66" text-anchor="middle">1100 (+100)</text><text class="tm sm" x="155" y="221" text-anchor="middle">year 1</text><rect class="bar" x="210" y="73" width="50" height="132"/><rect class="bar2" x="210" y="59.8" width="50" height="13.2"/><text class="tx sm" x="235" y="52.8" text-anchor="middle">1210 (+110)</text><text class="tm sm" x="235" y="221" text-anchor="middle">year 2</text><rect class="bar" x="290" y="59.8" width="50" height="145.2"/><rect class="bar2" x="290" y="45.28" width="50" height="14.52"/><text class="tx sm" x="315" y="38.28" text-anchor="middle">1331 (+121)</text><text class="tm sm" x="315" y="221" text-anchor="middle">year 3</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Each year's rise is taken on the latest figure, so the extra piece (dark top) keeps getting bigger.

blocks.q: A mask manufacturing company manufactured ‘X’ number of masks in 2018. It increased its manufacturing capacity by 30% in 2019 and further increased its manufacturing by 15% in 2020. In 2021, due to the machinery breakdown, its manufacturing declined by 40%. What is the value of ‘X’ if it manufactured 179400 masks in 2021?
steps: Turn each year into a multiplier: +30% → 1.3, +15% → 1.15, −40% → 0.6.
So the 2021 output is 0.897X = 1,79,400.
blocks.trick: Check the options: 2,00,000 × 0.897 = 1,79,400 at once.

blocks.q: In the first year the population of a town decreased by 5% due to the Corona virus first wave. In the next year it decreased again by 5% due to the second wave and in the third year it increased by 5%. At the end of the third year the population was 9,47,625. What was the population at the beginning of the first year?
blocks.trick: The final figure has the same digits as the multiplier 0.947625, so the start must be a round 10,00,000.

blocks.q: 20% of the inhabitants of a village having died of malaria, a panic set in, during which 30% of the remaining inhabitants left the village. The population was then reduced to 12,000. What was the number of inhabitants initially (Consider integral part only)
steps: 20% died, so 80% remained: multiplier 0.8.
30% of the rest left, so 70% of them stayed: multiplier 0.7.
Remaining = 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.56 of the start = 12,000.
Start = 12,000 ÷ 0.56 = 21,428.57..., whose integral part is 21,428.
blocks.trick: The 30% acts on the survivors, not on the original; never add 20% and 30% to get 50%.

blocks.body: When the final value is given, try the options backwards: multiply the neatest option by the combined factor and see if it lands on the given number. Round options such as 10,000 or 62,500 are usually right.
blocks.title: Test the round option

chapters.intro: An election question is a chain of shrinking quantities. Registered voters shrink to votes cast when some do not vote, votes cast shrink to valid votes when some are invalid, and only the valid votes are split between candidates. The whole skill is knowing which stage each percentage belongs to.

steps: Registered voters
Votes cast = registered minus non-voters
Valid votes = votes cast minus invalid votes
Candidates share the valid votes, and the margin is the gap between them
blocks.title: The election chain

items.f: Two-candidate margin = (2p - 100)% of valid votes
items.note: The winner has p% of the valid votes.

items.f: Valid votes = registered × cast% × valid%
items.note: Walk down the chain by multiplying.

steps: 80% vote, 5% of those are invalid, the winner gets 70% of valid votes and wins by 36,480.
The margin is 70 - 30 = 40% of valid votes, so valid votes = 36,480 ÷ 0.4 = 91,200.
Registered voters = 96,000 ÷ 0.8 = 1,20,000.
blocks.title: Working back up the chain

items: With three candidates, express everyone in terms of one: if P gets 35% more than Q and R gets 15% more than Q, then P - R = 20% of Q.
A winner with '110% of the loser's votes' has 10% more than the loser, so the margin is 10% of the loser's votes.

blocks.title: The election chain
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 206" role="img" aria-label="Registered, cast, valid, then winner and loser"><rect class="fl ln" x="30" y="30" width="360" height="28"/><text class="tx sm" x="210" y="49" text-anchor="middle">registered 1,20,000</text><rect class="fl ln" x="66" y="70" width="288" height="28"/><text class="tx sm" x="210" y="89" text-anchor="middle">cast 96,000 (80%)</text><rect class="fl ln" x="73.2" y="110" width="273.6" height="28"/><text class="tx sm" x="210" y="129" text-anchor="middle">valid 91,200 (95% of cast)</text><rect class="fa ln" x="73.2" y="150" width="191.52" height="28"/><rect class="fa2 ln" x="264.72" y="150" width="82.08" height="28"/><text class="tx sm" x="169" y="169" text-anchor="middle">winner 63,840 (70%)</text><text class="tx sm" x="305.8" y="169" text-anchor="middle">loser 27,360</text><text class="tb sm" x="210" y="198" text-anchor="middle">margin 36,480 = 70% − 30% = 40% of valid votes</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Each bar is a stage; every percentage in the question belongs to exactly one of these bars.

blocks.q: In an election between two candidates, y% of the voters did not vote. 10% of the votes cast were declared invalid, while all the valid votes were cast in favour of either of the two candidates. The candidate who got 59.375% of the valid votes cast was declared elected by 2484 votes. If the number of people eligible to vote in that election was 16,000, what is the value of y?
steps: The winner got 59.375% of valid votes, so the loser got 100 − 59.375 = 40.625%.
Valid votes are 90% of votes cast (10% invalid), so votes cast = 13,248 ÷ 0.9 = 14,720.

blocks.q: In an election between two candidates, 12% of voters did not cast their votes. The winner by obtaining 68% of the total votes defeated his contestant by 2880 votes. What was the total number of voters who cast their votes in the election?
steps: Here 'total votes' means all registered voters. Take the voters as 100.
12% did not vote, so 88 voted.
The winner got 68 (68% of all voters), so the loser got 88 − 68 = 20.
Margin = 68 − 20 = 48% of all voters = 2,880, so the voters number 2,880 ÷ 0.48 = 6,000.
Votes cast = 88% of 6,000 = 5,280.
blocks.trick: Trap: if you take 68% of the votes cast you get 8,000, which is an option but wrong. Check which base the 68% is on.

blocks.q: In an election, 2% persons enrolled in the voter list did not participate and 500 votes were invalid. Two candidates A and B fought the election, and A defeated B by 200 votes. If 43% of the persons enrolled in the voter list casted their votes in favour of A, then what is the number of the total casted votes?
steps: Let N people be enrolled. 2% did not vote, so votes cast = 0.98N.
500 were invalid, so valid votes = 0.98N − 500.
A got 43% of those enrolled: 0.43N. B got 200 fewer: 0.43N − 200.
A + B = valid votes: 0.86N − 200 = 0.98N − 500.
Total votes cast = 0.98 × 2,500 = 2,450.

blocks.q: At the election for the President of Students' Union in a university, the number of votes not cast for the person A increased by 25% over those not cast for her in the previous election, and A lost by a majority twice as large as that by which she had won the previous election. If a total of 26000 students voted each time, how many voted for A in the previous election?
steps: Previous election: A got x votes, the rest got 26000 − x; A won by x − (26000 − x) = 2x − 26000.
Now votes against A = 1.25(26000 − x) and votes for A = 26000 − 1.25(26000 − x); A loses by 2.5(26000 − x) − 26000.
The new losing margin is twice the old winning margin: 2.5(26000 − x) − 26000 = 2(2x − 26000).
Check: before 14000 vs 12000 (won by 2000); now 11000 vs 15000 (lost by 4000).
Answer: 14000
blocks.trick: Test options: x = 14000 gives margin 2000; against becomes 15000, so A has 11000 and loses by 4000 = 2 × 2000.

blocks.body: Draw the chain once: registered → cast → valid → candidates. Put every number on its own stage, then walk up or down by multiplying or dividing. The margin between two candidates is (winner% − loser%) of whatever stage their percentages are of.
blocks.title: One chain, one base per step

chapters.intro: The pass mark is a fixed number of marks, so a student who fails by k marks has k fewer than the pass mark and a student who passes by k has k more. When two students are compared, the difference in their percentages equals the difference in their marks, including both margins.

items.title: Fails by k
points: Marks scored + k = pass mark.
The k marks are added to reach the pass mark.

items.title: Passes by k
points: Marks scored - k = pass mark.
The k marks are the surplus over the pass mark.

items.f: Maximum marks = difference in marks ÷ difference in percentages × 100
items.note: For fail by x and pass by y, the difference in marks is x + y.

items.f: Weighted % = Σ(weight × score%) ÷ Σweight
items.note: Use it for several papers with different weights.

rows: 20% fails by 10; 35% is 20 more than the pass mark
15% of max = 30, so max = 200 and pass = 40 + 10 = 50

blocks.title: Fail by, pass by

blocks.cap: The pass mark sits between the two students; the gap in marks, 10 + 20, equals the gap in percentages.

blocks.q: Pass percentage of an examination is 35%. If a student who got 210 marks, failed by 14 marks, then what are the maximum marks of the examination?
steps: Failing by 14 marks means the pass mark is 14 more than 210: 210 + 14 = 224.
The pass mark is 35% of the maximum: 0.35 × max = 224.

blocks.q: In a competitive exam with 120 questions, there are three sections: General Knowledge (20 questions), Reasoning (50 questions) and English (50 questions). A candidate answered 70% of General Knowledge, 50% of Reasoning and 30% of English questions correctly. If the minimum passing score is 60%, how many more questions did the candidate need to answer correctly to pass?
steps: Correct in General Knowledge: 70% of 20 = 14.
Correct in Reasoning: 50% of 50 = 25.
Correct in English: 30% of 50 = 15.
Total correct = 14 + 25 + 15 = 54.
To pass he needs 60% of 120 = 72 correct.
He needs 72 − 54 = 18 more correct answers.

blocks.body: With 'x% fails by a' and 'y% passes by b', the maximum marks = 100(a + b)/(y − x) in one line; the pass mark is then x% of max + a. With 'x% fails by a' and 'y% also fails by b' (b < a), use a − b instead of a + b.
blocks.title: One-line maximum

chapters.h: Percentage equations, errors and money applications
chapters.intro: Some questions are really equations dressed in percentages, and some ask how far a wrong calculation is from the right one. In every error question the error is measured on the correct value. SSC also sets short money applications such as commission, rent for a target return and fuel price hikes, which are percentages of an amount.

items.f: a% of N - b% of N = k gives N = 100k ÷ (a - b)
items.note: 45% and 30% of a number differ by 0.9, so N = 6.

items.f: Wrong quotient = true quotient × (dividend factor) ÷ (divisor factor)
Error % = (wrong - correct) ÷ correct × 100
items.note: Measure every error on the correct value.

items.f: Error percentage in measurement = |measured - true| ÷ true × 100
items.note: The true value is the base.

rows: 75% of a number is 15 more than 2/3 of it
Increased by 25% instead of decreased by 20%
Flat costing ₹8,00,000 must earn 9% a year after ₹2,000 monthly maintenance
Petrol rises 5% from ₹82; 3045 km a month at 15 km per litre

blocks.body: For a commission, multiply each item's price by its commission rate and by the number sold, then add. For a target return, add the required return and the running costs before dividing by 12.

blocks.title: Measure the error on the correct value
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 380 162" role="img" aria-label="Bars 80 and 125"><text class="tb sm" x="52" y="52" text-anchor="end">correct</text><text class="tb sm" x="52" y="102" text-anchor="end">wrong</text><rect class="bar" x="60" y="35" width="192" height="25"/><text class="tx sm" x="156" y="52" text-anchor="middle">80</text><rect class="bar" x="60" y="85" width="192" height="25"/><rect class="bar2" x="252" y="85" width="108" height="25"/><text class="tx sm" x="156" y="102" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text class="tx sm" x="306" y="102" text-anchor="middle">45</text><line class="lt" x1="252" y1="28" x2="252" y2="116"/><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="136" text-anchor="middle">wrong 125 is 45 above the correct 80</text><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="153" text-anchor="middle">error = 45/80 = 56.25% (base = the correct value)</text></svg>
blocks.cap: A +25% slip instead of −20% gives 125 instead of 80; the extra 45 is compared with 80, not 125.

blocks.q: During a division, Suhas mistakenly took as the dividend a number that was 10% less than the original dividend. He also mistakenly took as the divisor a number that was 20% less than the original divisor. If the correct quotient of the original division problem was 24 and the remainder was 0, what was the quotient that Suhas obtained, assuming his calculations had no error?
steps: Quotient = dividend ÷ divisor. Let the true dividend be D and divisor d, with D/d = 24.
Suhas used 0.9D (10% less) and 0.8d (20% less).
blocks.trick: Dividend factor over divisor factor: 9/8 × 24 = 27.

blocks.q: A vendor sells shirts at 500 each, earning a 2% commission, and ties at 150 each, with a 12% commission. if he sells 3 shirts and 4ties per day, what will be his total commission earned in 30 days?
steps: Commission on shirts each day: 3 × ₹500 = ₹1,500 of sales, and 2% of 1,500 = ₹30.
Commission on ties each day: 4 × ₹150 = ₹600 of sales, and 12% of 600 = ₹72.
Commission per day = 30 + 72 = ₹102.

blocks.q: The difference between 20% of a number and 10% of the same number is 120. What is the number?

blocks.body: In any wrong-operation question, take the original number as 100, write the correct and the wrong results, and divide the gap by the correct one. For wrong division, multiply the true quotient by (dividend factor ÷ divisor factor).
blocks.title: Take 100, then compare with the correct result

chapters.intro: Real SSC CGL questions worked from the first line. Try each one, then open the solution.

blocks.q: In an election between two candidates, the defeated candidate secured 42% of the valid votes polled and lost the election by 7,68,400 votes. If 82,560 votes were declared invalid and 20% people did NOT cast their vote, then the invalid votes were what percentage (rounded off to 1 decimal place) of the votes which people did NOT cast?
steps: The loser got 42% of valid votes, so the winner got 58%; margin = 16% of valid votes = 7,68,400.
Votes cast = valid + invalid = 48,02,500 + 82,560 = 48,85,060.
20% did not vote, so votes cast are 80% of voters: voters = 48,85,060 ÷ 0.8 = 61,06,325.
blocks.trick: Non-votes are a quarter of the votes cast (20 : 80), so 12,21,265 = 48,85,060 ÷ 4.
blocks.title: Elections: non-voters, invalid votes and margins

blocks.q: In an election contested between two candidates, 15% of the total voters did not cast their votes and 100 votes got disqualified. The candidate who won the election won it by securing 45% of the total votes and won by a margin of 400 votes. Find the total number of voters?
steps: Let the total voters be T. 15% did not vote, so votes cast = 0.85T; 100 were disqualified, so valid = 0.85T − 100.
The winner got 45% of all voters: 0.45T. The loser got 400 fewer: 0.45T − 400.
Winner + loser = valid votes: 0.9T − 400 = 0.85T − 100.

blocks.q: In an election between two candidates, P received 42% of the valid votes and Q won by 45,360 votes. 20% people did not cast their vote. If 10% of the votes cast were found invalid, what is the total number of votes registered in the poll booth?
steps: P got 42% of valid votes, so Q got 58%. Margin = 16% of valid votes = 45,360.
10% of votes cast were invalid, so valid = 90% of cast: cast = 2,83,500 ÷ 0.9 = 3,15,000.
20% did not vote, so cast = 80% of registered: registered = 3,15,000 ÷ 0.8 = 3,93,750.

blocks.q: In an election between two candidates P and Q, P got 78% of the total valid votes. If the total votes of the electorate were 75,60,000, then what was the number of valid votes that Q got if 10% of the voters did not cast their vote and 15% of the votes polled were declared invalid?
steps: 10% did not vote: votes polled = 90% of 75,60,000 = 68,04,000.
15% of these were invalid: valid = 85% of 68,04,000 = 57,83,400.
P got 78% of valid votes, so Q got 22%.
blocks.trick: One chain: 75,60,000 × 0.9 × 0.85 × 0.22. A rough check, 22% of about 58 lakh is about 12.7 lakh, rules out the three small options.

blocks.q: In an election between Sunita and Mamata, 85% of voters cast their votes but 2% of votes were invalid. If Sunita got 64,974 votes which is 78% of valid votes, then the total number of voters enrolled in the election was:
steps: Sunita's 64,974 votes are 78% of valid votes: valid = 64,974 ÷ 0.78 = 83,300.
2% of votes cast were invalid, so valid = 98% of cast: cast = 83,300 ÷ 0.98 = 85,000.
85% of voters cast votes: enrolled = 85,000 ÷ 0.85 = 1,00,000.

blocks.q: In a constituency, 90% of the total number of people on the electoral roll cast their votes during an election. 15% of the votes cast were declared invalid. Jeeta secured 60% of the valid votes. If Jeeta secured 91,800 valid votes, what was the total number of people on the electoral roll?
steps: Jeeta's 91,800 are 60% of valid votes: valid = 91,800 ÷ 0.6 = 1,53,000.
15% of cast votes were invalid, so valid = 85% of cast: cast = 1,53,000 ÷ 0.85 = 1,80,000.
90% of the roll voted: roll = 1,80,000 ÷ 0.9 = 2,00,000.

blocks.q: In the election, 8% of the voters did not cast their votes. Two candidates contested the election in which the winning cadidate got 48% of the total votes and won election by 1100 votes. Find the total number of voters in the election, given that all the votes cast were valid?
steps: Take the voters as 100. 8% did not vote, so 92 votes were cast, all valid.
The winner got 48 (48% of all voters), so the loser got 92 − 48 = 44.
Margin = 48 − 44 = 4% of the voters = 1,100.
blocks.trick: The 48% is of total voters, not of votes cast; keep one base.

blocks.q: Three candidates were participating in an election. The person at third place got 20% of the total votes while the difference between the votes of the winner and the first runner up was 20% of the total votes. If the difference between the votes of the first runner up and the second runner up was 37,000, how many votes did the winner receive?
steps: Take the total votes as 100. Third place got 20, so winner + runner-up = 80.
Winner − runner-up = 20. Adding: 2 × winner = 100, so winner = 50 and runner-up = 30.
Runner-up − third = 30 − 20 = 10% of the total = 37,000, so the total = 3,70,000.
blocks.title: Elections: several candidates, supporters and 'more than'

blocks.q: Three candidates P, Q and R participated in an election. P got 35% more votes than Q, and R got 15% more votes than Q. P overtook R by 2,412 votes. If 90% voters voted and no invalid or illegal votes were cast, then what was the number of voters in the voting list?
steps: Let Q get 100. Then P gets 135 (35% more) and R gets 115 (15% more).
These are 90% of the voters: list = 42,210 ÷ 0.9 = 46,900.

blocks.q: Three candidates X, Y and Z participated in an election. X got 30% more votes than Y, whereas Z got 25% more votes than Y. X also overtook Z by 5000 votes. If 71% of the voters voted and no invalid votes were cast, then what was the total number of voters in the voting list?
steps: Let Y get 100. Then X gets 130 and Z gets 125.
X − Z = 5 parts = 5,000, so 1 part = 1,000.
These are 71% of the voters: list = 3,55,000 ÷ 0.71 = 5,00,000.

blocks.q: Raju, Ravi and Ashok contested an election. 5% votes polled were invalid. Raju got 30% of the total votes. Ravi got 32% of the total votes. The winner got 5136 more votes than the person who received the least number of votes. Find the total number of votes polled.
steps: Take the votes polled as 100. 5% were invalid, so the valid votes are 95.
Raju got 30 and Ravi got 32 (both % of the total), so Ashok got 95 − 30 − 32 = 33.
The winner is Ashok (33) and the lowest is Raju (30): gap = 3% of the total = 5,136.
Total votes polled = 5,136 × 100/3 = 1,71,200.
blocks.trick: The third candidate's share comes from the valid 95%, not from 100%.

blocks.q: In an election between R and S, R gets 110% of the votes of S and beats S by 770 votes. If there were no invalid votes, then the total number of votes polled is:
steps: R gets 110% of S, so if S = 100, R = 110.
R beats S by 10 parts = 770, so 1 part = 77.
blocks.trick: '110% of S' means 10% more than S; the margin is 10% of S's votes.

blocks.q: Two candidates P and Q contested in an election. 70% of the registered voters are P supporters. If 60% of the P supporters and 30% of the Q supporters are expected to vote for candidate P, then what percentage of the registered voters are expected to vote for candidate P?
steps: Take 100 registered voters: 70 support P and 30 support Q.
60% of P's supporters vote for P: 60% of 70 = 42.
30% of Q's supporters also vote for P: 30% of 30 = 9.
Votes for P = 42 + 9 = 51 out of 100, that is 51%.

blocks.q: The expenditure on the cost of living of a man and his family is 60% of his salary. He gets two increment of 30% and 60% in his salary. If his saving increases by 250% of his initial saving, then the new cost of living expenditure is what percentage (rounded off to the nearest integer) of the increased salary?
steps: Take the salary as 100: cost of living 60, savings 40.
Two increments of 30% and 60%: new salary = 100 × 1.3 × 1.6 = 208.
Savings increase by 250% of the initial savings: increase = 2.5 × 40 = 100, so new savings = 40 + 100 = 140.
New cost of living = 208 − 140 = 68.
blocks.trick: Read 'increases by 250%' as adding 100, not as becoming 100.
blocks.title: Income, expenditure and savings

blocks.q: Ajay spends 66⅔% of his income on different household items. If his income increases by 25% and expenditure increases by 20%, then the effect on his savings will be:
steps: 66⅔% = 2/3, so take income = 3, expenditure = 2, savings = 1.
New income = 3 × 1.25 = 3.75.
New expenditure = 2 × 1.2 = 2.4.
New savings = 3.75 − 2.4 = 1.35, up from 1: an increase of 35%.

blocks.q: Mr. X has a monthly income of $26,500 and his monthly expenditure is $20,500. The next year, his salary is increased by 12% and expenditure is increased by 6%. His savings increase by how much percent?
steps: Expenditure rises 6%: 6% of 20,500 = 1,230.
Savings rise by 3,180 − 1,230 = 1,950.

blocks.q: Kalyan spends 80% of his income. His income increases by 15% and his expenditure also increases by 5%. The percentage of increase in his savings is:
steps: Take income = 100: expenditure 80, savings 20.
New income = 115; new expenditure = 80 × 1.05 = 84.
New savings = 115 − 84 = 31.
Increase = 31 − 20 = 11 on 20, which is 55%.

blocks.q: If an employee's income is ₹72,000, the amount he spends is 40% higher than his savings. Therefore, his savings (in ₹) is:
steps: Let savings = S. Spending is 40% higher: 1.4S.
blocks.trick: Savings : spending = 10 : 14 = 5 : 7, so savings = 5/12 × 72,000 = 30,000.

blocks.q: Rima spends 35% of her monthly income on food articles and 15% of the remaining on clothes. She saves 40% of the remaining income. If her monthly salary is ₹27,500, how much does she save (in ₹) every month?
steps: After clothes (15% of that), 85% is left: 0.85 × 17,875 = 15,193.75.
She saves 40% of what remains: 0.4 × 15,193.75 = ₹6,077.50.

blocks.q: A father gives 8% of his monthly income to both his sons as pocket money. The elder son gets 85% of the total amount given to both the sons. He spend 90% of the amount and saves ₹17. What is the monthly income of father?
steps: Let the income be I. The sons get 8% of I = 0.08I.
The elder son gets 85% of that: 0.85 × 0.08I = 0.068I.
He spends 90%, so he saves 10%: 0.1 × 0.068I = 0.0068I = 17.

blocks.q: During the first year, the strength of a school increased by 12%, in the second year it decreased by 12% and in the third year it increased by 10%. At the end of the third year its strength was nearly 10842. What was the strength at the beginning of the first year?
blocks.title: Successive changes and working backwards

blocks.q: A man loses 20% of his money and after spending 85% of the remainder, he is left with Rs.120. How much did he have at first?
steps: After losing 20%, 80% of the money is left.
He spends 85% of that, so 15% of the 80% remains: 0.8 × 0.15 = 0.12 of the start.

blocks.q: The salary of a worker is first increased by 25%, then it is decreased by 12%. The percentage change in his salary is:
steps: The salary is now 110% of the old one: a 10% increase.

blocks.q: The price of an article is increased by r%. The new price was decreased by r% later. Now the latest price is Rs.1.What was the original price of the article?
steps: Let the original price be P.
After a rise of r%: P(1 + r/100). After a fall of r%: P(1 + r/100)(1 − r/100).
blocks.trick: Check with r = 10: the net change is −1%, so P = 1/0.99 = 100/99, and 10000/9900 = 100/99.

blocks.q: A school organized a field trip for 100 students and 10 chaperones. Each student was given a snack pack containing items equal to 15% of the total number of students. Each chaperone received a snack pack with items equal to 25% of the total number of students. How many snack items were distributed in total?
steps: Each student's pack has 15% of 100 students = 15 items; 100 students get 100 × 15 = 1,500 items.
Each chaperone's pack has 25% of 100 = 25 items; 10 chaperones get 10 × 25 = 250 items.
blocks.title: Percentage equations and applications

blocks.q: A person having bought goods for Rs.400 sells half of it at a gain of 5%. At what gain percentage must he sell the remainder, so as to gain 25% on the whole?
steps: For 25% gain on the whole ₹400, he must receive 1.25 × 400 = ₹500.
Half the goods cost ₹200 and sell at 5% gain: 1.05 × 200 = ₹210.
The other half must bring 500 − 210 = ₹290.
Its cost is ₹200, so the gain is 90 on 200 = 45%.
blocks.trick: The two halves are equal, so their gains average to 25%: (5 + x)/2 = 25, x = 45.

blocks.q: Piyush sold a guitar to Anuj at 16% gain and Anuj sold it to Mayank at 32% gain. If Mayank paid Rs.3,828 for the guitar, what amount did Piyush pay for the same?
steps: Each sale multiplies the price: 16% gain → × 1.16, 32% gain → × 1.32.
Mayank's price = Piyush's cost × 1.16 × 1.32 = 1.5312 × cost.

chapters.intro: Elections and savings dominated 2024, while 2025 leaned towards fraction-equivalent evaluations, percentage equations and chains of 'more than'. Wrong options are built from the reversed base (20% instead of 25%) and from the right number with the wrong direction. Knowing this pattern helps you pause on the right step.

items.what: Population and depreciation, elections, price and consumption, pass and fail marks, 'x% more than y' reversals, and salary and savings were common.
Elections with non-voters and invalid votes were the most frequent, alongside successive changes, population over three years, rice price cuts and losses followed by spending of the remainder.
Savings with income and spending rising at different rates, pass marks, weighted paper marks, mistaken dividends and divisors, pocket money chains and 'which is the least' comparisons appeared.
Savings increases came in four shifts and elections in five shifts, with successive share-price moves, employees versus wages, price hike versus consumption and a second rise twice the first.
Fraction-equivalent evaluations, percentage equations, chains of 'more than', weighted budget change, income and savings, commission, a fuel price hike and rent for a target return were asked.

blocks.body: Before marking, say the answer aloud as a sentence, such as 'savings rose by 60% of the old savings'. If the sentence sounds wrong, the base or the direction is wrong.

chapters.intro: Counts come from the 240 Mathematical Abilities questions of the eight Tier 2 Paper I sets on the site: 2, 3, 6 and 7 March 2023, 26 October 2023, 18 and 20 January 2025, and the CGL 2025 set of 19 January 2026. Percentage gave 10 questions, about 1.25 a paper, and it also sits inside most profit, interest and population work. Tier 2 percentage questions are mostly direct, but the elections and population items add a twist: a candidate with "42% more than the other two together", or population data given for one period and asked for another.

blocks.title: Percentage questions in Tier 2 Paper I
rows: Basic percentage and ratio from percentages
Numbers 10% and 25% more than a third, 12% rotten eggs, 20% of (A + B) = 30% of (A - B), 60% of 75 against 1/5 of 25.
Winner with 64% wins by 434, three candidates with one 42% more than the other two together.
Decrease 8% a year for 2 years, sales up 6% then 20%, growth at 6% read backwards and forwards.

blocks.title: Read which years the rate covers
blocks.body: On 18 January 2025 the population reached 50,000 in 2018 after two years of 6% growth, so 2016 = 50000/1.06² ≈ 44,500 and 2020 = 50000 × 1.06² = 56,180. The difference is 11,680. The words "for the next 3 years" are only a distractor, because 2020 is just two years after 2018.

blocks.title: Tier 2 checks
items: Two numbers a% and b% more than a third number are in the ratio (100 + a) : (100 + b).
In a two-candidate election the margin is (winner% - loser%) of the total votes polled.
If K = (1 + k/100)(H + L) and all three total N, then H + L = N/(2 + k/100).
Going back n years at r% growth divides by (1 + r/100)ⁿ; going back under decline divides by (1 - r/100)ⁿ.

formulas.f: x% of N = xN/100
formulas.note: This is the basic definition.

formulas.f: A as a % of B = A/B × 100
formulas.note: The base is the 'of' quantity.

formulas.f: % change = (new - old)/old × 100
formulas.note: The base is the original value.

formulas.f: Increase r%: × (100 + r)/100; decrease r%: × (100 - r)/100
formulas.note: This is the multiplier method.

formulas.f: Original = final × 100/(100 ± r)
formulas.note: Use it to undo a change.

formulas.f: A r% more than B means B is 100r/(100 + r)% less than A
formulas.note: Use it to reverse a comparison.

formulas.f: A r% less than B means B is 100r/(100 - r)% more than A
formulas.note: Use it to reverse a comparison.

formulas.f: Successive a%, b%: net = a + b + ab/100
formulas.note: Use negative numbers for decreases.

formulas.f: Three successive changes: multiply (1 + a/100)(1 + b/100)(1 + c/100)
formulas.note: Alternatively, apply the two-step rule twice.

formulas.f: +r% then -r%: net = -r²/100 %
formulas.note: This is always a loss, in either order.

formulas.f: Two equal rises of r%: net = +(2r + r²/100)%
formulas.note: The same result gives the area change of a square whose side rises r%.

formulas.f: Area change = (a + b + ab/100)% for length +a% and breadth +b%
formulas.note: Use it for rectangles.

formulas.f: Volume change of a cube with side +r% = (1 + r/100)³ - 1
formulas.note: Use it for three dimensions.

formulas.f: Price up r%, spending fixed: consumption down 100r/(100 + r)%
formulas.note: This is the price-consumption rule.

formulas.f: Price down r%, spending fixed: consumption up 100r/(100 - r)%
formulas.note: This is the price-consumption rule in reverse.

formulas.f: Expenditure change = price change combined with consumption change by the successive rule
formulas.note: Use it when both change.

formulas.f: Price cut r% on amount M buys q more: new price = (rM/100)/q; old price = new × 100/(100 - r)
formulas.note: This solves the rice ₹450 case.

formulas.f: Income = Expenditure + Savings
formulas.note: Track each part separately.

formulas.f: Savings % change = (ΔI - ΔE)/S × 100, in money terms
formulas.note: Use it when income and spending change by different rates.

formulas.f: Population after n years = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ
formulas.note: Use a minus sign for a decline.

formulas.f: Population n years ago = P/(1 + r/100)ⁿ
formulas.note: This reverses growth.

formulas.f: Two-candidate margin = (2p - 100)% of valid votes
formulas.note: The winner has p% of the valid votes.

formulas.f: Valid votes = registered × cast% × valid%
formulas.note: This is the election chain.

formulas.f: Maximum marks = (difference in marks)/(difference in %) × 100
formulas.note: With 'fail by x' and 'pass by y', the difference in marks is x + y.

formulas.f: a% of N - b% of N = k gives N = 100k/(a - b)
formulas.note: Use it for percentage equations.

formulas.f: Wrong quotient = true quotient × (dividend factor)/(divisor factor)
formulas.note: Use it for a mistaken division.

formulas.f: Error in result = (wrong - correct)/correct × 100
formulas.note: Use it for wrong-operation questions.

formulas.f: Weighted % = Σ(wᵢ × pᵢ)/Σwᵢ
formulas.note: Use it for papers or a portfolio.

formulas.f: Weighted change of a total = Σ(shareᵢ × changeᵢ)
formulas.note: Use it for a budget whose parts change differently.

formulas.f: Two numbers x% and y% more than a third are in the ratio (100 + x) : (100 + y)
formulas.note: Use it for chains and ratios.

formulas.f: x% of y = y% of x
formulas.note: Swap for easier mental calculation.

method: 1. Pick a base of 100, or the LCM of the denominators, unless the actual amount is given.
2. Turn every change into a multiplier, so +25% becomes 5/4 and -20% becomes 4/5.
3. Chain the multipliers for successive changes, and divide by them to go backwards.
4. For structures such as elections, budgets and exams, write the chain of quantities before computing anything.
5. For comparisons, identify the base first: in 'than B', the base is B.
6. Use fraction equivalents for evaluation items instead of decimals.
7. Check the direction (increase or decrease) and the base of the final percentage before marking.
traps: Using the wrong base is the top mistake: '% more than B' divides by B, and '% less than A' divides by A.
Adding successive percentages directly is wrong: +12%, +23% and -34% make about -9%, not +1%.
Picking the right number with the wrong direction, such as a 6% increase instead of a 6% decrease, loses the mark.
In elections, taking percentages of registered voters when they are of valid votes, or forgetting invalid votes, breaks the chain.
In savings questions, the percentage change must be computed on the old savings, not on income.
In price-consumption questions, the cut is 100r/(100 + r) %, not r%.
In wrong-operation questions, divide the error by the correct value: 45/80, not 45/125.
'A is 110% of B' means A is 10% more than B, not 110% more.
A change in percentage points is not the same as a percentage change.
In population questions, compound the rates year by year instead of applying each to the original.
In pass-fail questions, add the 'fails by' marks on the correct side of the pass mark.
Rounding too early spoils two-decimal answers: 21.875 rounds to 21.88 only at the end.

examples.q: If x% of 280 = 15% of 240 + 20% of 310, the value of x is: (CGL 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: 15% of 240 = 36 and 20% of 310 = 62, so the right side is 98. Step 2: x = 98/280 × 100 = 35.

examples.q: Seventy-five percent of a number is 15 more than two-thirds of that number. Find the number. (CGL 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: 3/4 - 2/3 = 1/12, so the difference is N/12. Step 2: N/12 = 15 gives N = 180.

examples.q: If A is 25% more than B, and B is 20% more than C, then what is A:C? (CGL 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: A = 1.25B and B = 1.2C. Step 2: A = 1.25 × 1.2C = 1.5C. Step 3: A : C = 3 : 2.

examples.q: If the price of petrol increases by 28%, by what percentage should consumption fall so that expenditure is unchanged? (Correct to 2 decimal places) (CGL 2022)
examples.how: Step 1: Use 100r/(100 + r). Step 2: 28/128 × 100 = 21.875%. Step 3: Rounded to two decimals, this is 21.88%.

examples.q: A number is increased by 12%, then by 23%, and the result is decreased by 34%. What is the net change (nearest integer)? (CGL 2024)
examples.how: Step 1: Multiply the factors: 1.12 × 1.23 × 0.66 = 0.9092. Step 2: The number is about 91% of the original, so it has decreased by about 9%.

examples.q: The population of a town increased by 12% in the first year and decreased by 8% in the next year to 64,400. Find the population at the beginning. (CGL 2022)
examples.how: Step 1: The combined factor is 1.12 × 0.92 = 1.0304. Step 2: P × 1.0304 = 64,400. Step 3: P = 62,500.

examples.q: A reduction of 20% in the price of rice enables a person to obtain 50 kg more for ₹450. Find the original price per kg. (CGL 2022)
examples.how: Step 1: The money saved is 20% of 450 = ₹90. Step 2: This buys 50 kg at the new price, so the new price is ₹1.80. Step 3: The original price is 1.80 × 100/80 = ₹2.25.

examples.q: The income of a person is ₹16,500 and expenditure ₹12,000. Next year income rises 24% and expenditure falls 10%. The percentage increase in savings (nearest integer) is: (CGL 2024)
examples.how: Step 1: New income = 20,460 and new expenditure = 10,800. Step 2: Savings rise from 4,500 to 9,660, an increase of 5,160. Step 3: 5,160/4,500 = 114.67%, which is about 115%.

examples.q: Vipul spends 30% of his income on rent, 60% of the remainder on groceries and 40% of the rest on others. If he saves ₹7,056, how much does he spend on groceries? (CGL 2024)
Two candidates contested; 80% of voters cast votes, 5% of these were invalid. The winner got 70% of valid votes and won by 36,480. Find the total number of voters. (CGL 2024)
examples.how: Step 1: The margin is 70 - 30 = 40% of valid votes, so valid votes = 91,200. Step 2: Votes cast = 91,200/0.95 = 96,000. Step 3: Registered voters = 96,000/0.8 = 1,20,000.

examples.q: John got 20% marks and failed by 10 marks. Jack got 35%, which was 20 more than the pass mark. Find the pass percentage. (CGL 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: The 15% gap equals 10 + 20 = 30 marks, so the maximum is 200. Step 2: The pass mark is 40 + 10 = 50. Step 3: 50/200 = 25%.

examples.q: The price of an item is raised twice from ₹1,000 to ₹2,295; the second percentage rise was twice the first. What was the second rise? (CGL 2024)
examples.how: Step 1: (1 + x)(1 + 2x) = 2.295 gives 2x² + 3x - 1.295 = 0. Step 2: The positive root is x = 0.35. Step 3: The second rise is 2 × 35% = 70%. Check: 1.35 × 1.7 = 2.295.

examples.q: Household spending on food, clothing and entertainment is 2:4:4. Food falls 10%, clothing rises 5%, entertainment falls 15%. Find the change in total expenditure. (CGL 2025)
examples.how: Step 1: Take the spending as 20, 40 and 40 out of 100. Step 2: The new amounts are 18, 42 and 34, a total of 94. Step 3: The total has fallen by 6%.

examples.q: During a division, Pranjal took a dividend 10% more and a divisor 25% more than the original. The correct quotient was 25 with remainder 0. What quotient did he get? (CGL 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: The quotient is multiplied by 1.1/1.25 = 0.88. Step 2: 25 × 0.88 = 22.

examples.q: Hari, Kamal and Lalit contested an election in which 6,050 votes were polled with none invalid. Kamal got 42% more votes than Hari and Lalit together. If Lalit got 8% of the votes, find Hari's votes. (CGL Tier 2, 26 October 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: Let H + L = x, so Kamal = 1.42x and 2.42x = 6050. Step 2: x = 2500. Step 3: Lalit = 8% of 6050 = 484. Step 4: Hari = 2500 - 484 = 2016.

examples.q: Two candidates contested an election. One got 64% of the votes and won by 434 votes. What was the total number of votes polled? (CGL Tier 2, 3 March 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: The loser got 36%, so the margin is 28% of the total. Step 2: 28% = 434, so 1% = 15.5. Step 3: Total = 1550.

examples.q: If 20% of (A + B) = 30% of (A - B), then what percentage of B is equal to A? (CGL Tier 2, 7 March 2023)
examples.how: Step 1: 2(A + B) = 3(A - B). Step 2: 2A + 2B = 3A - 3B, so A = 5B. Step 3: A is 500% of B.

examples.q: The population of a place increased to 50,000 from 2016 to 2018 at 6% per annum and continued the same trend. If A is the population in 2016 and B the population in 2020, each rounded to the next integer, find B - A. (CGL Tier 2, 18 January 2025)
Two years ago the population of a town was 94,87,500. It decreases every year at 8% because of migration. What is the present population? (CGL Tier 2, 20 January 2025)

revise: The base is the original value, or the quantity written after 'than'.
r% more reverses to 100r/(100 + r)% less, and r% less reverses to 100r/(100 - r)% more.
Two successive changes give a + b + ab/100, and longer chains are handled by multiplying factors.
An equal rise and fall of r% leaves a loss of r²/100 %.
When price rises r% with fixed spending, consumption falls by r/(100 + r) of itself.
Income = Expenditure + Savings, and the savings change is measured on the old savings.
Population follows P(1 ± r/100)ⁿ, and you go back by dividing.
Elections run registered, cast, valid, candidates, and the margin is (2p - 100)% of valid votes.
In exams, the difference of percentages equals the difference of marks, including fail and pass margins.
If a% of N exceeds b% of N by k, then N = 100k/(a - b).
A wrong-operation error is measured on the correct value.
Learn the eighths, sixths, ninths and elevenths as percentages.
Check increase versus decrease in the options before marking.
facts: Fraction equivalents: 1/15 = 6.67%, 1/16 = 6.25%, 1/17 is about 5.88% and 1/19 is about 5.26%.
Successive results: +10% and +10% give +21%, +20% and +20% give +44%, and -10% and -10% give -19%.
Successive results: +10% then -10% gives -1%, and +25% then -20% gives no change.
Reversals: 10% more reverses to 9.09% less, 20% more to 16.67% less, 25% more to 20% less and 50% more to 33.33% less.
Reversals: 10% less reverses to 11.11% more, 20% less to 25% more and 25% less to 33.33% more.

Q|Profit & Loss.why: Profit & Loss is one of the steadiest Quant topics, averaging about 1.9 questions per shift across CGL 2021-2025 and about 2.1 per shift in CGL 2025. Marked price and discount questions dominate, followed by false weights, free-item offers, dealer chains and several items sold together. A few questions tagged here each year are really partnership problems, so those basics are included too.

lines: Cost price is what the seller pays, including transport and repairs, selling price is what the buyer pays, and marked price is the number printed on the tag.
Profit and markup are always calculated on the cost price, while discount is always calculated on the marked price.
Turn every percentage into a multiplier, so a 20% profit becomes ×1.2 and a 25% loss becomes ×0.75, and then just multiply along the story.
Learn the fraction ladder by heart, because 1/6 is 16⅔%, 1/7 is 14 2/7%, 1/8 is 12.5% and 1/9 is 11 1/9%.
When the cost price of x items equals the selling price of y items, the profit is (x − y)/y, with the number sold in the denominator.
Markup m followed by discount d gives a net result of m − d − md/100, which is why 20% up and 20% off is a 4% loss.
Two successive discounts a and b equal one discount of a + b − ab/100, and the order in which they are applied never matters.
In a 'buy x, get y free' offer the customer pays for x but takes x + y, so the discount is y/(x + y).
A dishonest trader who sells at cost price but gives 900 g for a kilogram gains 100/900, which is 11 1/9%, not 10%.
When a false weight is combined with a profit or loss, divide the price factor by the fraction of weight actually given.
In a dealer chain, multiply all the factors from the first seller to the last buyer, and divide back when you need the first cost price.
Two items sold at the same price, one at x% profit and one at x% loss, always give a net loss of x²/100 %.
When several items are sold, find each cost price separately, add them, and compute the percentage only once on the total.
If no amount is given, take the cost price as 100, and finish by checking whether the answer is a profit or a loss.

Take x + y -> he takes home x + y items
Discount -> free items over items taken, y/(x + y)
