chapters.intro: Profit and loss is the maths of a shop. A shopkeeper buys something, puts a price tag on it, and sells it. Only three prices matter: what he paid, what the tag says, and what the customer finally paid. If you can say which price each percentage is taken on, every question in this topic becomes one or two multiplications.

items: Cost price (CP) is the money the shopkeeper spends to get the article. If he also pays for transport or repair, that is added to the CP.
Selling price (SP) is the money the customer pays him.
If SP is more than CP, the extra money is profit (or gain). If SP is less than CP, the shortfall is loss.
Example: a pen bought for ₹10 and sold for ₹12 gives a profit of ₹2. Sold for ₹8, it gives a loss of ₹2.
A percentage needs a base. Profit % and loss % are always out of CP, because CP is the money the shopkeeper risked.
So a profit of ₹2 on a CP of ₹10 is 2/10 × 100 = 20%. The same ₹2 on a CP of ₹40 is only 5%.

blocks.title: Profit and loss on one bar
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 170" role="img" aria-label="Bars for CP 10, SP 12 and SP 8"><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="16" text-anchor="middle">Buy a pen for ₹10. Sell it for ₹12, or for ₹8.</text><text class="tb sm" x="72" y="48" text-anchor="end">CP ₹10</text><rect class="fl ln" x="80" y="32" width="200" height="22"/><text class="tb sm" x="72" y="82" text-anchor="end">SP ₹12</text><rect class="fl ln" x="80" y="66" width="200" height="22"/><rect class="fa ln" x="280" y="66" width="40" height="22"/><text class="tx sm" x="326" y="82" text-anchor="start">profit ₹2</text><text class="tb sm" x="72" y="116" text-anchor="end">SP ₹8</text><rect class="fl ln" x="80" y="100" width="160" height="22"/><rect class="lt" x="240" y="100" width="40" height="22"/><text class="tx sm" x="286" y="116" text-anchor="start">loss ₹2</text><line class="ac" x1="280" y1="26" x2="280" y2="128"/><text class="tm sm" x="280" y="142" text-anchor="middle">the CP line</text><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="162" text-anchor="middle">profit % = 2/10 × 100 = 20%;  loss % = 2/10 × 100 = 20%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The CP bar is the yardstick: profit sticks out past it, loss falls short of it, and both are measured against it.

items: Going the other way: a 20% profit on a CP of ₹50 means SP = 50 + 20% of 50 = 50 + 10 = ₹60.
Shorter: SP = CP × 1.2. A 20% profit multiplies CP by 1.2, and a 25% loss multiplies CP by 0.75.
When no rupee amount is given, take CP = ₹100. Then every percentage is simply a number of rupees.
Backwards: if SP = ₹60 after a 20% profit, then CP = 60 ÷ 1.2 = ₹50. Divide when you go back from SP to CP.

blocks.title: Blocks for a 25% profit
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 152" role="img" aria-label="Four blocks of cost and five blocks of selling price"><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="16" text-anchor="middle">25% profit: cut CP into 4 equal blocks of 25%</text><text class="tb sm" x="62" y="48" text-anchor="end">CP</text><rect class="fl ln" x="70" y="30" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tm sm" x="95" y="48" text-anchor="middle">25</text><rect class="fl ln" x="120" y="30" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tm sm" x="145" y="48" text-anchor="middle">25</text><rect class="fl ln" x="170" y="30" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tm sm" x="195" y="48" text-anchor="middle">25</text><rect class="fl ln" x="220" y="30" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tm sm" x="245" y="48" text-anchor="middle">25</text><text class="tb sm" x="62" y="90" text-anchor="end">SP</text><rect class="fl ln" x="70" y="72" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tm sm" x="95" y="90" text-anchor="middle">25</text><rect class="fl ln" x="120" y="72" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tm sm" x="145" y="90" text-anchor="middle">25</text><rect class="fl ln" x="170" y="72" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tm sm" x="195" y="90" text-anchor="middle">25</text><rect class="fl ln" x="220" y="72" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tm sm" x="245" y="90" text-anchor="middle">25</text><rect class="fa ln" x="270" y="72" width="50" height="26"/><text class="tx sm" x="295" y="90" text-anchor="middle">profit</text><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="124" text-anchor="middle">CP : SP = 4 : 5.  Profit = 1 block = 1/4 of CP = 25%,</text><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="142" text-anchor="middle">but the same block is only 1/5 of SP = 20% on SP.</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Cutting CP into equal blocks turns a percentage into a ratio: 25% profit means CP : SP = 4 : 5.

items: Marked price (MP) is the price on the tag. It is also called list price, labelled price or printed price.
A discount is a cut from the marked price, and discount % is always out of MP.
Example: a shirt tagged ₹500 with 10% off costs 500 − 50 = ₹450. That ₹450 is the SP.
Markup is how far the tag sits above CP, and like profit it is out of CP. A ₹400 shirt tagged ₹500 has a markup of 100/400 = 25%.
So a shopkeeper who marks up and then gives a discount still makes a profit as long as SP stays above CP.

blocks.title: Every question in four moves
steps: Write down which prices are given: CP, MP or SP.
Turn each percentage into a multiplier: +p% is × (1 + p/100) and −d% is × (1 − d/100).
Multiply along the story (CP → MP → SP), or divide to go back.
Compare SP with CP, always on CP, to get the profit or loss %.

blocks.title: The one rule to never forget
blocks.body: Profit, loss and markup are out of CP. Discount is out of MP. Almost every wrong answer in this topic comes from using the wrong base.

chapters.h: The language of buying and selling
chapters.intro: Every Profit & Loss question uses three prices: what the seller paid, what the price tag says, and what the buyer finally paid. Once you know which percentage sits on which price, most questions become one line of multiplication. The single most important rule is that profit is on cost price and discount is on marked price.

rows: What the seller pays, including overheads such as transport, repair or tax paid by him
The price written on the article, also called list, printed, labelled, tag or catalogue price
The reduction from the marked price
blocks.title: Three prices, three differences

items.b: only when the question says so

items.f: Profit % = (SP − CP)/CP × 100
Discount % = (MP − SP)/MP × 100

items.note: For a profit of p% or a loss of l%.
Working back from SP to CP.

blocks.title: Which base does each gap use?
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 156" role="img" aria-label="Number line with CP 100, SP 117 and MP 130"><line class="ln" x1="40" y1="70" x2="380" y2="70"/><circle class="dota" cx="82.5" cy="70" r="4.5"/><text class="tb sm" x="82.5" y="90" text-anchor="middle">CP 100</text><circle class="dota" cx="227" cy="70" r="4.5"/><text class="tb sm" x="227" y="90" text-anchor="middle">SP 117</text><circle class="dota" cx="337.5" cy="70" r="4.5"/><text class="tb sm" x="337.5" y="90" text-anchor="middle">MP 130</text><line class="lt" x1="227" y1="46" x2="337.5" y2="46"/><line class="lt" x1="227" y1="51" x2="227" y2="45"/><line class="lt" x1="337.5" y1="51" x2="337.5" y2="45"/><text class="tm sm" x="282.2" y="40" text-anchor="middle">discount 13 = 13/130 of MP = 10%</text><line class="lt" x1="82.5" y1="104" x2="227" y2="104"/><line class="lt" x1="82.5" y1="99" x2="82.5" y2="105"/><line class="lt" x1="227" y1="99" x2="227" y2="105"/><text class="tm sm" x="154.8" y="118" text-anchor="middle">profit 17 = 17/100 of CP = 17%</text><line class="lt" x1="82.5" y1="132" x2="337.5" y2="132"/><line class="lt" x1="82.5" y1="127" x2="82.5" y2="133"/><line class="lt" x1="337.5" y1="127" x2="337.5" y2="133"/><text class="tm sm" x="210" y="146" text-anchor="middle">markup 30 = 30/100 of CP = 30%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The same three prices give three different percentages: profit and markup are measured from CP, discount from MP.

blocks.q: The difference between the cost price and selling price of a pair of shoes is Rs.1,200. If the profit is 15%, the selling price is:
steps: The difference between CP and SP is the profit, and here it is ₹1,200.
The profit is 15%, and profit % is always out of CP, so 15% of CP = ₹1,200.

blocks.q: In a clearance sale, a sari whose marked price was ₹10,490 is now sold for ₹9,441. What is the discount percentage on the sari?
steps: Discount in rupees = MP − SP = 10,490 − 9,441 = ₹1,049.
Discount % is always out of MP: 1,049/10,490 × 100.
1,049 × 10 = 10,490, so the fraction is exactly 1/10 = 10%.
blocks.trick: Check the options: 10% of 10,490 is 1,049, and 10,490 − 1,049 = 9,441. Done.

blocks.body: Before you calculate, write the base under each percentage: 'profit /CP', 'discount /MP'. It takes two seconds and removes the most common mistake in the topic.

chapters.h: Ratios and profit on selling price
chapters.intro: Instead of writing equations, it is often faster to think of CP and SP as a ratio. A profit of 10% simply means CP : SP = 10 : 11. Occasionally a question asks for profit as a percentage of SP, which needs a different denominator.

items.f: CP : SP = a : b  ⇒  profit % = (b − a)/a × 100
Profit as % of SP = p/(100 + p) × 100
items.note: A 25% profit on CP is a 20% profit on SP.

blocks.body: If the profit is 320% of the cost, take the cost as 1. Then the profit is 3.2 and the SP is 4.2, so profit as a share of SP is 3.2/4.2, about 76.2%.
blocks.title: Same profit, different base

blocks.body: Profit % is on CP unless the question clearly says 'profit on SP'. Using SP as the base by habit is one of the commonest errors.

blocks.title: 250% profit as blocks
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 156" role="img" aria-label="Two blocks of cost price against seven blocks of selling price"><text class="tb sm" x="210" y="16" text-anchor="middle">Profit 250% of CP: CP = 2 blocks, profit = 5 blocks</text><text class="tb sm" x="52" y="48" text-anchor="end">CP</text><rect class="fl ln" x="60" y="30" width="42" height="26"/><rect class="fl ln" x="102" y="30" width="42" height="26"/><text class="tb sm" x="52" y="92" text-anchor="end">SP</text><rect class="fl ln" x="60" y="74" width="42" height="26"/><rect class="fl ln" x="102" y="74" width="42" height="26"/><rect class="fa ln" x="144" y="74" width="42" height="26"/><rect class="fa ln" x="186" y="74" width="42" height="26"/><rect class="fa ln" x="228" y="74" width="42" height="26"/><rect class="fa ln" x="270" y="74" width="42" height="26"/><rect class="fa ln" x="312" y="74" width="42" height="26"/><line class="lt" x1="144" y1="112" x2="354" y2="112"/><line class="lt" x1="144" y1="107" x2="144" y2="113"/><line class="lt" x1="354" y1="107" x2="354" y2="113"/><text class="tm sm" x="249" y="126" text-anchor="middle">profit = 5 blocks = 5/2 of CP = 250%</text><text class="tb sm" x="210" y="146" text-anchor="middle">CP : SP = 2 : 7</text></svg>
blocks.cap: A profit of r% of CP means SP is (100 + r)% of CP: here 350%, so CP : SP = 100 : 350 = 2 : 7.

blocks.q: An article is sold at a profit of 250%. What is the ratio of its cost price to selling price?
steps: A profit of 250% means profit = 2.5 × CP.
SP = CP + profit = CP + 2.5 CP = 3.5 CP.
CP : SP = 1 : 3.5. Multiply both by 2 to clear the decimal: 2 : 7.

blocks.q: The profit gained on selling a certain product is 320% of the cost. If the cost increases by 10% but the selling price remains constant, then what percentage of the selling price is the profit (correct to one decimal place)?
steps: Take the cost as 100. The profit is 320% of cost = 320, so SP = 100 + 320 = 420.
The cost rises by 10%, so the new cost = 110. The SP stays 420.
New profit = 420 − 110 = 310.
The question asks for profit as a percentage of SP: 310/420 × 100 = 73.81%.
To one decimal place this is 73.8%.
blocks.trick: Profit as % of SP = (SP − new CP)/SP = 1 − 110/420 = 1 − 0.262 = 73.8%.

blocks.q: From the given data, find the ratio of the cost prices of a shirt and a trouser. Shirt: selling price ₹1,200, profit 20%. Trouser: selling price ₹660, profit 10%.
steps: Shirt: SP ₹1,200 at a 20% profit, so CP = 1,200 ÷ 1.2 = ₹1,000.
Trouser: SP ₹660 at a 10% profit, so CP = 660 ÷ 1.1 = ₹600.
Ratio of CPs = 1,000 : 600 = 5 : 3.

blocks.body: Profit r% on CP gives CP : SP = 100 : (100 + r). Cancel the ratio and you have the answer to most 'ratio of CP to SP' questions without writing an equation.

chapters.h: Multipliers and fractions: the fastest tool
chapters.intro: The best way to handle any chain of percentages is to turn each one into a multiplier and multiply them in the order of the story. Fractions make the numbers cancel neatly, so learn the common percentage-fraction pairs by heart. A profit of 1/8 means CP : SP = 8 : 9, and a loss of 1/6 means CP : SP = 6 : 5.

items: A 20% profit is ×1.2 or ×6/5, and a 25% loss is ×0.75 or ×3/4. {PYQ 2026}
Profit 1/8 means CP : SP = 8 : 9, and loss 1/6 means CP : SP = 6 : 5.
Use these ratios directly instead of forming equations.

blocks.body: Keep fractions exact until the last step. Options are often close, such as 9.25% and 9.5%, so early rounding can pick the wrong one.

blocks.title: One CP, two multipliers
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 410 168" role="img" aria-label="One cost price with two multipliers"><rect class="fl ln" x="20" y="58" width="90" height="34"/><text class="tb sm" x="65" y="80" text-anchor="middle">CP = 200</text><rect class="fa ln" x="290" y="12" width="100" height="34"/><text class="tb sm" x="340" y="34" text-anchor="middle">SP ₹144</text><rect class="fa2 ln" x="290" y="104" width="100" height="34"/><text class="tb sm" x="340" y="126" text-anchor="middle">SP ₹288</text><line class="arr" x1="110" y1="68" x2="288" y2="32"/><path class="arr" d="M283.5 36 L288 32 L282.3 30.1"/><line class="arr" x1="110" y1="82" x2="288" y2="118"/><path class="arr" d="M282.3 119.9 L288 118 L283.5 114"/><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="38" text-anchor="middle">× 0.72  (28% loss)</text><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="126" text-anchor="middle">× 1.44  (44% gain)</text><text class="tm sm" x="200" y="158" text-anchor="middle">144 ÷ 0.72 = 200 first; then 288 ÷ 200 = 1.44</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Find the CP once by dividing, then any new SP ÷ CP gives the new multiplier directly.

blocks.q: A man loses 28% by selling an article for ₹144. If he sells it for ₹288, what will be his gain/loss percentage?
steps: A 28% loss means SP = CP × 0.72.
The new SP is ₹288, which is more than ₹200, so it is a gain.
blocks.trick: The new SP is exactly double the old one, so the multiplier doubles: 0.72 × 2 = 1.44, a 44% gain.

blocks.q: Sofia sold an iPhone at the cost of Rs.46,068 at a loss of 12%. At what cost will she have to sell it to get a profit of 18%?
steps: For an 18% profit, SP = 52,350 × 1.18.
blocks.trick: Go straight from one SP to the other: new SP = 46,068 × 118/88 = 46,068 × 59/44 = ₹61,773.

blocks.q: A horse was sold for Rs.60,000 at a profit of 20%. For what price should he have sold to gain a 30% profit?
steps: A 20% profit means SP = CP × 1.2, so CP = 60,000 ÷ 1.2 = ₹50,000.

blocks.q: An item is sold at 20% profit. If CP and SP increase by Rs. 50 and Rs. 30 respectively, profit becomes 10%. Find original CP.
steps: Let CP = C. A 20% profit means SP = 1.2C.
New CP = C + 50 and new SP = 1.2C + 30, with a 10% profit: 1.2C + 30 = 1.1(C + 50).
C = ₹250 (check: CP 300, SP 330, profit 10%).
Answer: Rs. 250.
blocks.trick: Test the options: CP 250 gives SP 300; new CP 300 and new SP 330 is exactly 10%.

blocks.q: An article is sold at a 15% profit. If its cost price was ₹ 20 less and selling price was ₹ 20 less, the profit would have been 20%. Find the original cost price.
steps: Let the cost price be x. A 15% profit means SP = 1.15x.
New CP = x − 20 and new SP = 1.15x − 20; a 20% profit means new SP = 1.2 × new CP.
Check: CP 80, SP 92; new CP 60, new SP 72, and 72 = 1.2 × 60.
Answer: ₹ 80.
blocks.trick: Test the options: CP 80 gives SP 92; 92 − 20 = 72 is exactly 120% of 80 − 20 = 60.

blocks.q: If the selling price of an item is increased by 25% and the profit also increases from 20% to 30%, what is the percentage increase in the cost price?
steps: Take CP = 100; a 20% profit gives SP = 120.
The SP rises by 25%: new SP = 120 × 1.25 = 150.
The new profit is 30%, so new SP = 1.3 × new CP: new CP = 150 ÷ 1.3 ≈ 115.38.
Answer: 15.38%

blocks.body: When the same article is sold twice with two different percentages, jump from one SP to the other: new SP = old SP × (new factor)/(old factor). There is no need to find the CP separately.

chapters.h: Two selling prices for the same article
chapters.intro: Many questions describe one article sold at two different prices with two different results. The key idea is that the gap between the two SPs equals the gap between the two percentages, taken on the same CP. Count a loss as a negative profit.

rows: 20% profit instead of 16% loss earns ₹324 more: 36% of CP = 324, so CP = 900
Profit % at S₁ equals loss % at S₂
₹2,000 and ₹1,200 give CP ₹1,600, so a 20% profit needs SP ₹1,920
Gain at S₁ is k times the loss at S₂
SP doubled makes profit four times
S = 1.5C, so the original profit is 50%

blocks.body: For 'SP multiplied by n gives profit multiplied by m', solve nS − C = m(S − C). This one equation covers every version of the question.

blocks.title: Equal gain % and loss %
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 148" role="img" aria-label="Number line with CP midway between 1200 and 2000"><line class="ln" x1="30" y1="60" x2="370" y2="60"/><circle class="dota" cx="64" cy="60" r="4.5"/><text class="tb sm" x="64" y="80" text-anchor="middle">₹1,200</text><circle class="dota" cx="200" cy="60" r="4.5"/><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="80" text-anchor="middle">CP ₹1,600</text><circle class="dota" cx="336" cy="60" r="4.5"/><text class="tb sm" x="336" y="80" text-anchor="middle">₹2,000</text><circle class="dot" cx="308.8" cy="60" r="4"/><text class="tx sm" x="308.8" y="44" text-anchor="middle">1,920</text><line class="lt" x1="64" y1="98" x2="200" y2="98"/><line class="lt" x1="64" y1="93" x2="64" y2="99"/><line class="lt" x1="200" y1="93" x2="200" y2="99"/><text class="tm sm" x="132" y="112" text-anchor="middle">loss 400 = 25%</text><line class="lt" x1="200" y1="98" x2="336" y2="98"/><line class="lt" x1="200" y1="93" x2="200" y2="99"/><line class="lt" x1="336" y1="93" x2="336" y2="99"/><text class="tm sm" x="268" y="112" text-anchor="middle">profit 400 = 25%</text><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="138" text-anchor="middle">Equal % on the same CP means equal rupees, so CP is the midpoint.</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Equal percentages on the same CP are equal rupee gaps, so CP sits exactly halfway between the two SPs.

blocks.q: The percentage profit earned by selling an article for ₹2,000 is the same as the percentage loss incurred by selling the same article for ₹1,200. At what price should that article be sold to make a profit of 20%?
steps: The profit % at ₹2,000 equals the loss % at ₹1,200. Both are on the same CP, so the rupee gaps are equal too.
So CP is the midpoint: (2,000 + 1,200)/2 = ₹1,600.

blocks.q: A watch is sold at a profit of 25%. Had it been sold for Rs.120 less then, there would have been a less then of 15%. What is the cost price in rupees?
steps: At the first price there is a 25% profit, so SP₁ = 125% of CP.
Selling for ₹120 less gives a 15% loss, so SP₂ = 85% of CP.
The gap between them is 125% − 85% = 40% of CP, and this gap is ₹120.
blocks.trick: Rupee gap ÷ percentage gap: 120 ÷ 40% = ₹300. Remember to add the percentages when one side is a profit and the other a loss.

blocks.q: On selling a painting at Rs.1,498, the gain is 25% more than the loss incurred on selling it at Rs.1,300. In order to gain 25%, the selling price will be:
steps: Let the CP be C. The gain at ₹1,498 is 1,498 − C, and the loss at ₹1,300 is C − 1,300.
The gain is 25% more than the loss: 1,498 − C = 1.25(C − 1,300).

blocks.body: Draw the two SPs on a line with CP between them (or both on one side). The rupee gap between the SPs always equals the percentage gap on CP, with a profit and a loss adding up.

chapters.h: Items bought and sold in numbers
chapters.intro: When prices are given for groups of items, compare the price of one item on each side. The most famous version says the cost price of x items equals the selling price of y items. Remember that the base is always the number of items sold.

items.f: CP of x items = SP of y items  ⇒  profit % = (x − y)/y × 100
items.note: Negative means a loss. CP of 20 = SP of 18 gives 11 1/9%; CP of 17 = SP of 28 gives a loss of 11/28 = 39 2/7%.

items.f: Gain = CP of g items on selling n  ⇒  profit % = g/n × 100
items.note: Selling 15 kg with gain equal to the CP of 5 kg gives 33⅓%.

items.f: Gain = SP of g items on selling n  ⇒  profit % = g/(n − g) × 100
items.note: The SP version has n − g in the denominator.

blocks.q: On selling 25 shirts, a retailer earns profit equal to the cost price of 8 shirts. What is the profit percentage?
steps: Profit % is always on the cost of the goods actually sold.
Profit on 25 shirts = CP of 8 shirts.
Answer: 32

items: Bought a items for ₹p and sold b items for ₹q: compare the per-item rates p/a and q/b. {PYQ 2026}
Buying 9 for ₹90 (₹10 each) and selling 10 for ₹95 (₹9.50 each) gives a 5% loss.
For rates like 'buy 3 for ₹1, sell 2 for ₹1', take the LCM of the counts or compare unit prices.
If a supplier gives n items for the price of m, the real CP of each item is m/n of its price.

steps: The price falls by ₹2, so a buyer gets 4 more apples for ₹720.
Let the original number be n: 720/n − 720/(n + 4) = 2.
This gives n(n + 4) = 1,440.
So n = 36, and the original price is ₹20 per apple.
blocks.title: Price cut gives more items

blocks.body: In 'CP of 20 = SP of 18', divide by 18, not 20. The base is the number actually sold. {PYQ 2026}

blocks.title: The missing cookie
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 128" role="img" aria-label="Twenty cookies with one held back"><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="16" text-anchor="middle">Charged for '1 kg' = 20 cookies, handed over 19</text><circle class="dota" cx="38" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="55" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="72" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="89" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="106" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="123" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="140" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="157" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="174" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="191" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="208" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="225" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="242" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="259" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="276" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="293" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="310" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="327" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="dota" cx="344" cy="44" r="7"/><circle class="lt" cx="361" cy="44" r="7"/><line class="lt" x1="31" y1="62" x2="351" y2="62"/><line class="lt" x1="31" y1="57" x2="31" y2="63"/><line class="lt" x1="351" y1="57" x2="351" y2="63"/><text class="tm sm" x="191" y="76" text-anchor="middle">19 given for ₹95</text><text class="tm sm" x="361" y="30" text-anchor="middle">kept</text><text class="tx sm" x="200" y="100" text-anchor="middle">Cost of 20 = ₹76, so cost of 19 = 76 × 19/20 = ₹72.20</text><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="118" text-anchor="middle">Gain = 95 − 72.20 = ₹22.80</text></svg>
blocks.cap: When fewer items are handed over than are charged for, cost only the items actually given.

blocks.q: A seller sold 19 cookies for ₹95 instead of 20 cookies in one kg, cheating a customer. What is the gain (in ₹) if the seller bought the cookies for ₹76?
steps: One 'kg' should have 20 cookies, and the seller's cost for those 20 is ₹76.
So one cookie costs him 76 ÷ 20 = ₹3.80.
He hands over only 19 cookies, so his real cost is 19 × 3.80 = ₹72.20.
He is paid ₹95, so his gain = 95 − 72.20 = ₹22.80.

blocks.q: The marked price of 55 items was equal to the cost price of 99 items. The selling price of 56 items was equal to the marked price of 35 items. Calculate the profit or loss percentage from the sale of each item.
steps: MP of 55 items = CP of 99 items, so MP of 1 item = 99/55 = 9/5 of the CP of 1 item.
SP of 56 items = MP of 35 items, so SP of 1 item = 35/56 = 5/8 of the MP of 1 item.
Take CP of 1 item = 5. Then MP = 9 and SP = 9 × 5/8 = 45/8 = 5.625.
Profit = 5.625 − 5 = 0.625 on a CP of 5, which is 0.625/5 × 100 = 12.5% profit.

blocks.q: A fruit vendor sells 15 kg of apples for ₹750, thereby gaining the cost price of 5 kg of apples. What is his profit percentage?
steps: On selling 15 kg he gains the cost price of 5 kg.
So profit/CP = (CP of 5 kg)/(CP of 15 kg) = 5/15 = 1/3.
Profit % = 1/3 × 100 = 33⅓%, which is about 33.33%. The ₹750 is not needed.

blocks.q: Total cost price of 1600 articles is Rs. 300. Total selling price of 10 articles is Rs. 3. What is the profit percentage? (Cost price of all the articles is same. Selling price of all the articles is same.)
steps: Compare the per-item rates.
CP per article = 300/1600 = ₹0.1875; SP per article = 3/10 = ₹0.30.
Profit per article = 0.30 − 0.1875 = ₹0.1125.
Answer: 60 percent.
blocks.trick: SP of 1600 articles = 160 × 3 = ₹480 against CP ₹300: profit 180/300 = 60%.

blocks.q: If the cost price of 15 articles is equal to the selling price of 12 articles, find the profit percentage.
steps: If CP of x items = SP of y items, the profit on y items sold equals the CP of (x − y) items.
Here x = 15 and y = 12, so the profit is the CP of 3 items on a cost of 12 items.
Answer: 25%.

blocks.body: Turn every 'CP of x = SP of y' or 'MP of a = CP of b' line into a per-item ratio, then multiply the ratios. The fraction left over is the profit or loss.

chapters.intro: This is the heart of the topic and appears in almost every shift. The seller first marks the price above cost, then gives a discount on the marked price, and what remains decides the profit. A handful of formulas answers nearly every version of the question.

steps: CP
Add markup m% on CP to get MP
Subtract discount d% on MP to get SP
Compare SP with CP for the profit or loss
blocks.title: The price journey

items.note: A 20% discount leaving SP ₹1,792 gives MP ₹2,240.
Discount 20% with a 10% gain gives CP : MP = 80 : 110 = 8 : 11.

items.f: Net % = m − d − md/100
items.note: 25% and 10% give 12.5%; 20% and 20% give a 4% loss; 26% and 32% give a 14.32% loss.

items.f: Discount for target profit p = (m − p)/(100 + m) × 100
Markup for profit p after discount d = (p + d)/(100 − d) × 100

blocks.q: A shopkeeper marks the price of his goods at 20% higher than the cost price and allows a discount of 10%. What is his profit percentage?
steps: A 10% discount on MP: SP = 120 × 90/100 = 108.
Answer: 8%

rows: No profit, no loss after markup m
Discount changes from d₁ to d₂
10% to 15% on ₹3,500 saves ₹175; a ₹400 saving means MP ₹8,000
Price raised x%, then y% discount

blocks.body: A trade discount is given by the manufacturer to the dealer on the list price, and a cash discount is given for immediate payment. Both are applied one after the other.

blocks.title: The price ladder
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 220" role="img" aria-label="Bars for CP 100, SP 110 and MP 137.5"><line class="ln" x1="30" y1="170" x2="390" y2="170"/><rect class="fl ln" x="60" y="70" width="70" height="100"/><text class="tb sm" x="95" y="64" text-anchor="middle">CP 100</text><rect class="fa2 ln" x="170" y="60" width="70" height="110"/><text class="tb sm" x="205" y="54" text-anchor="middle">SP 110</text><rect class="fa ln" x="280" y="32.5" width="70" height="137.5"/><text class="tb sm" x="315" y="26.5" text-anchor="middle">MP 137.5</text><text class="tx sm" x="115" y="188" text-anchor="middle">SP = CP × 1.1</text><text class="tx sm" x="262" y="188" text-anchor="middle">SP = MP × 0.8</text><text class="tm sm" x="210" y="210" text-anchor="middle">MP/CP = 110/80 = 1.375, so mark 37.5% above cost</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Profit 10% on CP and discount 20% on MP: the ladder shows why MP/CP = (100 + p)/(100 − d) = 110/80.

blocks.q: An article is marked at ₹550. If it is sold at a discount of 40%, then the selling price becomes 10% more than its cost price. What is the cost price (in ₹)?
steps: The MP is ₹550 and the discount is 40%, so SP = 550 × 0.6 = ₹330.
This SP is 10% more than CP, so SP = CP × 1.1.

blocks.q: Raghav purchased a shirt at Rs.1,500 and marked up the price of the shirt by 40%. What is the discount percentage he has to offer in order to get a profit of Rs.75?
steps: He wants a profit of ₹75, so SP = 1,500 + 75 = ₹1,575.
Discount % is out of MP: 525/2,100 × 100 = 25%.

blocks.q: Amit and Bilal buy goods for ₹1,500 and ₹2,000, respectively. Amit marks his goods up by y%, while Bilal marks his goods up by 2y% and offers a discount of y%. If both make the same profit, then find the value of y.
steps: Amit: CP ₹1,500, marked up y%, no discount. His profit = 1,500 × y/100 = 15y.
Both profits are equal: 2,000(1 + 2y/100)(1 − y/100) − 2,000 = 15y.

blocks.q: A dealer buys an article at a discount of 25% on its list price and marks it at 35% above the list price. If he allows a discount of 20% on the new marked price, find his profit percent.
steps: Take the list price as 100.
Cost price = 100 − 25% = 75.
Marked price = 100 + 35% = 135; selling price = 135 × 0.8 = 108.
The profit is 44%.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper buys an item at a discount of 20% on the marked price. He then marks it up by 50% above his cost price. If he offers a discount of 10% on this new marked price, what is his overall profit percentage on his cost price?
steps: Take the original marked price as 100; he buys at 20% off, so CP = 80.
He marks 50% above his CP: new MP = 80 × 1.5 = 120.
He gives 10% discount: SP = 120 × 0.9 = 108.
Answer: 35%
blocks.trick: Markup 50% then discount 10% on the same CP: 1.5 × 0.9 = 1.35, so 35% profit; the 20% purchase discount does not matter.

blocks.body: Keep one line in your head: MP/CP = (100 + profit %)/(100 − discount %). With any two of markup, discount and profit you can find the third in one step. {PYQ 2026}

chapters.intro: When two or more discounts are applied one after another, the second one works on an already reduced price. So the combined discount is always less than the simple sum. Multiply the remaining factors, and the order never changes the final price.

items.f: Single equivalent of a% and b% = a + b − ab/100
Three or more: 1 − (1 − a)(1 − b)(1 − c)
Single (a + b)% vs a% then b%: gap = ab/100 % of MP
items.note: 25% single vs 15% and 10% in succession: gap 1.5%.

blocks.title: Farther apart means a bigger discount

steps: MP ₹1,600, first discount 17%, final price ₹747.
After the first discount the price is 1,600 × 0.83 = 1,328.
747/1,328 = 0.5625 is what remains.
So the second discount is 1 − 0.5625 = 43.75%.
blocks.title: Finding a missing discount

items: A flat cash discount mixed with percentage discounts is applied in the stated order: ₹1,285 with ₹85 off, then 10% and 2%, gives 1,200 × 0.9 × 0.98 = ₹1,058.40.
For tier offers such as 10% above ₹500 plus 1% extra for cash, check which slab the bill falls in after each step, then multiply.

blocks.body: A bill had a gap of ₹28 between one 25% discount and successive discounts of 15% and 20%. The successive pair is 32%, so the gap is 7% of the bill, and the bill is ₹400.
blocks.title: CGL 2024
Why 10% + 20% is not 30%
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 430 170" role="img" aria-label="Bars showing successive discounts of 10 and 20 percent"><text class="tb sm" x="215" y="16" text-anchor="middle">10% off, then 20% off  vs  one 30% off</text><text class="tb sm" x="112" y="43" text-anchor="end">MP</text><rect class="fa ln" x="120" y="28" width="260" height="20"/><text class="tx sm" x="250" y="43" text-anchor="middle">100</text><text class="tb sm" x="112" y="73" text-anchor="end">after 10%</text><rect class="fa ln" x="120" y="58" width="234" height="20"/><rect class="lt" x="354" y="58" width="26" height="20"/><text class="tx sm" x="237" y="73" text-anchor="middle">90</text><text class="tb sm" x="112" y="103" text-anchor="end">after 20% more</text><rect class="fa ln" x="120" y="88" width="187.2" height="20"/><rect class="lt" x="307.2" y="88" width="46.8" height="20"/><text class="tx sm" x="213.6" y="103" text-anchor="middle">72</text><text class="tb sm" x="112" y="133" text-anchor="end">single 30%</text><rect class="fa2 ln" x="120" y="118" width="182" height="20"/><rect class="lt" x="302" y="118" width="78" height="20"/><text class="tx sm" x="211" y="133" text-anchor="middle">70</text><text class="tm sm" x="215" y="160" text-anchor="middle">second cut is 20% of 90 = 18, not 20% of 100</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The second discount works on the already reduced price, so two discounts together always take off less than their sum.

blocks.q: If, on a marked price, the difference between selling prices with a discount of 65% and with two successive discounts of 30% and 40% is ₹105, then the marked price (in ₹) is:
steps: Take MP = 100. A single 65% discount leaves 35.
Discounts of 30% and 40% leave 100 × 0.7 × 0.6 = 42.
The difference between the two selling prices is 42 − 35 = 7, that is 7% of MP.
blocks.trick: 30 and 40 combine to 30 + 40 − 12 = 58%. The gap from 65% is 7% of MP = 105, so MP = 1,500.

blocks.q: If successive discounts of 5%, 10% and p% are equivalent to a single discount of 31.6%, then the value of p is:
steps: A single discount of 31.6% leaves 68.4% of the price.
Discounts of 5% and 10% leave 0.95 × 0.9 = 0.855 of the price.
So the third factor is 0.684 ÷ 0.855 = 0.8.
A factor of 0.8 means p = 20%.

blocks.q: The printed price of a TV set is ₹14,500. It is sold for ₹10,000 with two consecutive discounts. If the first discount is 10%, then what is the second discount?
steps: Printed price ₹14,500. After the first 10% discount: 14,500 × 0.9 = ₹13,050.
The final price is ₹10,000, so the second discount = 13,050 − 10,000 = ₹3,050.

blocks.q: The difference between the selling prices with a discount of 32% and two successive discounts of 20% and 12% is ₹36. What is the marked price (in ₹) of the article?
steps: A single 32% discount leaves 68% of the MP.
Successive 20% and 12% discounts leave 0.80 × 0.88 = 0.704, i.e. 70.4% of the MP.
Difference = 70.4% − 68% = 2.4% of the MP = ₹36.
Answer: ₹1,500.
blocks.trick: Equivalent of 20% and 12% = 20 + 12 − 240/100 = 29.6%; the gap from 32% is 2.4%.

blocks.q: The marked price of an article is ₹ 2,500. A shopkeeper gives two successive discounts of 20% and 10%. What is the selling price of the article?
steps: Successive discounts are applied one after another, each on the price left by the previous one.
After 20% off, the price is 2,500 × 0.8 = 2,000.
After a further 10% off, it is 2,000 × 0.9 = 1,800.
Answer: ₹ 1,800.
blocks.trick: Single equivalent discount = 20 + 10 − 20 × 10/100 = 28%, and 72% of 2,500 = 1,800.

blocks.body: For any string of discounts, multiply what is left (0.9 × 0.8 × ...) and subtract from 1. To compare schemes with the same total, the pair that is farther apart gives the bigger discount. {PYQ 2026}

chapters.intro: Some questions give a bill and a set of rules: a discount that depends on the bill size, an extra cut for cash, students or a card, reward points worth a fixed sum, or a choice between two coupons. Nothing new is needed; the skill is reading the rules in order. Apply each rule to the amount that is left at that moment, and check each condition on the right amount.

blocks.title: A slab offer, then a cash offer
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 530 110" role="img" aria-label="Flow of a slab discount followed by a cash discount"><rect class="fl ln" x="10" y="26" width="150" height="50"/><text class="tx sm" x="85" y="46" text-anchor="middle">bill 25 × 30</text><text class="tb sm" x="85" y="66" text-anchor="middle">= ₹750</text><rect class="fl ln" x="190" y="26" width="150" height="50"/><text class="tx sm" x="265" y="46" text-anchor="middle">≥ ₹500: 10% off</text><text class="tb sm" x="265" y="66" text-anchor="middle">= ₹675</text><rect class="fa ln" x="370" y="26" width="150" height="50"/><text class="tx sm" x="445" y="46" text-anchor="middle">cash: 1% off</text><text class="tb sm" x="445" y="66" text-anchor="middle">= ₹668.25</text><line class="arr" x1="160" y1="51" x2="188" y2="51"/><path class="arr" d="M182.8 54 L188 51 L182.8 48"/><line class="arr" x1="340" y1="51" x2="368" y2="51"/><path class="arr" d="M362.8 54 L368 51 L362.8 48"/><text class="tm sm" x="265" y="100" text-anchor="middle">check the slab on the bill first, then apply each extra offer to what is left</text></svg>
blocks.cap: 25 packets at ₹30: the bill of ₹750 falls in the 10% slab, and the 1% cash cut is taken on ₹675, not on ₹750.

items: A percentage discount multiplies what is left; a flat rupee discount (cash back, reward points, a ₹85 coupon) subtracts.
The order matters when flat and percentage cuts are mixed: follow the order the question states.
Slabs ('more than ₹2,000', '₹500 and above') are checked on the amount the rule names, usually the amount after the earlier discount.
When only one coupon may be used, work out each one fully and pick the smaller bill.
Discounts that depend on how many items are bought (one rate for 1 book, another for 2) must be matched to the buyer's case first.

blocks.q: Raghav went to a shopping mall to purchase clothes. He had two coupons with him, but only one can be used on a single day. Using the first coupon, a total discount of 30% could be obtained on the total amount. Using the second coupon, he will get 80% off on the price of the costliest shirt if he buys at least 3 shirts. What is the price at which Raghav can purchase 3 shirts at a minimum price if the prices of the three shirts are Rs.1,250, Rs.1,540 and Rs.1,375?
steps: Total of the three shirts = 1,250 + 1,540 + 1,375 = ₹4,165.
Coupon 1 takes 30% off the total: 4,165 × 0.7 = ₹2,915.50.
Coupon 2 takes 80% off the costliest shirt only: 80% of 1,540 = ₹1,232, so he pays 4,165 − 1,232 = ₹2,933.
Only one coupon can be used, so the minimum is ₹2,915.50 with coupon 1.

blocks.q: An electronic store owner allows two successive discounts of 20% and 25% on each item. The store has a reward points scheme which enables a customer to get free shopping worth ₹0.10 on every 1 reward point credited to the customer’s account on previous purchases from the store. A customer decides to buy a laptop that is marked at ₹72,000. What will be its net selling price if he has 2850 reward points to his credit?
steps: Two successive discounts of 20% and 25%: 72,000 × 0.8 × 0.75 = ₹43,200.
Reward points: 2,850 × ₹0.10 = ₹285 of free shopping.

blocks.q: A discount of 20% is given for the purchase of two books by a bookseller and a discount of 25% is offered if a customer buys more than two books. A 10% discount is being offered to all the customers on purchase of one book. An additional 5% discount will be given to students. Sohan, a student of M.Com. in college, bought a book for Rs.513. What was the marked price of the book?
steps: Sohan bought one book, so the one-book discount of 10% applies (not the 20% or 25%).
He is a student, so a further 5% is taken off: factor = 0.9 × 0.95 = 0.855.

blocks.body: Write the bill as a chain: amount → check slab → × factor → − flat amount → × next factor. Doing one line per rule stops you from applying a slab to the wrong amount.

chapters.h: Free items and 'buy x, get y' offers
chapters.intro: In a free-item offer the customer pays for some items but carries home more. The discount is the number of free items divided by the number taken home. Read the wording carefully, because 'buy 4, get 6' and 'buy 4, get 6 free' are very different deals.

items.f: Buy x, get y free  ⇒  discount = y/(x + y) × 100
items.note: Pay for x, take x + y.

items.f: n items for the price of m, sold at d% off  ⇒  profit factor = (1 − d/100) × n/m

items: When y items are free with every x sold, as in a bakery giving 1 free with every 9, revenue comes from x out of every x + y items.
Combine this with any percentage discount and any promotional give-aways before computing the total SP. {PYQ 2026}
To compare schemes, turn every scheme into one effective discount percentage, then compare.

blocks.title: Paid and free boxes
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 390 128" role="img" aria-label="Seven boxes, five paid and two free"><text class="tb sm" x="195" y="16" text-anchor="middle">Buy 5, get 2 free</text><rect class="fl ln" x="40" y="30" width="38" height="34"/><text class="tm sm" x="59" y="52" text-anchor="middle">paid</text><rect class="fl ln" x="84" y="30" width="38" height="34"/><text class="tm sm" x="103" y="52" text-anchor="middle">paid</text><rect class="fl ln" x="128" y="30" width="38" height="34"/><text class="tm sm" x="147" y="52" text-anchor="middle">paid</text><rect class="fl ln" x="172" y="30" width="38" height="34"/><text class="tm sm" x="191" y="52" text-anchor="middle">paid</text><rect class="fl ln" x="216" y="30" width="38" height="34"/><text class="tm sm" x="235" y="52" text-anchor="middle">paid</text><rect class="fa ln" x="260" y="30" width="38" height="34"/><text class="tm sm" x="279" y="52" text-anchor="middle">free</text><rect class="fa ln" x="304" y="30" width="38" height="34"/><text class="tm sm" x="323" y="52" text-anchor="middle">free</text><line class="lt" x1="40" y1="76" x2="342" y2="76"/><line class="lt" x1="40" y1="71" x2="40" y2="77"/><line class="lt" x1="342" y1="71" x2="342" y2="77"/><text class="tm sm" x="191" y="90" text-anchor="middle">takes home 7</text><text class="tx sm" x="195" y="118" text-anchor="middle">discount = free/taken = 2/7 = 28 4/7%   (not 2/5)</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The discount is measured on everything the customer takes home, so the free items go over the total, not over the paid ones.

blocks.q: During a new-year sale, a shopkeeper offers a discount scheme to his customers, ‘Buy 5 Sweaters, Get 2 Sweaters Free’. Find the effective percentage discount given by the shopkeeper.
steps: The customer pays for 5 sweaters and takes home 5 + 2 = 7.
He gets 2 of the 7 free, so the discount = 2/7 of the price of what he takes.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper offers the following two discount schemes. A) Buy 3 get 4 free B) Buy 5 get 6 free Which scheme has the maximum discount percentage?
o: A does not give any discount
A and B both have the same discount percentage
steps: Scheme A, buy 3 get 4 free: pay for 3, take 7. Discount = 4/7 = 57.14%.
Scheme B, buy 5 get 6 free: pay for 5, take 11. Discount = 6/11 = 54.55%.
57.14% > 54.55%, so scheme A gives the bigger discount.
blocks.trick: Compare free/total: 4/7 against 6/11. Cross-multiply: 4 × 11 = 44 and 6 × 7 = 42, so 4/7 is larger.

blocks.q: A sweet shop owner buys 10 boxes of sweets for the price of 8 boxes from a wholesaler. If he sells each box at a 2% discount on its marked price, what is his profit percentage?
steps: Take the marked price of one box as ₹1. He buys 10 boxes for the price of 8, so he pays ₹8 for 10 boxes.
His CP per box = 8 ÷ 10 = ₹0.80.
He sells each box at a 2% discount, so SP = ₹0.98.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper offers a fixed discount of 15% on rice and 100 gm rice free with every purchase of 1.9 kg rice. Find the overall discount percent offered by him on rice.
steps: The free rice is a hidden discount: pay for 1.9 kg, take 2 kg, so 0.1/2 = 5% of the goods is free.
Combine it with the 15% discount: let the marked price be ₹1 per kg; 2 kg is worth ₹2.
blocks.trick: Successive discounts of 15% and 5%: 15 + 5 − (15 × 5)/100 = 19.25%.

blocks.body: Change every offer into one number, the fraction of the goods that is free: buy x get y free is y/(x + y), and n for the price of m is (n − m)/n. Then compare the numbers.

chapters.intro: A dishonest trader gains by charging for more than he gives. If he charges for 1,000 g but hands over only 900 g, he earns on the 100 g he kept back, and his gain is measured against what he actually gave. Every false-weight question uses one factor: price factor divided by the fraction of weight actually given.

items.f: Profit factor = (SP factor) × (weight charged for)/(weight actually given)
Sold at CP with w g for 1 kg  ⇒  gain % = (1000 − w)/w × 100
items.note: 900 g gives 11 1/9%; 870 g gives 14.94%; 800 g gives 25%.

items.f: Weight used for gain g at CP = 1000/(1 + g/100)
items.note: 12.5% gain uses 888.9 g; 15% gain uses 869.6 g.

rows: ₹48 claimed for a ₹50 cost, 900 g given

items: A faulty metre scale works the same way, using centimetres instead of grams.
An advertised 7% loss that is really a 24% gain means 0.93/L = 1.24, so the scale is 0.75 m, or 75 cm.
A machine that shows 400 g for 350 g gives the customer only 350/400 of what he pays for, so scale all quantities by that ratio.

blocks.body: When a trader cheats by x% while buying and x% while selling, SSC keys used (1 + x)/(1 − x) for 'gets 10% more and gives 10% less'. For 'cheats by 12% each time' the 2022 key used 1.12 × 1.12 = 25.44%, so check which result appears in the options.
blocks.title: Read the cheating wording
Charged for 1 kg, given 800 g
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 430 128" role="img" aria-label="Bars comparing 1000 g charged with 800 g given"><text class="tb sm" x="215" y="16" text-anchor="middle">Sold at CP, but 800 g given for every 1 kg</text><text class="tb sm" x="112" y="45" text-anchor="end">charged for</text><rect class="fl ln" x="120" y="30" width="260" height="22"/><text class="tx sm" x="250" y="45" text-anchor="middle">1000 g</text><text class="tb sm" x="112" y="83" text-anchor="end">actually given</text><rect class="fa ln" x="120" y="68" width="208" height="22"/><text class="tx sm" x="224" y="83" text-anchor="middle">800 g</text><rect class="lt" x="328" y="68" width="52" height="22"/><text class="tm sm" x="354" y="83" text-anchor="middle">kept</text><text class="tx sm" x="215" y="118" text-anchor="middle">gain = 200/800 = 25%, because his cost is only for 800 g</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The gain is the weight kept back divided by the weight actually given, because only the given weight cost him money.

blocks.q: A grocer professes to sell rice at the cost price, but uses a fake weight of 870 g for 1 kg. Find his profit percentage (correct to two decimal places).
steps: He charges for 1,000 g at cost price but gives only 870 g.
What he gains per 'kilogram' is the cost of 1,000 − 870 = 130 g.
His real cost is for 870 g, so gain % = 130/870 × 100.

blocks.q: Ramesh sells rice at ₹36 per kg, which he purchased for ₹30 per kg. Moreover, he gives only 800 g of rice instead of 1 kg while selling. Find the actual profit percentage of Ramesh.
steps: Ramesh pays ₹30 for 1 kg, so 800 g costs him 30 × 0.8 = ₹24.
He charges ₹36 for what he calls 1 kg, but hands over only those 800 g.
Profit = 36 − 24 = ₹12 on a cost of ₹24.
blocks.trick: Price factor 36/30 = 1.2; weight factor 0.8. 1.2 ÷ 0.8 = 1.5, so 50%.

blocks.q: A dishonest merchant sells goods at a 12.5% loss on the cost price, but uses 28 g weight instead of 36 g. What is his percentage profit or loss?
steps: The 12.5% loss on cost price means he charges 0.875 of the true price of the weight he claims.
He claims 36 g but gives only 28 g, so he gives 28/36 of the goods.
1.125 means a gain of 12.5%.
blocks.trick: In fractions: loss 1/8 gives 7/8; 7/8 × 36/28 = 7/8 × 9/7 = 9/8, a gain of 1/8.

blocks.body: One formula covers every false-weight question: profit factor = (price factor) × (weight charged)/(weight given). Put a profit as 1 + p, a loss as 1 − l, then subtract 1 at the end.

chapters.intro: When an article passes from a manufacturer to a wholesaler to a retailer, each person applies his own percentage to his own buying price. So the final price is the first CP multiplied by every factor in turn. To go backwards, divide by the same factors.

steps: Manufacturer's CP
× (1 + wholesaler's profit)
× (1 + retailer's profit)
= price paid by the customer
blocks.title: The chain

rows: ₹1,250 sold at 18% gain, then at 10% loss
Three hands, total 65%, first two 20% and 25%
₹42,000 sold at 20% loss, proceeds reinvested at 30% gain

items.title: Same SP, x% gain and x% loss
points: The result is always a net loss of x²/100 %.
Two cows at ₹15,640 each with ±15% cost 13,600 and 18,400.
The total loss is ₹720.

items.title: Same CP, gains a% and b%
points: The overall result is the simple average (a + b)/2 %.
8% gain and 6% loss on ₹4,000 each give a net 1% of 8,000.
That is a gain of ₹80.

items: A wholesaler's markup and trade discount plus a retailer's markup and festival discount make four factors.
Multiply all four, then divide the customer price by the product to get the first CP.

blocks.title: A two-dealer chain
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 134" role="img" aria-label="A chain of two dealers"><rect class="fl ln" x="20" y="30" width="80" height="34"/><text class="tb sm" x="60" y="52" text-anchor="middle">CP 100</text><rect class="fl ln" x="180" y="30" width="80" height="34"/><text class="tb sm" x="220" y="52" text-anchor="middle">130</text><rect class="fa ln" x="340" y="30" width="80" height="34"/><text class="tb sm" x="380" y="52" text-anchor="middle">140</text><line class="arr" x1="100" y1="47" x2="178" y2="47"/><path class="arr" d="M172.8 50 L178 47 L172.8 44"/><line class="arr" x1="260" y1="47" x2="338" y2="47"/><path class="arr" d="M332.8 50 L338 47 L332.8 44"/><text class="tx sm" x="139" y="24" text-anchor="middle">dealer 1: × 1.3</text><text class="tx sm" x="299" y="24" text-anchor="middle">dealer 2: × ?</text><line class="lt" x1="20" y1="82" x2="420" y2="82"/><line class="lt" x1="20" y1="77" x2="20" y2="83"/><line class="lt" x1="420" y1="77" x2="420" y2="83"/><text class="tm sm" x="220" y="96" text-anchor="middle">whole journey: × 1.4 (40% on the first CP)</text><text class="tb sm" x="220" y="124" text-anchor="middle">? = 1.4 ÷ 1.3 = 14/13, so dealer 2 gains 1/13 = 7 9/13%</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Each dealer's percentage is on his own buying price, so the factors multiply; dividing the total factor by one dealer's factor gives the other.

blocks.q: An article passing through two hands is sold at a total profit of 40% of the original cost price. If the first dealer makes a profit of 30%, then the profit percentage made by the second dealer is:
steps: Take the original CP as 100. The total profit is 40%, so the final price is 140.
The first dealer makes 30%, so he sells to the second dealer at 130.
The second dealer buys at 130 and sells at 140, a profit of 10 on 130.
blocks.trick: 1.4 ÷ 1.3 = 14/13, so the second dealer's profit is 1/13 = 7 9/13%.

blocks.q: A wholesaler sells a packet of tea to a retailer at a profit of 20%. The retailer then marks up the price by 50% and offers a discount of 20% to the customer. If the customer pays Rs. 480, find the cost price of the packet for the wholesaler.
steps: Let the wholesaler's cost be C. He sells at a 20% profit, so the retailer's CP = 1.2C.
The retailer marks up 50%: MP = 1.2C × 1.5 = 1.8C.
He gives a 20% discount: SP = 1.8C × 0.8 = 1.44C.
The customer pays ₹480, so 1.44C = 480 and C = 480 ÷ 1.44 = ₹333.33.

blocks.q: A wholesaler marks up the price of a microwave oven by 60% above its cost price. He gives a 15% trade discount to a retailer. The retailer, in turn, marks up the price by 25% above his purchase price and offers a 10% festival discount to the customer. If the customer finally pays ₹14,490 for the microwave, what is the original approximate cost price of the oven to the wholesaler?
steps: Wholesaler: MP = 1.6 × CP, then a 15% trade discount, so the retailer pays 1.6 × 0.85 = 1.36 × CP.
Retailer: marks up 25% and gives a 10% festival discount, a factor of 1.25 × 0.9 = 1.125.
Total factor = 1.36 × 1.125 = 1.53, so the customer pays 1.53 × CP.

blocks.q: Arvind bought an article for ₹x. He sold it to Biru at a loss of 20%. Biru spent ₹140 on its transportation and sold it to Minu at a profit of 46%. If Minu bought it for ₹1,752, then what is the value of x?
steps: Work backwards from Minu's price.
Biru sold at 46% profit: his total cost = 1752 ÷ 1.46 = ₹1,200.
This includes ₹140 transport, so Biru paid Arvind 1200 − 140 = ₹1,060.
Arvind sold at 20% loss: 0.8x = 1060, so x = 1060 ÷ 0.8 = 1325.

blocks.q: Ravi sold an item to Shyam at a profit of 20%. Shyam spent ₹200 on repairs and sold it to Mohan at a loss of 10%. If Mohan bought it for ₹1,620, what was the original cost price for Ravi?
steps: Work backwards from Mohan's price. Shyam sold at a 10% loss, so his total cost = 1,620 ÷ 0.9 = ₹1,800.
Shyam's total cost includes ₹200 of repairs, so he paid Ravi 1,800 − 200 = ₹1,600.
Ravi sold at 20% profit: 1,600 = 1.2 × Ravi's cost.
Answer: ₹1,333

blocks.body: Write one factor per step of the chain (markups and profits above 1, discounts and losses below 1), multiply them, and divide the last price by the product to get the first CP.

chapters.intro: When more than one item or lot is involved, percentages cannot simply be averaged, because each sits on a different cost price. Find each cost price in rupees, add them up, and compute the overall percentage once. For two profit rates, alligation gives the quantities quickly.

steps: Take the SPs in the given ratio, for example 5, 6 and 7.
Add the CPs to get 16.22 and compare with the total SP of 18.
Overall profit = 1.78/16.22, about 10.99%.
blocks.title: Items with SPs in a ratio

items.f: qty₁ : qty₂ = (p₂ − p̄) : (p̄ − p₁)
items.note: Alligation on profit %. 1,000 kg sold partly at 10% and partly at 40% for 20% overall gives 2 : 1, so 333⅓ kg at 40%.

items.f: Loss fraction on cutting = 1 − Σaᵢ²/(Σaᵢ)²

items: For a lot sold in fractions at different rates, add the SPs so far and see what the last part must fetch.
For example, ₹3,600 of apples with a 27% overall target leaves ₹1,584 for the last part.
For a mixture sold at one rate, total CP = Σ quantity × rate and total SP = total quantity × selling rate.
Prices like '5 for ₹20' or '2 for ₹9' must be changed to a price per item before weighting by the mixing ratio.
Investment split: ₹5,000 at +10% and −5% with a net ₹100 profit gives 0.15x − 250 = 100, so x = ₹2,333.33 at +10%.
Wastage: 200 flowers for ₹800 with 20 wasted and a 30% target means ₹1,040 from 180 flowers, so ₹5.78 each.

blocks.body: A 20% profit on one item and a 10% loss on another is not a 5% profit overall, because the two percentages sit on different cost prices.

blocks.title: Alligation on profit %
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 196" role="img" aria-label="Alligation cross for 20 and 12 percent giving 18 percent"><text class="tb lg" x="70" y="30" text-anchor="middle">20%</text><text class="tb lg" x="250" y="30" text-anchor="middle">12%</text><text class="tm sm" x="70" y="48" text-anchor="middle">part A</text><text class="tm sm" x="250" y="48" text-anchor="middle">part B</text><circle class="fl ln" cx="160" cy="96" r="26"/><text class="tb sm" x="160" y="101" text-anchor="middle">18%</text><line class="lt" x1="90" y1="56" x2="140" y2="80"/><line class="lt" x1="230" y1="56" x2="180" y2="80"/><line class="lt" x1="140" y1="112" x2="90" y2="138"/><line class="lt" x1="180" y1="112" x2="230" y2="138"/><text class="tx sm" x="70" y="156" text-anchor="middle">18 − 12 = 6</text><text class="tx sm" x="250" y="156" text-anchor="middle">20 − 18 = 2</text><text class="tb sm" x="160" y="186" text-anchor="middle">A : B = 6 : 2 = 3 : 1</text></svg>
blocks.cap: The quantities go in the ratio of the opposite distances from the overall profit %: the rate closer to the average gets the bigger share.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper has 2220 kg of rice. A part of which he sells at a 20% profit and the rest at a 12% profit. He gains 18% on the whole. The quantity (in kg) sold at a 12% profit is:
steps: Part A is sold at 20% profit and part B at 12% profit; the whole gives 18%.
The 12% part is 1 of 4 parts: 2,220 × 1/4 = 555 kg.

blocks.q: Samreen sells a keyboard for ₹1,260 at a profit of 25%, and another keyboard for ₹1,440 at a loss of 10%. What is her total gain or loss percentage?
steps: Keyboard 1: SP ₹1,260 at a 25% profit, so CP = 1,260 ÷ 1.25 = ₹1,008.
Keyboard 2: SP ₹1,440 at a 10% loss, so CP = 1,440 ÷ 0.9 = ₹1,600.
575/163 = 3 86/163, so the answer is a gain of 3 86/163% (about 3.53%).

blocks.q: During a sale, 50% of the goods are sold at 37% profit, 30% of the remaining goods are sold at 26% profit and the still remaining goods are sold at a loss of 24%. If there is an overall profit of x%, then what is the value of x?
steps: Rule: do not average the percentages; turn each part into rupees of profit on a common cost.
Take a cost of ₹100 for all the goods. The first 50% (₹50) at 37% profit gives ₹18.50.
30% of the remaining ₹50 is ₹15, sold at 26% profit: ₹3.90.
The last ₹35 at a 24% loss: −₹8.40.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper mixes two types of rice costing ₹250/5 kg and ₹280/5 kg in the ratio 7 : 8. Find the net cost of the resultant mixture (per kg).
steps: First rice: ₹250 for 5 kg = ₹50 per kg. Second rice: ₹280 for 5 kg = ₹56 per kg.
Mixed 7 : 8, so take 7 kg and 8 kg: cost = 7 × 50 + 8 × 56 = 350 + 448 = ₹798.
Total weight = 15 kg, so cost per kg = 798 ÷ 15 = ₹53.20.

blocks.body: Never average percentages that sit on different CPs. Turn every item into rupees (CP and SP), add, and take one percentage at the end. Use alligation only when the parts are measured on the same base. {PYQ 2026}

chapters.intro: SSC tags a few partnership questions under Profit & Loss each year. Profit is shared in the ratio of capital multiplied by the time it was invested. Anything set aside first, such as charity or a working partner's salary, comes off before the split.

steps: Take the total profit.
Remove charity, reserve or the working partner's salary first.
Share the rest in the capital × time ratio.
Add the salary back to the working partner.
blocks.title: Order of sharing

blocks.body: With 9% charity on ₹2,50,000 and a split of 2 : 3 : 5, the shareable profit is ₹2,27,500, so C gets half of it, which is ₹1,13,750.

blocks.title: Charity first, then the split
blocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 380 122" role="img" aria-label="Profit bar with charity and the 9 to 5 split"><text class="tb sm" x="200" y="16" text-anchor="middle">Whole profit P</text><rect class="fa2 ln" x="30" y="28" width="32" height="30"/><rect class="fa ln" x="62" y="28" width="185.1" height="30"/><rect class="fl ln" x="247.1" y="28" width="102.9" height="30"/><text class="tx sm" x="46" y="47" text-anchor="middle">10%</text><text class="tx sm" x="154.6" y="47" text-anchor="middle">A: 9 parts</text><text class="tx sm" x="298.6" y="47" text-anchor="middle">B: 5 parts</text><text class="tm sm" x="46" y="22" text-anchor="middle">charity</text><line class="lt" x1="62" y1="72" x2="350" y2="72"/><line class="lt" x1="62" y1="67" x2="62" y2="73"/><line class="lt" x1="350" y1="67" x2="350" y2="73"/><text class="tm sm" x="206" y="86" text-anchor="middle">90% of P shared 9 : 5</text><text class="tb sm" x="190" y="112" text-anchor="middle">A = 0.9P × 9/14 = ₹29,840</text></svg>
blocks.cap: Anything set aside comes off the whole profit before the partners' ratio is applied.

blocks.q: A and B invested their money in a business in the ratio of 9 : 5. If 10% of the total profit goes for charity and A’s share is Rs.29,840, what is the total profit (in Rs., to the nearest integer)?
steps: Let the total profit be P. Charity takes 10%, so 0.9P is shared.
A and B share in the ratio of their money, 9 : 5, so A gets 9/14 of 0.9P.

blocks.body: Profit shares follow capital × time. Make the money-months for each partner, cancel to a small ratio, remove any charity or salary first, and then share.

chapters.intro: Real SSC CGL questions, plus practice questions for the kinds SSC has not asked yet, each worked from the first line. Try each one, then open the solution.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper makes a net profit of 44% on selling an article at successive discounts of 10% and 20%. Find the net profit percentage, if the shopkeeper sells the same article at a discount of 15%.
steps: Take CP = 100. With successive discounts of 10% and 20%, SP = MP × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72 × MP.
This gives a 44% profit, so SP = 144.
With a single 15% discount instead, SP = 200 × 0.85 = 170.
Profit = 170 − 100 = 70 on a CP of 100, so the profit is 70%.
blocks.title: Markup, discount and profit

blocks.q: A Microwave oven is sold in Hyderabad for Rs.M. A retailer, Elahi from Hyderabad went to Madras and bought it for 25% less (when compared to the price in Hyderabad). He spends Rs.1,000 on transport to bring it from Madras to Hyderabad. He sold it in Hyderabad for Rs.M making a profit of 10%. Find the value of M (in Rs.).
steps: In Madras the oven costs 25% less than M, so Elahi pays 0.75M.
He adds ₹1,000 for transport, so his total cost = 0.75M + 1,000.
He sells it for M at a 10% profit: M = 1.1 × (0.75M + 1,000) = 0.825M + 1,100.

blocks.q: A furniture store marks its items at 80% above the cost price. They offer a discount of 30% on the marked price. If a customer receives an additional loyalty discount of ₹250, and the store still makes a 12% profit on the cost price, what is the cost price of the furniture item?
steps: Let the CP be x. The store marks it 80% above cost: MP = 1.8x.
A 30% discount gives 1.8x × 0.7 = 1.26x.
The loyalty discount takes off a flat ₹250, so SP = 1.26x − 250.
The store still makes 12%, so SP = 1.12x.
blocks.trick: The ₹250 flat cut is the gap between 126% and 112% of CP, that is 14% of CP.

blocks.q: An article costs Rs.4,000 to a shopkeeper, who marks its price at Rs.8,400. The shopkeeper sells it to a customer at a discount of 25%. The customer gets a further discount of 15% on the discounted price if the customer redeems a coupon issued by the store previously. What is the profit percentage (to the nearest integer) earned by the shopkeeper in this transaction?
steps: The coupon takes a further 15% off: 6,300 × 0.85 = ₹5,355.
Profit % = 1,355/4,000 × 100 = 33.875%, which is 34% to the nearest integer.

blocks.q: After allowing a discount of 15%, the value of a washing machine is ₹29,750. If no discount is allowed, then the shopkeeper gains 12%. The cost price of the washing machine is:
steps: After a 15% discount the price is ₹29,750, so MP = 29,750 ÷ 0.85 = ₹35,000.
With no discount the shopkeeper sells at MP and gains 12%, so 35,000 = CP × 1.12.

blocks.q: A saree bought for ₹500 is marked at 16% profit and later on sold at a sales discount of x% on the marked price. If the selling price of the saree is ₹493, find the value of x.
steps: The saree costs ₹500 and is marked at a 16% profit: MP = 500 × 1.16 = ₹580.
It is sold for ₹493, so the discount = 580 − 493 = ₹87.
Discount % is on MP: 87/580 × 100 = 15%. So x = 15.

blocks.q: A merchant marked an article such that its price was 25% above its cost price. He offered two consecutive discounts of 10% and 20% to a buyer. If he incurred a loss of ₹400, what was the marked price of the article?
steps: Take CP = 100. The MP is 25% above cost: MP = 125.
Successive discounts of 10% and 20%: SP = 125 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 90.
SP = 90 on CP = 100 is a 10% loss.
This loss is ₹400, so 10% of CP = 400 and CP = ₹4,000.

blocks.q: The difference between a discount of 40% and two successive discounts of 30% on a certain bill was ₹220. Find the amount of the bill (in ₹).
steps: Take the bill as 100. A single 40% discount leaves 60.
Two successive 30% discounts leave 100 × 0.7 × 0.7 = 49, a total discount of 51%.
The difference between the two discounts = 51 − 40 = 11% of the bill.
blocks.title: Successive discounts and schemes

blocks.q: Applied to a bill for ₹50,000, the difference between a discount of 40% and two successive discounts of 36% and 4%,is :
steps: A single 40% discount leaves 60% of ₹50,000 = ₹30,000.

blocks.q: A trader offers the following discount schemes on the purchase of a refrigerator. ( I ) a discount of 10% followed by a discount of 8% ( ii ) successive discounts of 12% and 10% ( iii ) two successive discounts of 12% ( iv ) a discount of 20% In which scheme is the selling price the lowest?
steps: Scheme (i): 10% then 8% leaves 0.9 × 0.92 = 0.828, a discount of 17.2%.
Scheme (ii): 12% then 10% leaves 0.88 × 0.9 = 0.792, a discount of 20.8%.
Scheme (iii): 12% twice leaves 0.88 × 0.88 = 0.7744, a discount of 22.56%.
Scheme (iv): a single 20% leaves 0.8.
The lowest SP comes from the smallest factor left, 0.7744, so scheme (iii).

blocks.q: A shopkeeper offers the following discount schemes for buyers on an article: i. Two successive discounts of 15% each ii. A discount of 25% followed by a discount of 5% iii. Two successive discounts of 20% and 10% iv. A discount of 30% Under which scheme will the selling price be maximum?
steps: The selling price is highest when the total discount is smallest.
(iv) a single 30%.
The smallest discount is 27.75%, so the SP is maximum under scheme i.
blocks.trick: Pairs (i), (ii), (iii) all add to 30; the equal pair (15, 15) has the biggest ab/100, so it is the weakest discount.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper gives a 12% additional discount on the discounted price, after giving an initial discount of 25% on the labelled price of a radio. If the final selling price of the radio is ₹792, then what is its labelled price (in ₹)?
steps: Discounts of 25% and then 12% leave 0.75 × 0.88 = 0.66 of the labelled price.
0.66 × labelled price = ₹792.
Labelled price = 792 ÷ 0.66 = ₹1,200.

blocks.q: An oven has a marked price of ₹12,000. It is sold with two successive discounts. If the second discount is 20% and the final selling price is ₹8,400, what is the percentage of the first discount?
steps: Let the first discount be x. Then 12,000 × (1 − x) × 0.8 = 8,400.

blocks.q: R’s weighing machine shows 400 gm when the actual weight is 350 gm. The cost price of almonds is ₹880 per kg and packets of 200 gm are made using the faulty machine. What should be the selling price (in ₹) of each packet to get a profit of 25%?
steps: The machine shows 400 g when the real weight is 350 g, so every reading is 350/400 = 7/8 of the truth.
A packet that shows 200 g really holds 200 × 7/8 = 175 g.
Almonds cost ₹880 per kg, so 175 g costs 880 × 0.175 = ₹154.
For a 25% profit, SP = 154 × 1.25 = ₹192.50 per packet.
blocks.title: False weights and faulty machines

blocks.q: The cost price and selling price of rice are the same. Due to a faulty weighing machine, the seller earns a 15% profit. If Rs. x is the cost price of 1000 gm rice and the machine is changed which shows 1000 gm instead of 950 gm, what should be the selling price (in ₹) now to get the same percentage of profit?
steps: Now the machine shows 1,000 g when only 950 g is on it, so a customer who pays for '1,000 g' gets 950 g.
The real cost of what he gives = 0.95x, since x is the cost of 1,000 g.
For the same 15% profit, SP = 1.15 × 0.95x = 1.0925x.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper has a fault of 100 g in a 3 kg weight. He sold 3 kg of potatoes to Charu using the same faulty weight for ₹46. The cost price of the potatoes for the seller was ₹12 per kg. How much profit (in ₹) did he earn on the potatoes?
steps: A fault of 100 g in a 3 kg weight means Charu gets 3,000 − 100 = 2,900 g, that is 2.9 kg.
Cost to the seller = 2.9 × 12 = ₹34.80.
He charges ₹46, so profit = 46 − 34.80 = ₹11.20.

blocks.q: A dishonest dealer sells the goods at 7% loss on cost price but uses 18% less weight. What is his percentage of profit? (Correct to 2 decimal places)
steps: A 7% loss on cost price means the price factor is 0.93.
18% less weight means he gives 0.82 of what he charges for.
So the profit is 13.41%.

blocks.q: A businessman cheats by using faulty weights, to the tune of 12% each time, when buying and selling material. What is the rise in his profit percentage using faulty weights only?
steps: While buying he takes 12% more goods than he pays for, so each rupee buys 1.12 times the goods.
While selling he charges for 12% more than he gives, so the goods earn 1.12 times as much again.
The two effects multiply: 1.12 × 1.12 = 1.2544.
So his profit from the faulty weights alone is 25.44%.
blocks.trick: Two successive 12% gains: 12 + 12 + 144/100 = 25.44%.

blocks.q: If a shopkeeper sells sugar at ₹44.8 per kg, he is able to make a 12% profit. Due to water seepage, 1/5 of the sugar is damaged. What should now be the selling price per kg of the rest of the sugar to have a 5% profit?
steps: At ₹44.8 per kg he makes 12%, so the CP = 44.8 ÷ 1.12 = ₹40 per kg.
Take 1 kg of sugar costing ₹40. One-fifth is damaged, so only 4/5 kg = 0.8 kg is left to sell.
For a 5% profit on the whole cost, he needs 40 × 1.05 = ₹42 from that 0.8 kg.
blocks.title: Several items, parts and damaged stock

blocks.q: Ramesh purchased 130 books at the rate of ₹200 each and sold half of them at the rate of ₹300 each, one-fifth of them at the rate of ₹350 each and the rest at the cost price. Find his profit percentage.
steps: Half the books, 65, sell at ₹300: 65 × 300 = ₹19,500.
blocks.trick: Per book: half gain 100 (50%), one-fifth gain 150 (75%), rest 0. Overall = ½ × 50% + ⅕ × 75% = 25% + 15% = 40%.

blocks.q: Three-fourth of a consignment was sold at a profit of 8% and the rest at a loss of 4%. If there was an overall profit of Rs.600, then find the value of the consignment.
steps: Let the value (cost) be V. Three-fourths earns 8%: profit = 0.75V × 0.08 = 0.06V.
One-fourth loses 4%: loss = 0.25V × 0.04 = 0.01V.

blocks.q: A shopkeeper earns 10% on an investment but loses 20% on another investment. If the ratio of the two investments is 2 : 3, then the combined loss percentage is:
steps: Take the investments as 2 and 3, a total of 5.
Gain on the first = 10% of 2 = 0.2. Loss on the second = 20% of 3 = 0.6.

blocks.q: A seller bought three different types of mobile covers, C1, C2 and C3. The ratio of their selling prices was 3 : 4 : 5. He made a profit of 25% on C1 and 10% on C2, but incurred a loss of 20% on C3. What was his approximate percent gain or loss in the entire transaction?
steps: Take the SPs as 3, 4 and 5 (total 12).
Total CP = 2.4 + 3.636 + 6.25 = 12.286, more than the total SP of 12, so it is a loss.

blocks.q: Sita sold a whiteboard marker set at 10% profit. On selling it for Rs.20 more, she would have earned a profit of 15%. What is the cost price of the whiteboard marker set? www.exammix.com
steps: At the first price the profit is 10%, so SP₁ = 1.10 × CP.
Selling for ₹20 more gives 15%, so SP₂ = 1.15 × CP.
The ₹20 is the extra 5% of CP: 0.05 × CP = 20.
blocks.title: Changing CP or SP

blocks.q: A pen was sold for Rs.166.44 with a profit of 14%. If it were sold for Rs.154.76, then what would have been the percentage of profit or loss?
steps: At ₹154.76, the SP is still above ₹146, so it is a profit.

blocks.q: By selling a watch for ₹2,000, a shopkeeper loses 20%. How much would he gain or lose by selling it for ₹3,000?
blocks.trick: 3,000/2,000 = 1.5, so the factor becomes 0.8 × 1.5 = 1.2, a 20% gain.

blocks.q: If books bought at prices ranging from ₹200 to ₹260 are sold at prices ranging from ₹250 to 300, what is the greatest possible profit that might be made in selling 25 books?
steps: The greatest profit comes from buying at the lowest cost and selling at the highest price.
Lowest CP = ₹200 and highest SP = ₹300, so the greatest profit on one book = ₹100.
blocks.trick: Greatest profit = (max SP − min CP) × number; least profit = (min SP − max CP) × number.
blocks.title: Price ranges

blocks.q: A starts a business with ₹12,000. After 4 months B joins with ₹15,000. At the end of the year the profit is ₹11,000. Find B's share.
steps: A is in for all 12 months: money-months = 12,000 × 12 = 1,44,000.
B joins after 4 months, so he is in for 12 − 4 = 8 months: 15,000 × 8 = 1,20,000.
Ratio A : B = 1,44,000 : 1,20,000 = 6 : 5, a total of 11 parts.
blocks.title: Practice: Partnership with time and salary

blocks.q: A and B invest ₹30,000 and ₹20,000 for a year. A runs the business and first takes 10% of the profit as his salary; the rest is shared in the ratio of capital. If the profit is ₹15,000, how much does A receive in all?
steps: Profit left to share = 15,000 − 1,500 = ₹13,500.
A receives 8,100 + 1,500 = ₹9,600 in all (B gets ₹5,400).
blocks.trick: Take the salary out first, split the rest, then add the salary back.

chapters.intro: The core has not changed in ten years: markup with discount, successive discounts and working back to CP or MP. Around this core SSC rotates false weights, free-item offers, dealer chains and several items sold together. Expect longer, story-style wording in 2026 with one numeric twist.

items.what: Papers used selling price ranges (greatest profit = max SP − min CP per item × number), overheads added to CP, the markup needed above CP, and articles bought and sold by count.
Every year had markup plus discount to profit %, successive discounts, SP to MP or CP, and CP : SP ratios.
False weights with profit or loss, 'CP of x = SP of y', profit change when SP or CP changes, two SPs, dealer chains and best-scheme comparisons were very frequent.
About two thirds of the questions involved MP or discount, with festive re-marking, n for the price of m with a discount, three items with SPs in a ratio, mixtures, free items and chains.
Expect the same MP and discount core with story-style wording (retailer, festive offer, loyalty discount) and one twist such as a flat cash discount.

items.f: Festive re-mark: profit factor = k(1 − d)(1 + p)
items.note: Sold at P with profit p, then re-marked at kP with discount d. 1.5 × 0.9 × 1.2 = 1.62, so 62%.

blocks.body: Options are often very close, such as 29.41% loss and 29.41% gain. Keep fractions exact and check the sign before marking.

chapters.intro: Counts come from the 240 Mathematical Abilities questions of the eight Tier 2 Paper I sets on the site: 2, 3, 6 and 7 March 2023, 26 October 2023, 18 and 20 January 2025, and the CGL 2025 set of 19 January 2026. Profit, loss and discount gave 14 questions, about 1.75 a paper. Tier 2 keeps the Tier 1 types but raises the step count: a markup, a discount and a faulty balance in one question, a buyer cheated by the wholesaler who cheats his own customers, or three successive discounts. Several questions ask for two-decimal answers, so the multiplier method must be carried out exactly.
